article_title: How Do We Make Sense of the Book of Genesis?
main_theme: God creates a good world and makes humans in his image to rule it; they reach for the knowledge of good and evil on their own terms and are sent out of Eden.
primary_threads: Creation and new creation; The image of God; Blessing and curse
supporting_threads: Temple and God's presence; Exile and return; The promised Messiah
pre_where: Today the story begins. Genesis opens before Israel, before Abraham and before any nation is formed, with God speaking the world into being, day by day.
pre_watch: Watch for what God says about the world he makes, what he gives the first humans to do, and what changes after they eat from the tree.
q1: God creates a good world and makes humans in his image to rule it; they reach for the knowledge of good and evil on their own terms and are sent out of Eden. What does this reveal about the practice of stewardship?
q2: Humanity made in God's image echoes in Colossians 1:15–16 (Day 323), where Christ is called the image of the invisible God, through whom all things were created. How does Colossians describe Christ as the image of the invisible God and his relationship to creation? How does that compare with the responsibility given to those God created "in the image of God" (Genesis 1:27, Day 1)? What does this reveal about God's people as those created in the image of God?
q3: In light of God entrusting his world to people made in his image, how might stewardship take shape in your life this week?
identity: Those created in the image of God

article_title: What Are Sin, Iniquity, and Transgression in the Bible?
main_theme: Sin spreads from Cain's murder of Abel until violence fills the earth, and God resolves to judge it by flood while preserving Noah.
primary_threads: Blessing and curse; Sacrifice and atonement; Creation and new creation; Covenant
pre_where: Yesterday the first humans left Eden. Today their family grows outside the garden, and the story follows Adam and Eve's sons and their descendants.
pre_watch: Watch for the two offerings in chapter 4, what God says to Cain before and after Abel's death, and how Noah is described.
q1: Sin spreads from Cain's murder of Abel until violence fills the earth, and God resolves to judge it by flood while preserving Noah. God sends Cain away as a restless wanderer, yet puts a mark on him so that no one who finds him would kill him (4:12–15). What does this reveal about the practice of justice and mercy?
q2: Abel's offering and Noah's faith are named in Hebrews 11:4–7 (Day 340), and Hebrews later describes the faithful as strangers seeking a homeland (11:13–16). How does Hebrews describe the faith of Abel and Noah, and how does its later description of strangers seeking a homeland connect with life outside Eden?
q3: In light of God's judgment on Cain together with his protection of him, how might justice and mercy take shape in your life this week?
identity: Foreigners and strangers on earth

article_title: If God Remembers, Does He Also Forget?
main_theme: After the flood God renews creation and covenants with Noah, but humanity grasps for its own name at Babel and is scattered.
primary_threads: Creation and new creation; Covenant; Sacrifice and atonement; The image of God; Blessing and curse
pre_where: The flood waters still cover the earth. Today they recede, and God makes his first covenant, with Noah and every living creature, before the story moves to a city called Babel.
pre_watch: Watch for the sign God gives, what God says about human life in 9:6, and what the builders at Babel want for themselves.
q1: After the flood God renews creation and covenants with Noah, but humanity grasps for its own name at Babel and is scattered. The builders say, "Come, let us build ourselves a city, with a tower that reaches to the heavens, so that we may make a name for ourselves" (11:4). What does this reveal about the practice of humility?
q2: God's covenant with Noah is explicitly compared to God's promise in Isaiah 54:9–10 (Day 122). How does Isaiah talk about the oath after the flood? Isaiah 54:10 says, "my unfailing love for you will not be shaken nor my covenant of peace be removed"; what does this reveal about God's people as those under his covenant of peace?
q3: In light of the builders' desire to make a name for themselves, how might humility take shape in your life this week?
identity: Those under his covenant of peace

article_title: Abraham, Melchizedek, and Jesus
main_theme: God calls Abram, promises him land, offspring and blessing for all nations, and binds himself to the promise by covenant.
primary_threads: Blessing and curse; Covenant; The people of God
pre_where: After Babel the nations are scattered. Today the story narrows to one man, Abram, as God calls him to leave his country for a land he will be shown.
pre_watch: Watch for the promises God makes in 12:1–3, how Abram responds when the promise seems slow, and the ceremony in chapter 15.
q1: God calls Abram, promises him land, offspring and blessing for all nations, and binds himself to the promise by covenant. Abram believed the LORD, and he credited it to him as righteousness (15:6). What does this reveal about the practice of trust?
q2: God's promise of blessing for all nations echoes in Galatians 3:6–9 (Day 316), where Paul quotes Genesis 12:3 and 15:6. How does Paul talk about Abraham's faith? Galatians 3:9 says, "those who rely on faith are blessed along with Abraham, the man of faith"; what does this reveal about God's people as those blessed along with Abraham?
q3: In light of Abram believing the LORD's promise, how might trust take shape in your life this week?
identity: Those blessed along with Abraham

main_theme: Human efforts to secure the promise bring conflict, yet God cares for Hagar, confirms his covenant with Abraham, promises Sarah a son and hears Abraham's intercession.
primary_threads: Covenant; The people of God; Blessing and curse
pre_where: God has promised Abram a son, but years pass and Sarai is still childless. Today the household tries to secure the promise another way, and God speaks again.
pre_watch: Watch for how God treats Hagar in the wilderness, the new names in chapter 17, and the visitors Abraham welcomes in chapter 18.
q1: Human efforts to secure the promise bring conflict, yet God cares for Hagar, confirms his covenant with Abraham, promises Sarah a son and hears Abraham's intercession. Abraham hurries to welcome three visitors, bringing water, bread and a choice calf (18:2–8). What does this reveal about the practice of hospitality?
q2: The LORD asks whether anything is too hard for him when promising Sarah a son (Genesis 18:14). In Luke 1:36–38 (Day 267) the angel tells Mary of Elizabeth's pregnancy and that no word from God will fail. How do these passages speak about God's promises? Mary answers, "I am the Lord's servant" (1:38); what does her response reveal about God's people as the Lord's servants?
q3: In light of Abraham's welcome to the visitors, how might hospitality take shape in your life this week?
identity: The Lord's servants

main_theme: God judges Sodom and rescues Lot, then gives Isaac to Abraham and Sarah as promised, even after Abraham again passes Sarah off as his sister.
primary_threads: Blessing and curse; Covenant; The people of God
pre_where: Yesterday Abraham pleaded with God for the city of Sodom. Today the visitors arrive there, and then the long-promised son is finally born.
pre_watch: Watch for how Lot's household responds to the warning, what Abraham does again in Gerar, and Sarah's words at Isaac's birth.
q1: God judges Sodom and rescues Lot, then gives Isaac to Abraham and Sarah as promised, even after Abraham again passes Sarah off as his sister. Abraham also prays for Abimelek and his household. What does this reveal about the practice of prayer?
q2: The birth of Isaac, the child of promise, echoes in Romans 9:7–9 (Day 297), where Paul quotes God's promise about Sarah's son. How does Paul talk about the children of promise? What does this reveal about the identity of God's people as children of the promise (9:8)?
q3: In light of Abraham praying for Abimelek's household, how might prayer take shape in your life this week?
identity: Children of the promise

main_theme: God tests Abraham in the region of Moriah and provides a ram in Isaac's place; the family line continues through Rebekah.
primary_threads: Sacrifice and atonement; Covenant; Blessing and curse; The people of God
pre_where: Isaac, the son God promised, is now growing up. Today God tests Abraham concerning him, and later Abraham's servant travels to find a wife for Isaac.
pre_watch: Watch for the question Isaac asks on the way up the mountain, the name Abraham gives the place, and the servant's prayer at the well.
q1: God tests Abraham in the region of Moriah and provides a ram in Isaac's place; the family line continues through Rebekah. What does this reveal about the practice of obedience?
q2: God's provision in the region of Moriah echoes in Hebrews 11:17–19 (Day 340). How does Hebrews describe Abraham's faith when he offered Isaac, and how does Abraham's response relate to God's covenant promise in Genesis 22:16–18? What does this reveal about God's people as those who, like Abraham, embraced the promises (11:17)?
q3: In light of Abraham listening to God and the command not to harm Isaac, how might obedience to God's instructions take shape in your life this week?
identity: Those who embrace the promises

article_title: Ruling the World Through Weakness in Psalm 8
main_theme: Jacob obtains Esau's birthright through a bargain and his father's blessing through deception, yet God meets him at Bethel and renews the promise.
primary_threads: Blessing and curse; Covenant; Temple and God's presence
pre_where: Abraham dies, and the promise passes to Isaac and Rebekah. Today their twin sons, Esau and Jacob, struggle with each other even before they are born.
pre_watch: Watch for what Esau gives up and for what, how Jacob obtains his father's blessing, and what God says to Jacob at Bethel.
q1: Jacob obtains Esau's birthright through a bargain and his father's blessing through deception, yet God meets him at Bethel and renews the promise. Jacob wakes and says, "Surely the LORD is in this place," then sets up the stone as a pillar and pours oil on it (28:16–18). What does this reveal about the practice of worship?
q2: God meeting Jacob at Bethel echoes in John 1:51 (Day 258). How does Jesus' description in John 1:51 recall Jacob's dream, and how does Ephesians 2:21–22 (Day 318) describe God's people as a dwelling for God?
q3: In light of Jacob's response to God's presence at Bethel, how might worship take shape in your life this week?
identity: A dwelling in which God lives by his Spirit

main_theme: Jacob the deceiver is deceived by Laban, yet God builds his family and prospers him far from home.
primary_threads: The people of God; Blessing and curse; Covenant
pre_where: Jacob has fled from Esau toward his mother's family in Harran. Today he arrives, meets Rachel, and works for her father, Laban.
pre_watch: Watch for how Jacob is deceived, how Leah names her sons, and what God tells Jacob to do in chapter 31.
q1: Jacob the deceiver is deceived by Laban, yet God builds his family and prospers him far from home. What does this reveal about the practice of gratitude?
q2: Jacob's years of service in Aram echo in Hosea 12:6, 12 (Day 158), where the prophet recalls Jacob serving for a wife and calls Israel to maintain love and justice. How does Hosea talk about Jacob's story? What does this reveal about the identity of God's people as those who maintain love and justice (12:6)?
q3: In light of Leah's praise at Judah's birth, how might gratitude take shape in your life this week?
identity: Those who maintain love and justice

main_theme: Jacob wrestles with God and is renamed Israel, then reconciles with Esau; the violation of Dinah leads to violence.
primary_threads: The people of God; Exile and return; Blessing and curse
pre_where: Twenty years after fleeing, Jacob heads home and must face Esau, the brother he deceived. Today he prepares for that meeting.
pre_watch: Watch for Jacob's prayer in 32:9–12, the new name he receives, and how Esau greets him. Chapter 34 is a hard passage; read it as the text tells it.
q1: Jacob wrestles with God and is renamed Israel, then reconciles with Esau; the violation of Dinah leads to violence. What does this reveal about the practice of forgiveness?
q2: Esau embraces Jacob after their separation (Genesis 33:4). In 2 Corinthians 5:18–20 (Day 311) Paul describes reconciliation to God through Christ and the ministry of reconciliation. How are these two accounts of reconciliation similar or different? What does Paul say about being Christ's ambassadors?
q3: In light of Esau running to embrace the brother who had deceived him, how might forgiveness take shape in your life this week?
identity: Christ's ambassadors

main_theme: God confirms Israel's new name at Bethel; Joseph's dreams provoke his brothers to sell him into Egypt.
primary_threads: Covenant; Temple and God's presence; The people of God
pre_where: Jacob has made peace with Esau and travels back toward Bethel, where God first met him. Today the story begins to turn from Jacob to his son Joseph.
pre_watch: Watch for what Jacob tells his household before going to Bethel, what God says to him there, and what Joseph's brothers decide to do.
q1: God confirms Israel's new name at Bethel; Joseph's dreams provoke his brothers to sell him into Egypt. Jacob tells his household to put away their foreign gods and purify themselves (35:2–4). What does this reveal about repentance?
q2: Hosea 12:4–6 (Day 158) recalls that God found Jacob at Bethel and talked with him there, then calls Israel to return to God and wait for him always. How does Hosea use Jacob's story? What does this reveal about God's people as a people who wait for God?
q3: In light of Jacob's household putting away their foreign gods, what might turning away from wrongdoing look like for you this week?
identity: A people who wait for God

main_theme: Judah fails Tamar while Joseph stays faithful in Egypt, where the LORD is with him in slavery and prison.
primary_threads: The people of God; Temple and God's presence; Blessing and curse
pre_where: Joseph has been sold to traders and taken to Egypt. Today the story pauses to follow his brother Judah, then returns to Joseph in Potiphar's house and in prison.
pre_watch: Watch for what Judah finally says about Tamar, how Joseph answers Potiphar's wife, and how often the text says the LORD was with Joseph.
q1: Judah fails Tamar while Joseph stays faithful in Egypt, where the LORD is with him in slavery and prison. Joseph asks the cupbearer to remember him, but the cupbearer forgets him (40:14–15, 23). What does this reveal about the practice of waiting on God?
q2: Psalm 105:16–19 recalls Joseph sold as a slave, his feet in shackles, until what he foretold came to pass. How does the psalm describe what happened to Joseph? Psalm 105:6 calls Abraham's descendants God's chosen ones; what does this reveal about God's people as his chosen ones?
q3: In light of Joseph's continued imprisonment after the cupbearer forgot him, how might waiting on God take shape in your life this week?
identity: His chosen ones

main_theme: God raises Joseph, a man in whom is the Spirit of God, to rule Egypt and save many from famine; his brothers come to buy grain.
primary_threads: Kingdom and kingship; The Spirit; Blessing and curse
pre_where: Joseph has interpreted dreams in prison and been forgotten. Today, two years later, Pharaoh has dreams that no one in Egypt can explain.
pre_watch: Watch for whom Joseph credits with the interpretation, what Pharaoh says about Joseph, and how Joseph's brothers act when they meet him.
q1: God raises Joseph, a man in whom is the Spirit of God, to rule Egypt and save many from famine; his brothers come to buy grain. Joseph tells Pharaoh that God, not he, will give the answer (41:16). What does this reveal about the practice of humility?
q2: Joseph's words to Pharaoh are similar to Daniel's words to Nebuchadnezzar: "There is a God in heaven who reveals mysteries" (Daniel 2:27–28, Day 208). Both Joseph and Daniel credit God rather than themselves for revealing mysteries. How are their responses similar or different? Daniel 3:26–28 describes his friends as servants of the Most High God who trusted him. What might these accounts reveal about serving God?
q3: In light of Joseph giving God the credit before Pharaoh, how might humility take shape in your life this week?
identity: Servants of the Most High God

main_theme: Judah offers himself in Benjamin's place, and Joseph reveals himself, seeing God's purpose to preserve life.
primary_threads: The people of God; Blessing and curse
pre_where: Famine has already brought Joseph's brothers to Egypt once. Today they must return with Benjamin, still unaware that the governor is their brother.
pre_watch: Watch for Judah's speech in 44:18–34 and what Joseph says about God when he reveals who he is.
q1: Judah offers himself in Benjamin's place, and Joseph reveals himself, seeing God's purpose to preserve life. Joseph tells his brothers not to be distressed or angry with themselves (45:5). What does this reveal about the practice of forgiveness?
q2: Acts 7:9–14 (Day 282) says God was with Joseph and rescued him from his troubles, and that on the brothers' second visit Joseph told them who he was and sent for his whole family. How does Stephen describe God's care for Joseph and the arrival of his family in Egypt? What does this reveal about God's people as a remnant God preserves (compare Genesis 45:7)?
q3: In light of Joseph's words to the brothers who sold him, how might forgiveness take shape in your life this week?
identity: A remnant God preserves

main_theme: God sends Jacob's family into Egypt with a promise to make them a great nation, and they flourish there.
primary_threads: Covenant; The people of God; Blessing and curse
pre_where: Joseph is alive and rules in Egypt. Today Jacob, now old, sets out with his whole family to join him.
pre_watch: Watch for what God tells Jacob at Beersheba, how Jacob describes his life to Pharaoh, and how Joseph manages the famine.
q1: God sends Jacob's family into Egypt with a promise to make them a great nation, and they flourish there. God tells Jacob not to be afraid to go down to Egypt (46:3). What does this reveal about the practice of trust?
q2: Deuteronomy 26:5 (Day 61) recalls that Israel's father went down into Egypt with a few people and became a great nation. How does Deuteronomy tell this part of the story? Deuteronomy 26:18 calls Israel God's treasured possession; what does this reveal about God's people as his treasured possession?
q3: In light of God's word to Jacob, "Do not be afraid," how might trust take shape in your life this week?
identity: His treasured possession

main_theme: Jacob blesses his family and speaks of Judah's future rule; Joseph affirms that God turned his brothers' intended harm toward preserving many lives.
primary_threads: Blessing and curse; Kingdom and kingship; The promised Messiah; Covenant
pre_where: Jacob has lived seventeen years in Egypt. Today, near the end of his life, he blesses Joseph's sons and his own twelve sons, and Genesis comes to a close.
pre_watch: Watch for which grandson Jacob blesses first, what he says about Judah in 49:8–12, and Joseph's words to his brothers in 50:19–21.
q1: Jacob blesses his family and speaks of Judah's future rule; Joseph affirms that God turned his brothers' intended harm toward preserving many lives. Joseph promises to provide for his brothers and their children (50:21). What does this reveal about the practice of service?
q2: Jacob calls Judah a lion (49:9); Revelation 5:5 (Day 351) speaks of "the Lion of the tribe of Judah." How does Revelation use this image? Revelation 5:10 says those purchased by the Lamb are made a kingdom and priests; what does this reveal about God's people as a kingdom and priests?
q3: In light of Joseph providing for the brothers who once harmed him, how might service take shape in your life this week?
identity: A kingdom and priests

article_title: 7 Powerful Women in the Bible Who Help Rescue God’s People
main_theme: Israel multiplies but is enslaved; God remembers his covenant and calls Moses from the burning bush.
primary_threads: Exodus and redemption; Covenant; Temple and God's presence; The people of God
pre_where: Genesis ended with Jacob's family settled in Egypt. Exodus opens generations later, when that family has grown into a people and a new king feels threatened by them.
pre_watch: Watch for the midwives Shiphrah and Puah, what God says he has seen and heard in 3:7–9, and the name God gives in 3:14.
q1: Israel multiplies but is enslaved; God remembers his covenant and calls Moses from the burning bush. The midwives fear God and refuse Pharaoh's order (1:17). What does this reveal about the practice of obedience?
q2: Acts 7:30–34 (Day 282) retells the burning bush: "I have indeed seen the oppression of my people… I have heard their groaning and have come down to set them free." How does Stephen tell the story? What does this reveal about God's people as those whose groaning God has heard?
q3: In light of the midwives fearing God more than Pharaoh, how might obedience to God take shape in your life this week?
identity: Those whose groaning God has heard

article_title: The Larger Story of Exodus
main_theme: Moses confronts Pharaoh and the oppression worsens, but God promises to redeem Israel and take them as his people.
primary_threads: Exodus and redemption; Covenant; The people of God
pre_where: God has called Moses at the burning bush. Today Moses returns to Egypt with Aaron and stands before Pharaoh for the first time.
pre_watch: Watch for Moses' objections to God, Pharaoh's reply in 5:2, and the "I will" promises in 6:6–8.
q1: Moses confronts Pharaoh and the oppression worsens, but God promises to redeem Israel and take them as his people. Moses asks the LORD why he has brought trouble on his people (5:22). What does this reveal about the practice of lament?
q2: God's promise, "I will take you as my own people, and I will be your God" (6:7), is echoed in Revelation 21:3 (Day 358): "God's dwelling place is now among the people." How does Revelation 21:3 echo God's promise in Exodus 6:7? Ephesians 2:22 (Day 318) describes believers being built together as a dwelling for God. What does this reveal about God's people?
q3: In light of Moses bringing his honest question to God, how might lament take shape in your life this week?
identity: A dwelling place for God

article_title: The Relationship Between Teaching and Signs in the Bible
main_theme: God strikes Egypt with signs so that Pharaoh and Israel will know that he is the LORD.
primary_threads: Exodus and redemption
pre_where: Pharaoh has refused to let Israel go and made their work harder. Today the signs begin.
pre_watch: Watch for the phrase "so that you may know" and how the text describes Pharaoh's heart after each sign.
q1: God strikes Egypt with signs so that Pharaoh and Israel will know that he is the LORD. God says his name is to be proclaimed in all the earth (9:16). What does this reveal about the practice of witness?
q2: Paul quotes Exodus 9:16 in Romans 9:17 (Day 297). How does Paul use God's words to Pharaoh? In Romans 9:25–26 Paul quotes Hosea: "children of the living God"; what does this reveal about God's people as children of the living God?
q3: In light of God's stated purpose that his name be proclaimed, how might you speak about him this week?
identity: Children of the living God

main_theme: The final plagues fall; Israel is spared by the blood of the Passover lamb and leaves Egypt.
primary_threads: Exodus and redemption; Sacrifice and atonement; The people of God
pre_where: Nine plagues have struck Egypt. Today comes the last, and with it the first Passover.
pre_watch: Watch for the instructions about the lamb and its blood, the meal eaten ready to travel, and the command to remember this day for generations.
q1: The final plagues fall; Israel is spared by the blood of the Passover lamb and leaves Egypt. Each household shares the Passover meal together (12:3–4). What does this reveal about the practice of fellowship?
q2: Paul writes, "Christ, our Passover lamb, has been sacrificed" (1 Corinthians 5:7, Day 303). How does Paul use the Passover? In 1 Corinthians 6:20 he says believers were bought at a price; what does this reveal about God's people as a people bought at a price?
q3: In light of Israel's households gathering for the Passover meal, how might fellowship take shape in your life this week?
identity: A people bought at a price

main_theme: God leads Israel through the sea and defeats Egypt; Moses and Miriam sing that the LORD will reign forever.
primary_threads: Exodus and redemption; Kingdom and kingship; Temple and God's presence
pre_where: Israel has left Egypt after the Passover. Today Pharaoh changes his mind and chases them to the edge of the sea.
pre_watch: Watch for the pillar of cloud and fire, Moses' words in 14:13–14, and the song in chapter 15.
q1: God leads Israel through the sea and defeats Egypt; Moses and Miriam sing that the LORD will reign forever. Moses, Miriam and Israel sing to the LORD (15:1, 20–21). What does this reveal about the practice of gratitude?
q2: Revelation 15:2–4 (Day 355) describes the victorious singing "the song of God's servant Moses and of the Lamb." How does Revelation use Moses' song? Compare Exodus 15:1–2, 20–21. What does this reveal about God's people as those who sing the song of Moses and of the Lamb?
q3: In light of Israel singing after the sea, how might gratitude take shape in your life this week?
identity: Those who sing the song of Moses and of the Lamb

main_theme: God provides manna and water in the wilderness, tests Israel with instructions for gathering manna and keeping the Sabbath, and Jethro counsels Moses to share the work of judging.
primary_threads: Exodus and redemption; Law and wisdom; The people of God
pre_where: Israel has crossed the sea into the wilderness. Today, with food and water running short, the people begin to grumble.
pre_watch: Watch for the instructions about gathering manna on the sixth and seventh days, the water from the rock, and Jethro's advice to Moses.
q1: God provides manna and water in the wilderness, tests Israel with instructions for gathering manna and keeping the Sabbath, and Jethro counsels Moses to share the work of judging. What does this reveal about the practice of Sabbath rest?
q2: In John 6:31–35 (Day 260) the crowd recalls the manna, and Jesus says, "I am the bread of life." How does Jesus talk about the bread from heaven? What does this reveal about God's people as those who come to him?
q3: In light of God's provision on the sixth day so Israel could rest on the seventh, how might Sabbath rest take shape in your life this week?
identity: Those who come to Jesus

article_title: What Does Psalm 23 (The Lord Is My Shepherd) Mean?
main_theme: At Sinai God calls Israel to be a kingdom of priests and gives the Ten Commandments.
primary_threads: Covenant; Law and wisdom; The people of God; Temple and God's presence
pre_where: Three months after leaving Egypt, Israel arrives at Mount Sinai. Today God meets them at the mountain and speaks the Ten Commandments.
pre_watch: Watch for what God says Israel will be in 19:5–6, how the people respond to God's presence, and how the commandments begin in 20:2.
q1: At Sinai God calls Israel to be a kingdom of priests and gives the Ten Commandments. God says, "You shall have no other gods before me" (20:3). What does this reveal about the practice of worship?
q2: Peter echoes Exodus 19:6 when he calls believers "a royal priesthood, a holy nation" (1 Peter 2:9, Day 343). How does Peter use these words? What does this reveal about God's people as a holy nation?
q3: In light of God's command to have no other gods, how might worship take shape in your life this week?
identity: A holy nation

main_theme: God's laws shape justice and care for the vulnerable; the covenant is sealed with blood and a meal before God on the mountain.
primary_threads: Law and wisdom; Covenant; Sacrifice and atonement
pre_where: God has spoken the Ten Commandments at Sinai. Today he gives laws for daily life, and the covenant is confirmed.
pre_watch: Watch for the laws about foreigners, widows and the poor, the people's words in 24:3 and 24:7, and the blood Moses sprinkles.
q1: God's laws shape justice and care for the vulnerable; the covenant is sealed with blood and a meal before God on the mountain. God forbids mistreating foreigners, widows and orphans and commands care for the poor (22:21–27; 23:6–9). What does this reveal about the practice of justice and mercy?
q2: Hebrews 9:18–20 (Day 339) quotes Moses: "This is the blood of the covenant." How does Hebrews use this moment? Hebrews 9:15 speaks of those who are called receiving the promised inheritance; what does this reveal about God's people as those who are called?
q3: In light of God's laws protecting foreigners, widows and the poor, how might justice and mercy take shape in your life this week?
identity: Those who are called

main_theme: God gives the pattern for a tabernacle so that he can dwell among his people.
primary_threads: Temple and God's presence; The people of God
pre_where: The covenant has been sealed at Sinai. Today Moses is on the mountain as God describes a tent where he will live among his people.
pre_watch: Watch for why the tabernacle is to be built (25:8), what goes in the Most Holy Place, and the instruction to follow the pattern exactly.
q1: God gives the pattern for a tabernacle so that he can dwell among his people. God asks for offerings from everyone whose heart prompts them (25:2). What does this reveal about the practice of generosity?
q2: Hebrews 8:5 (Day 338) quotes Exodus 25:40: "Make everything according to the pattern." How does Hebrews talk about the tabernacle? Hebrews 8:10 quotes God's promise, "I will be their God, and they will be my people"; what does this reveal about God's people as those of whom God says, "they will be my people"?
q3: In light of offerings given by everyone whose heart prompted them, how might generosity take shape in your life this week?
identity: Those God calls "my people"

article_title: Why Do Israel’s Priests Shine?
main_theme: Aaron and his sons are clothed and ordained as priests to serve in God's presence.
primary_threads: Temple and God's presence; Sacrifice and atonement
pre_where: God has described the tabernacle. Today he describes the priests who will serve in it: Aaron and his sons.
pre_watch: Watch for what is engraved on the high priest's garments, why Aaron carries the tribes' names before the LORD, and God's promise in 29:45–46.
q1: Aaron and his sons are clothed and ordained as priests to serve in God's presence. Aaron bears the names of Israel's tribes on his heart before the LORD (28:29). What does this reveal about the practice of service?
q2: Hebrews 5:1–5 (Day 337) describes how Aaron was called to be high priest and compares Christ's calling. How does Hebrews describe these callings? First Peter 2:5 (Day 343) calls believers a holy priesthood; what does this reveal about God's people as a holy priesthood?
q3: In light of Aaron carrying the people's names before the LORD, how might service take shape in your life this week?
identity: A holy priesthood

main_theme: God gives instructions for incense, oil and the Sabbath, and fills Bezalel with his Spirit to build the tabernacle.
primary_threads: Temple and God's presence; The Spirit; Law and wisdom
pre_where: The priests have been described. Today God adds the incense altar, the anointing oil and the craftsmen who will build everything, and repeats the Sabbath command.
pre_watch: Watch for what Bezalel is filled with in 31:3 and why the Sabbath is called a sign in 31:13–17.
q1: God gives instructions for incense, oil and the Sabbath, and fills Bezalel with his Spirit to build the tabernacle. God gives skill to all the craftsmen to make what he commanded (31:6). What does this reveal about the practice of stewardship?
q2: Bezalel is filled with God's Spirit for his work; in 1 Corinthians 12:4–7 (Day 306) Paul says the Spirit gives gifts for the common good. How are these two descriptions similar or different? Paul says in 12:27, "You are the body of Christ"; what does this reveal about God's people as the body of Christ?
q3: In light of God giving skill to the craftsmen for his work, how might stewardship take shape in your life this week?
identity: The body of Christ

main_theme: Israel worships the golden calf; Moses intercedes, and God reveals himself as compassionate and gracious and renews the covenant.
primary_threads: Covenant; Temple and God's presence; Blessing and curse
pre_where: While Moses is on the mountain receiving God's instructions, the people below grow impatient. Today they ask Aaron to make them gods.
pre_watch: Watch for Moses' prayers in 32:11–13 and 32:31–32, and the words the LORD proclaims about himself in 34:6–7.
q1: Israel worships the golden calf; Moses intercedes, and God reveals himself as compassionate and gracious and renews the covenant. What does this reveal about the practice of prayer?
q2: God's words about himself in 34:6 are echoed in Joel 2:13 (Day 159): "He is gracious and compassionate, slow to anger and abounding in love." How does Joel use the LORD's description in Exodus 34:6 to call the people to return (Joel 2:12–13)? What does Joel's later promise to pour out God's Spirit (2:28–29) reveal about God's people as those on whom God pours out his Spirit?
q3: In light of Moses praying for the people after the golden calf, how might prayer take shape in your life this week?
identity: Those on whom God pours out his Spirit

main_theme: The people give generously, the tabernacle is built, and the glory of the LORD fills it.
primary_threads: Temple and God's presence; The people of God
pre_where: After the golden calf, God renewed his covenant. Today the people bring their offerings, and the tabernacle is built and set up.
pre_watch: Watch for how the people give in 36:3–7, how often the text says "as the LORD commanded," and what happens when the work is finished in 40:34–38.
q1: The people give generously, the tabernacle is built, and the glory of the LORD fills it. The text repeats that everything was done as the LORD commanded (39:42–43). What does this reveal about the practice of obedience?
q2: The glory filling the tabernacle (40:34) is echoed in John 1:14 (Day 258): "The Word became flesh and made his dwelling among us. We have seen his glory." How does John use the language of God dwelling and glory? Ephesians 2:22 (Day 318) says believers are built together to become a dwelling for God; what does this reveal about God's people as a dwelling in which God lives by his Spirit?
q3: In light of the work done just as the LORD commanded, how might obedience take shape in your life this week?
identity: A dwelling in which God lives by his Spirit

article_title: Why Leviticus Is Worth Your Time
main_theme: God gives instructions for burnt, grain, fellowship and sin offerings, including atonement for unintentional sins.
primary_threads: Sacrifice and atonement; Temple and God's presence; Law and wisdom
pre_where: The tabernacle is complete and filled with God's glory. Leviticus opens with the LORD calling to Moses from it, giving instructions for the offerings.
pre_watch: Watch for the different kinds of offerings, what the person bringing an animal does with their hand (1:4), and the phrase "they will be forgiven" in chapter 4.
q1: God gives instructions for burnt, grain, fellowship and sin offerings, including atonement for unintentional sins. The offerings are described as an aroma pleasing to the LORD (1:9). What does this reveal about the practice of worship?
q2: Hebrews 10:1–4, 11–14 (Day 339) speaks of the sacrifices offered year after year and of Christ's one sacrifice. How does Hebrews compare them? Hebrews 10:14 speaks of "those who are being made holy"; what does this reveal about God's people as those being made holy?
q3: In light of offerings brought to the LORD as a pleasing aroma, how might worship take shape in your life this week?
identity: Those being made holy

main_theme: Further offerings address guilt and restitution, with instructions for the priests who handle each offering.
primary_threads: Sacrifice and atonement; Law and wisdom
pre_where: Leviticus has described the main offerings. Today it adds the guilt offering, for wrongs done against God and against other people, with instructions for the priests.
pre_watch: Watch for the command to confess in 5:5, the added fifth paid back in 6:4–5, and the offering given in thanksgiving in 7:12.
q1: Further offerings address guilt and restitution, with instructions for the priests who handle each offering. For specified offenses, a person must confess the sin (5:1–5); for specified property wrongs, the offender must restore what was taken and add a fifth (6:1–5). What does this reveal about confession and repentance?
q2: In Matthew 5:23–24 (Day 238) Jesus tells his hearers to leave their gift at the altar and first be reconciled. How are this teaching and Leviticus's guilt offering similar or different? Matthew 5:9 calls peacemakers children of God; what does this reveal about God's people as peacemakers?
q3: In light of these instructions, how might acknowledging wrongdoing and making appropriate restitution take shape in your life this week?
identity: Peacemakers

main_theme: Aaron and his sons are ordained, the LORD's glory appears and fire consumes the offering, and Nadab and Abihu die after offering unauthorized fire.
primary_threads: Temple and God's presence; Sacrifice and atonement; Blessing and curse
pre_where: God has given the offerings and described the priests. Today Aaron and his sons are ordained, and the priests offer sacrifices for the first time.
pre_watch: Watch for what happens when the glory of the LORD appears in 9:23–24, what Nadab and Abihu do in 10:1, and what Moses says to Aaron afterward.
q1: Aaron and his sons are ordained, the LORD's glory appears and fire consumes the offering, and Nadab and Abihu die after offering unauthorized fire. The people shout for joy and fall facedown (9:24). What does this reveal about the practice of humility?
q2: Hebrews 12:28–29 (Day 340) urges worship "with reverence and awe, for our God is a consuming fire." How are this call and the fire in Leviticus 9–10 similar or different? Hebrews 12:28 speaks of receiving a kingdom that cannot be shaken; what does this reveal about God's people as those receiving a kingdom that cannot be shaken?
q3: In light of the people falling facedown before the LORD's glory, how might humility take shape in your life this week?
identity: Those receiving a kingdom that cannot be shaken

main_theme: God distinguishes clean from unclean animals, gives purification laws after childbirth and for skin diseases, and calls Israel to be holy because he is holy.
primary_threads: Law and wisdom; The people of God
pre_where: The priests are now serving at the tabernacle. Today God teaches Israel to tell clean from unclean in food, after childbirth and in skin disease.
pre_watch: Watch for the reason God gives in 11:44–45 and the priest's role in examining people with skin diseases.
q1: God distinguishes clean from unclean animals, gives purification laws after childbirth and for skin diseases, and calls Israel to be holy because he is holy. What does this reveal about the practice of holiness?
q2: Peter quotes Leviticus 11:44: "Be holy, because I am holy" (1 Peter 1:15–16, Day 343). How does Peter use this command? In 1 Peter 1:14 he addresses his readers as obedient children; what does this reveal about God's people as obedient children?
q3: In light of God's call to be holy because he is holy, how might holiness take shape in your life this week?
identity: Obedient children

main_theme: God gives cleansing rituals for people and houses affected by skin disease or mold, and laws on bodily discharges to prevent uncleanness from defiling his dwelling.
primary_threads: Law and wisdom; Sacrifice and atonement; Temple and God's presence
pre_where: God has explained how a priest identifies skin diseases. Today he gives cleansing rituals for people and houses, and instructions concerning bodily discharges.
pre_watch: Watch for the two birds in 14:4–7, when the cleansed person may come back into the camp (14:8), and the reason given in 15:31.
q1: God gives cleansing rituals for people and houses affected by skin disease or mold, and laws on bodily discharges to prevent uncleanness from defiling his dwelling. After cleansing, the person may come back into the camp (14:8). What does this reveal about the practice of fellowship?
q2: In Luke 17:11–19 (Day 275) Jesus sends ten men with leprosy to show themselves to the priests, as the law required. How does Luke tell this story? Only one returns to praise God; what does this reveal about God's people as those who return to give praise to God (17:18)?
q3: In light of the cleansed person's return to the camp, how might welcoming someone back into community take shape in your life this week?
identity: Those who return to give praise to God

main_theme: On the Day of Atonement the high priest cleanses the sanctuary and the people; God forbids eating blood and the sexual practices of Egypt and Canaan.
primary_threads: Sacrifice and atonement; Temple and God's presence; Law and wisdom; The people of God
pre_where: After the deaths of Nadab and Abihu, God tells Aaron how he may enter the Most Holy Place. Today comes the Day of Atonement.
pre_watch: Watch for the two goats in 16:7–10, what the high priest confesses over the live goat, and the reason given about blood in 17:11.
q1: On the Day of Atonement the high priest cleanses the sanctuary and the people; God forbids eating blood and the sexual practices of Egypt and Canaan. The people are to deny themselves on that day (16:29). What does this reveal about the practice of humility?
q2: Hebrews 9:7, 11–12 (Day 339) recalls the high priest entering the Most Holy Place once a year and speaks of Christ entering once for all. How does Hebrews compare them? Hebrews 9:14 speaks of being cleansed "so that we may serve the living God"; what does this reveal about God's people as those who serve the living God?
q3: In light of the people denying themselves on the Day of Atonement, how might humility take shape in your life this week?
identity: Those who serve the living God

video_title: Wisdom Within Laws About Oaths, Retaliation, and Enemy Love
main_theme: God calls Israel to be holy as he is holy, including loving their neighbor and the foreigner, and sets penalties for serious offenses.
primary_threads: Law and wisdom; The people of God
pre_where: God has given the Day of Atonement and laws for holy living. Today he calls the whole community to be holy in everyday life.
pre_watch: Watch for how often a command ends with "I am the LORD," the laws about harvest edges in 19:9–10, and the commands in 19:18 and 19:34.
q1: God calls Israel to be holy as he is holy, including loving their neighbor and the foreigner, and sets penalties for serious offenses. Israel is to leave the edges of the harvest for the poor and the foreigner (19:9–10). What does this reveal about the practice of justice and mercy?
q2: A legal expert quotes the command to love one's neighbor and asks Jesus who his neighbor is (Luke 10:25–29, Day 272; Leviticus 19:18). Jesus tells the parable of the good Samaritan (10:30–37). How does Jesus answer the question, and what does this reveal about being a neighbor who has mercy (10:36–37)?
q3: In light of leaving the harvest edges for the poor and the foreigner, how might justice and mercy take shape in your life this week?
identity: Neighbors who have mercy

article_title: Rosh Hashanah: How the Jewish New Year Connects to Jesus
main_theme: God sets holiness standards for priests and offerings and gives the calendar of Sabbath and appointed festivals.
primary_threads: Law and wisdom; Temple and God's presence; Sacrifice and atonement
pre_where: God has called all Israel to be holy. Today he sets standards for the priests and gives Israel a yearly calendar of Sabbath and festivals.
pre_watch: Watch for the list of appointed festivals in chapter 23 and the command in 23:22 to leave harvest edges for the poor.
q1: God sets holiness standards for priests and offerings and gives the calendar of Sabbath and appointed festivals. The Sabbath is a day of sacred assembly and rest (23:3). What does this reveal about the practice of Sabbath rest?
q2: At the Festival of Tabernacles (23:33–43), Jesus calls out, "Let anyone who is thirsty come to me and drink" (John 7:37–39, Day 261). How does John connect this festival with the Spirit? What does this reveal about God's people as those who believe and receive the Spirit (7:39)?
q3: In light of the Sabbath as a day of rest and gathering, how might Sabbath rest take shape in your life this week?
identity: Those who believe and receive the Spirit

main_theme: The lamp and bread are kept before the LORD, blasphemy is punished, and God commands a Sabbath year and Jubilee, when property returns and Israelites in servitude are released.
primary_threads: Law and wisdom; Exodus and redemption; Temple and God's presence
pre_where: God has set Israel's festivals. Today he adds the lamp and bread kept before him, a case of blasphemy, and two kinds of release: the Sabbath year and the Jubilee.
pre_watch: Watch for why the land may not be sold permanently (25:23) and what God says about Israelites in servitude in 25:42 and 25:55.
q1: The lamp and bread are kept before the LORD, blasphemy is punished, and God commands a Sabbath year and Jubilee, when property returns and Israelites in servitude are released. God says, "The land is mine" (25:23). What does this reveal about the practice of stewardship?
q2: The Jubilee's proclamation of liberty (25:10) is similar to Isaiah 61:1–2 (Day 125): "to proclaim freedom for the captives… the year of the LORD's favor." How are these two proclamations similar or different? Isaiah 61:6 says, "You will be called priests of the LORD"; what does this reveal about God's people as priests of the LORD?
q3: In light of God's words, "The land is mine," how might stewardship take shape in your life this week?
identity: Priests of the LORD

main_theme: God promises blessing for obedience and curse for disobedience, including exile, yet promises to remember his covenant; vows and dedications are regulated.
primary_threads: Blessing and curse; Covenant; Exile and return; Temple and God's presence
pre_where: Leviticus is drawing to a close. Today God sets out the blessings that follow faithfulness and the warnings that follow rebellion, including exile, and what he will remember.
pre_watch: Watch for God's promise in 26:11–12, the warning in 26:33, and what God says he will remember in 26:40–45.
q1: God promises blessing for obedience and curse for disobedience, including exile, yet promises to remember his covenant; vows and dedications are regulated. God speaks of the people confessing their sins, their uncircumcised hearts being humbled and their making amends (26:40–42). What does this reveal about confession and repentance?
q2: Paul quotes Leviticus 26:12 in 2 Corinthians 6:16 (Day 311): "I will live with them and walk among them, and I will be their God, and they will be my people." How does Paul use this promise? He writes, "We are the temple of the living God"; what does this reveal about God's people as the temple of the living God?
q3: In light of the call to confess wrongdoing and humble their hearts, how might confession and repentance take shape in your life this week?
identity: The temple of the living God

article_title: What Does the Book of Numbers Teach Us?
main_theme: Israel is counted and arranged in camp around the tabernacle, and the Levites are assigned to carry and guard it.
primary_threads: The people of God; Temple and God's presence
pre_where: Leviticus set out how a holy God can live among his people. Numbers opens on the first day of the second month of the second year after Israel left Egypt, as Israel prepares to leave Sinai.
pre_watch: Watch for how the tribes are arranged around the tabernacle in chapter 2 and the Levites' duties in chapters 3–4.
q1: Israel is counted and arranged in camp around the tabernacle, and the Levites are assigned to carry and guard it. The Levites are given to serve at the tabernacle (3:5–8). What does this reveal about the practice of service?
q2: Israel camps tribe by tribe around God's dwelling; in Revelation 7:9–15 (Day 352) a great multitude from every nation stands before the throne, and God shelters them with his presence. How are these two pictures similar or different? What does this reveal about God's people as a great multitude from every nation?
q3: In light of the Levites assigned to serve at the tabernacle, how might service take shape in your life this week?
identity: A great multitude from every nation

main_theme: Laws keep the camp pure, the Nazirite vow is described, the priestly blessing is given, and the tribal leaders bring offerings to dedicate the altar.
primary_threads: Law and wisdom; Blessing and curse; Temple and God's presence
pre_where: Israel has been counted and arranged around the tabernacle. Today come laws for keeping the camp pure, the Nazirite vow, and the blessing the priests are to speak over the people.
pre_watch: Watch for the blessing in 6:24–26 and how each tribal leader brings the same offering for the altar.
q1: Laws keep the camp pure, the Nazirite vow is described, the priestly blessing is given, and the tribal leaders bring offerings to dedicate the altar. The priests are to bless the Israelites with the words the LORD gives them (6:23–27). What does this reveal about the practice of blessing others?
q2: Jesus tells his disciples they are witnesses and promises power from on high before blessing them (Luke 24:48–51, Day 278). How do this blessing and the priestly blessing in Numbers 6:23–27 compare, and what does Jesus' commission reveal about the disciples as witnesses?
q3: In light of the blessing God gives the priests to speak, how might blessing others take shape in your life this week?
identity: Witnesses

main_theme: The Levites are dedicated, Israel keeps the Passover, and the people set out from Sinai following the cloud of God's presence.
primary_threads: Temple and God's presence; Exodus and redemption; The people of God
pre_where: The tabernacle and its leaders are ready. Today the Levites are dedicated, Israel keeps its second Passover, and the people set out from Sinai.
pre_watch: Watch for the provision for those who could not keep the Passover on time (9:6–13), how the cloud guides the camp in 9:15–23, and Moses' words when the ark sets out (10:35–36).
q1: The Levites are dedicated, Israel keeps the Passover, and the people set out from Sinai following the cloud of God's presence. Israel sets out or stays in camp whenever the cloud lifts or remains, at the LORD's command (9:18–23). What does this reveal about the practice of waiting on God?
q2: Paul writes that "our ancestors were all under the cloud" (1 Corinthians 10:1–4, Day 305). How does Paul use Israel's journey? In 10:11 he says these things were written down as warnings for us; what does this reveal about God's people as those on whom the culmination of the ages has come (10:11)?
q3: In light of Israel staying put or setting out as the cloud led, how might waiting on God take shape in your life this week?
identity: Those on whom the culmination of the ages has come

main_theme: Israel complains about food, God puts his Spirit on seventy elders, Miriam and Aaron oppose Moses, and spies are sent into Canaan.
primary_threads: The Spirit; The people of God; Blessing and curse
pre_where: Israel has just left Sinai. Today the journey's hardships bring complaints, and Moses feels the weight of leading the people alone.
pre_watch: Watch for Moses' prayer in 11:10–15, his wish in 11:29, and what the spies report about the land.
q1: Israel complains about food, God puts his Spirit on seventy elders, Miriam and Aaron oppose Moses, and spies are sent into Canaan. Moses tells the LORD that the burden of the people is too heavy for him alone (11:14). What does this reveal about the practice of lament?
q2: Moses wishes that all the LORD's people were prophets and that the LORD would put his Spirit on them (11:29). In Acts 2:17–18 (Day 279) Peter announces God's promise, "I will pour out my Spirit on all people." How are these two passages similar or different? What does this reveal about God's people as those on whom God pours out his Spirit?
q3: In light of Moses bringing the weight of his task to God, how might lament take shape in your life this week?
identity: Those on whom God pours out his Spirit

main_theme: Israel refuses to enter the land; Moses intercedes and God forgives, yet that generation must die in the wilderness; Korah's rebellion is judged.
primary_threads: Blessing and curse; The people of God; Sacrifice and atonement
pre_where: The spies have returned from Canaan with mixed reports. Today the people must decide whether to go in.
pre_watch: Watch for Joshua and Caleb's words in 14:6–9, Moses' prayer in 14:17–19, and Aaron standing between the living and the dead in 16:47–48.
q1: Israel refuses to enter the land; Moses intercedes and God forgives, yet that generation must die in the wilderness; Korah's rebellion is judged. Moses asks the LORD to forgive the people, quoting his own words: "slow to anger, abounding in love" (14:17–19). What does this reveal about the practice of prayer?
q2: Hebrews 3:6–19 (Day 336) calls its readers God's house if they hold firmly to their confidence, and warns them using Israel's wilderness rebellion. How does that warning connect with Numbers 14:9–11, 22–23? What does this reveal about belonging to God's house and holding firmly to hope?
q3: In light of Moses praying for the people after their refusal, how might prayer take shape in your life this week?
identity: God's house

main_theme: Aaron's staff buds to confirm his priesthood, and the duties and provision of priests and Levites are set.
primary_threads: Temple and God's presence; Law and wisdom
pre_where: Korah's rebellion challenged Aaron's priesthood. Today God settles the question with twelve staffs.
pre_watch: Watch for what happens to Aaron's staff overnight (17:8) and what God tells Aaron is his share and inheritance (18:20).
q1: Aaron's staff buds to confirm his priesthood, and the duties and provision of priests and Levites are set. The Israelites' tithes are given to the Levites in return for their work at the tent of meeting (18:21). What does this reveal about the practice of generosity?
q2: Hebrews 9:4 (Day 339) lists "Aaron's staff that had budded" among the contents of the ark. How does Hebrews describe the tabernacle and its service? Hebrews 9:14 speaks of being cleansed "so that we may serve the living God"; what does this reveal about God's people as those who serve the living God?
q3: In light of the tithe given for the Levites' service, how might generosity take shape in your life this week?
identity: Those who serve the living God

main_theme: God gives instructions for purification with water; Miriam and Aaron die, Moses strikes the rock at Meribah and is barred from bringing Israel into the land, and those bitten by snakes live when they look at the bronze serpent.
primary_threads: Law and wisdom; Blessing and curse; The people of God
pre_where: God has confirmed Aaron's priesthood. Today he gives a rite of purification, and the story moves to the deaths of Miriam and Aaron and to Moses' own failure at Meribah.
pre_watch: Watch for what Moses is told to do at the rock and what he does (20:8–11), and what the people bitten by snakes are told to do in 21:8.
q1: God gives instructions for purification with water; Miriam and Aaron die, Moses strikes the rock at Meribah and is barred from bringing Israel into the land, and those bitten by snakes live when they look at the bronze serpent. Those who are bitten and look at the bronze snake live (21:9). What does this reveal about the practice of trust?
q2: Jesus says, "Just as Moses lifted up the snake in the wilderness, so the Son of Man must be lifted up" (John 3:14–15, Day 259). How does Jesus use this event? John 3:16 speaks of "whoever believes"; what does this reveal about God's people as those who believe?
q3: In light of the people looking to the bronze snake as God instructed, how might trust take shape in your life this week?
identity: Those who believe

main_theme: Balak hires Balaam to curse Israel, but God turns his words into blessing, including an oracle of a star and scepter rising from Israel.
primary_threads: Blessing and curse; Kingdom and kingship; The Spirit
pre_where: Israel has reached the plains of Moab, near the Jordan. Today Moab's king, Balak, fears them and hires Balaam to curse them.
pre_watch: Watch for Balaam's donkey, what Balaam says he can speak in 22:38, and the oracle of a star and scepter in 24:17.
q1: Balak hires Balaam to curse Israel, but God turns his words into blessing, including an oracle of a star and scepter rising from Israel. Balaam says he can speak only what God puts in his mouth (22:38; 23:12, 26), even when Balak wants a curse. What does this reveal about the practice of obedience?
q2: Micah 6:5 (Day 165) tells Israel to remember what Balak plotted and what Balaam answered, so they may know the LORD's righteous acts. How does Micah use this story? Micah 6:8 calls God's people to act justly, love mercy and walk humbly with God; what does this reveal about God's people as a people who walk humbly with God?
q3: When others pressure you to act against what God has commanded, how might obedience take shape this week?
identity: A people who walk humbly with God

main_theme: Israel joins in Baal worship at Peor and Phinehas acts; a second census counts the new generation, Zelophehad's daughters receive an inheritance, and Joshua is appointed.
primary_threads: The people of God; Blessing and curse; Covenant; The Spirit; Sacrifice and atonement
pre_where: Balaam's curses became blessings. Today, still in Moab, Israel joins in the worship of the Baal of Peor, and a new generation is counted.
pre_watch: Watch for Zelophehad's daughters' request in 27:1–4 and Moses' prayer for a successor in 27:15–17.
q1: Israel joins in Baal worship at Peor and Phinehas acts; a second census counts the new generation, Zelophehad's daughters receive an inheritance, and Joshua is appointed. Zelophehad's daughters bring their request to Moses, and the LORD says they are right (27:1–7). What does this reveal about the practice of justice and mercy?
q2: Moses prays that the LORD's people will not be "like sheep without a shepherd" (27:17); Mark 6:34 (Day 252) says Jesus saw a crowd "like sheep without a shepherd." How do these two passages use the image? In John 10:27 (Day 262) Jesus says, "My sheep listen to my voice"; what does this reveal about God's people as sheep who listen to the shepherd?
q3: In light of Zelophehad's daughters bringing their case and being heard, how might justice and mercy take shape in your life this week?
identity: Sheep who listen to the shepherd

main_theme: God sets the daily, Sabbath and festival offerings and gives laws about keeping vows.
primary_threads: Sacrifice and atonement; Law and wisdom
pre_where: A new generation has been counted and Joshua appointed. Today God sets out the regular offerings for every day, Sabbath and festival, and gives laws about vows.
pre_watch: Watch for the daily offering morning and evening (28:3–4) and the command in 30:2 about keeping one's word.
q1: God sets the daily, Sabbath and festival offerings and gives laws about keeping vows. A man who makes a vow to the LORD must not break his word (30:2). What does this reveal about the practice of keeping one's word?
q2: Jesus teaches his disciples to speak plainly and calls them the light of the world, whose good deeds are to glorify their Father (Matthew 5:14–16, 33–37, Day 238). How does his teaching on truthful speech compare with Numbers 30:2? How might truthful speech relate to being the light of the world?
q3: In light of the command to keep one's word, how might keeping your word take shape in your life this week?
identity: The light of the world

main_theme: At God’s command Israel takes vengeance on Midian, and Reuben and Gad promise to fight alongside the other tribes in exchange for land east of the Jordan; half the tribe of Manasseh also receives land there.
primary_threads: The people of God; Blessing and curse
pre_where: The laws for offerings and vows are complete. Today Israel goes to war against Midian, and two tribes ask to settle east of the Jordan.
pre_watch: Watch for Moses' concern in 32:6–15 and the agreement Reuben and Gad make in 32:16–27.
q1: At God’s command Israel takes vengeance on Midian, and Reuben and Gad promise to fight alongside the other tribes in exchange for land east of the Jordan; half the tribe of Manasseh also receives land there. Reuben and Gad promise not to return home until every Israelite has received an inheritance (32:18). What does this reveal about the practice of service?
q2: Years later, Joshua commends the eastern tribes for keeping this promise and sends them home (Joshua 22:1–5, Day 69). How does Joshua describe what they did? Joshua 22:5 urges them to serve the LORD with all their heart and soul; what does this reveal about God's people as a people who serve with all their heart?
q3: In light of Reuben and Gad promising to stand with the other tribes, how might service take shape in your life this week?
identity: A people who serve with all their heart

main_theme: Israel's journey from Egypt is recorded stage by stage, and God commands them to drive out the land's inhabitants and sets Canaan's borders.
primary_threads: Exodus and redemption; The people of God
pre_where: Israel is camped on the plains of Moab. Today Moses records every stage of the journey from Egypt, and God sets out the land's borders.
pre_watch: Watch for how the journey began in 33:3–4 and the command in 33:50–56.
q1: Israel's journey from Egypt is recorded stage by stage, and God commands them to drive out the land's inhabitants and sets Canaan's borders. Moses records the stages of the journey at the LORD's command, beginning with Israel's departure from Egypt (33:2–4). As you consider this record of their departure, what does it invite you to reflect on about gratitude?
q2: Hebrews 11:13–16 (Day 340) describes people of faith as "foreigners and strangers on earth," looking for a country of their own. How is this similar to or different from Israel's journey toward the land? What does this reveal about God's people as foreigners and strangers on earth?
q3: As you recall events in your own life, what might you give thanks for this week?
identity: Foreigners and strangers on earth

main_theme: Towns for the Levites and cities of refuge are set apart, and inheritance laws keep land within each tribe.
primary_threads: Law and wisdom; The people of God; Temple and God's presence
pre_where: The borders have been set. Today God provides towns for the Levites and cities of refuge, and settles a question about inheritance.
pre_watch: Watch for who may flee to a city of refuge (35:11–15) and the reason God gives in 35:34.
q1: Towns for the Levites and cities of refuge are set apart, and inheritance laws keep land within each tribe. Anyone who kills a person accidentally may flee to a city of refuge (35:11). What does this reveal about the practice of justice and mercy?
q2: Hebrews 6:18 (Day 337) speaks of "we who have fled to take hold of the hope set before us." How are this image and the cities of refuge similar or different? What does this reveal about God's people as those who have fled to take hold of the hope?
q3: In light of the refuge God provides for those who caused death by accident, how might justice and mercy take shape in your life this week?
identity: Those who have fled to take hold of the hope

main_theme: Moses recounts Israel's journey from Horeb, the refusal at Kadesh, and the victories east of the Jordan.
primary_threads: The people of God; Blessing and curse
pre_where: Numbers ended with Israel on the plains of Moab. Deuteronomy opens in the fortieth year after the exodus, with Moses speaking to Israel east of the Jordan and retelling the journey from Horeb.
pre_watch: Watch for Moses' words about God carrying Israel in 1:31 and why the people refused to go up in 1:26–32.
q1: Moses recounts Israel's journey from Horeb, the refusal at Kadesh, and the victories east of the Jordan. Moses reminds them that the LORD carried them as a father carries his son (1:31). What does this reveal about the practice of trust?
q2: Acts 13:17–18 (Day 285) retells how God led Israel out of Egypt and endured their conduct in the wilderness for about forty years. How does Paul tell this story? In 13:26 he says the message of salvation has been sent "to us"; what does this reveal about God's people as those to whom this message has been sent?
q3: In light of Moses' words that God carried Israel like a father, how might trust take shape in your life this week?
identity: Those to whom the message of salvation has been sent

main_theme: Moses urges Israel to keep God's commands, repeats the Ten Commandments, and calls them to love the LORD with all their heart, soul and strength.
primary_threads: Law and wisdom; Covenant; The people of God; Exile and return
pre_where: Moses has retold the journey. Today he urges Israel to remember what they saw at Horeb, and he repeats the Ten Commandments.
pre_watch: Watch for the warning about exile and return in 4:25–31 and the command in 6:4–9.
q1: Moses urges Israel to keep God's commands, repeats the Ten Commandments, and calls them to love the LORD with all their heart, soul and strength. Moses tells parents to impress these commands on their children and talk about them at home and on the road (6:7). What does this reveal about the practice of meditating on Scripture?
q2: Jesus quotes Deuteronomy 6:4–5 as the most important commandment (Mark 12:28–30, Day 255). How does Jesus use these words? What does this reveal about God's people as those who love God with all their heart?
q3: In light of the command to talk about God's words at home and on the road, how might meditating on Scripture take shape in your life this week?
identity: Those who love God with all their heart

main_theme: God chose Israel because he loved them, not for their size or righteousness, and warns them not to forget him in prosperity; Moses recalls the golden calf.
primary_threads: The people of God; Covenant; Blessing and curse
pre_where: Moses has called Israel to love the LORD with all their heart. Today he tells them why God chose them and warns them not to forget him.
pre_watch: Watch for the reason given in 7:7–8, what Moses says about manna and living by every word from the LORD in 8:3, and the warning in 9:4–6.
q1: God chose Israel because he loved them, not for their size or righteousness, and warns them not to forget him in prosperity; Moses recalls the golden calf. Moses tells them to remember how God led them and humbled them in the wilderness, feeding them with manna (8:2–3). What does this reveal about the practice of humility?
q2: Deuteronomy 7:6 calls Israel "his treasured possession"; Titus 2:14 (Day 333) says Christ gave himself "to purify for himself a people that are his very own." How does Titus echo this language? What does this reveal about God's people as a people that are his very own?
q3: In light of God humbling and feeding Israel in the wilderness, how might humility take shape in your life this week?
identity: A people that are his very own

article_title: What Does the Bible Say About Blessing and Curse?
main_theme: God calls Israel to fear, love and serve him and to worship at the place he will choose, and sets blessing and curse before them.
primary_threads: Law and wisdom; Blessing and curse; Temple and God's presence; Covenant
pre_where: Moses has recalled the golden calf. Today he tells how God gave the tablets again and asks what the LORD requires.
pre_watch: Watch for the question and answer in 10:12–13, God's care for the fatherless, widow and foreigner in 10:18–19, and the place God will choose in chapter 12.
q1: God calls Israel to fear, love and serve him and to worship at the place he will choose, and sets blessing and curse before them. God defends the fatherless and the widow and loves the foreigner, and Israel is to love foreigners too (10:18–19). What does this reveal about the practice of hospitality?
q2: Hebrews 13:1–2 (Day 340) says, "Do not forget to show hospitality to strangers." How are this command and Deuteronomy 10:19 similar or different? What does this reveal about God's people as those who show hospitality to strangers?
q3: In light of God's command to love the foreigner, how might hospitality take shape in your life this week?
identity: Those who show hospitality to strangers

main_theme: Israel must reject anyone who leads them to other gods, keep food laws as a holy people, and use the tithe to provide for the Levite, foreigner, orphan and widow.
primary_threads: Law and wisdom; The people of God
pre_where: Moses has begun to set out laws for life in the land. Today he warns against anyone who leads Israel to other gods and gives laws about food and the tithe.
pre_watch: Watch for why Israel is to be different in 14:1–2 and who shares in the third-year tithe in 14:28–29.
q1: Israel must reject anyone who leads them to other gods, keep food laws as a holy people, and use the tithe to provide for the Levite, foreigner, orphan and widow. Every third year the tithe is stored so the Levite, foreigner, fatherless and widow may eat and be satisfied (14:28–29). What does this reveal about the practice of generosity?
q2: Deuteronomy 13 warns against being led to other gods; 1 John 5:21 (Day 347) ends, "Dear children, keep yourselves from idols." How are these warnings similar or different? First John 3:1 says we are called children of God; what does this reveal about God's people as children of God?
q3: In light of the tithe shared with the Levite, foreigner, fatherless and widow, how might generosity take shape in your life this week?
identity: Children of God

main_theme: Debts are to be released every seventh year, and Hebrew servants are to be freed after six years of service, with Israel reminded of its redemption from slavery; the pilgrimage festivals and duties of judges are set.
primary_threads: Law and wisdom; Exodus and redemption
pre_where: Moses has given laws about the tithe. Today he turns to the seventh-year release of debts and servants and the three yearly festivals.
pre_watch: Watch for the reason given for releasing servants in 15:15 and the command about judges in 16:18–20.
q1: Debts are to be released every seventh year, and Hebrew servants are to be freed after six years of service, with Israel reminded of its redemption from slavery; the pilgrimage festivals and duties of judges are set. Judges are to follow justice and justice alone (16:20). What does this reveal about the practice of justice and mercy?
q2: Deuteronomy 15:4 says there need be no poor people among them; Acts 4:34 (Day 280) says there were no needy persons among the believers. How does Acts echo this? Acts 4:32 says the believers were one in heart and mind; what does this reveal about God's people as a people one in heart and mind?
q3: In light of the command to follow justice and justice alone, how might justice and mercy take shape in your life this week?
identity: A people one in heart and mind

main_theme: God gives laws for kings, priests, prophets, cities of refuge and warfare, and promises to raise up a prophet like Moses.
primary_threads: Kingdom and kingship; Law and wisdom
pre_where: Moses has set out the yearly festivals. Today he gives laws for Israel's leaders: judges, kings, priests and prophets.
pre_watch: Watch for what the king must do with the law in 17:18–20 and the promise of a prophet in 18:15–19.
q1: God gives laws for kings, priests, prophets, cities of refuge and warfare, and promises to raise up a prophet like Moses. The king is to read the law all the days of his life and not consider himself better than his fellow Israelites (17:19–20). What does this reveal about the practice of humility?
q2: Peter quotes Deuteronomy 18:15 in Acts 3:22–23 (Day 280). How does Peter use the promise of a prophet like Moses? In Acts 3:25 he calls his hearers heirs of the prophets and of the covenant; what does this reveal about God's people as heirs of the covenant?
q3: In light of the king reading God's law so as not to think himself better than others, how might humility take shape in your life this week?
identity: Heirs of the covenant

main_theme: Laws address unsolved murder, family matters, care for neighbors and animals, and who may enter the assembly.
primary_threads: Law and wisdom; The people of God
pre_where: Moses has given laws for Israel's leaders. Today come laws for everyday life: family, neighbors, animals and the assembly.
pre_watch: Watch for the command to return a neighbor's lost animal in 22:1–4 and the laws about a neighbor's vineyard and field in 23:24–25.
q1: Laws address unsolved murder, family matters, care for neighbors and animals, and who may enter the assembly. If you see your neighbor's animal straying, you must not ignore it but take it back (22:1–3). What does this reveal about the practice of service?
q2: Paul quotes Deuteronomy 21:23, "Cursed is everyone who is hung on a pole," in Galatians 3:13–14 (Day 316). How does Paul use this verse? Galatians 3:14 says "by faith we might receive the promise of the Spirit"; what does this reveal about God's people as those who receive the promise of the Spirit by faith?
q3: In light of the command not to ignore a neighbor's lost animal, how might service take shape in your life this week?
identity: Those who receive the promise of the Spirit by faith

video_title: Wisdom Within Laws About Murder, Adultery, and Divorce
main_theme: Laws protect the poor, widows and foreigners; Israel brings firstfruits remembering the exodus and is told to write the law on stones and pronounce curses at Mount Ebal.
primary_threads: Law and wisdom; Blessing and curse; Exodus and redemption; Covenant
pre_where: Moses continues the laws for life in the land. Today he gives laws protecting the poor, a ceremony of firstfruits and instructions for renewing the covenant.
pre_watch: Watch for the reason given in 24:18 and 24:22, the words the worshiper says in 26:5–10, and the curses spoken at Mount Ebal.
q1: Laws protect the poor, widows and foreigners; Israel brings firstfruits remembering the exodus and is told to write the law on stones and pronounce curses at Mount Ebal. Israel is to leave sheaves, olives and grapes for the foreigner, the fatherless and the widow (24:19–21). What does this reveal about the practice of generosity?
q2: Israel brings the firstfruits of the land to the LORD (26:2); James 1:18 (Day 341) says God chose to give us birth "that we might be a kind of firstfruits of all he created," and 1:27 calls for looking after orphans and widows. How do these passages echo Deuteronomy? What does this reveal about God's people as a kind of firstfruits?
q3: In light of the harvest left for the foreigner, fatherless and widow, how might generosity take shape in your life this week?
identity: A kind of firstfruits

main_theme: Moses sets out blessings for obedience and curses for disobedience, including exile, and renews the covenant in Moab.
primary_threads: Blessing and curse; Covenant; Exile and return
pre_where: The covenant ceremony at Mount Ebal has been commanded. Today Moses sets out the blessings and curses and renews the covenant in Moab.
pre_watch: Watch for the opening blessings in 28:1–14, the warning of exile in 28:64, and what belongs to the LORD in 29:29.
q1: Moses sets out blessings for obedience and curses for disobedience, including exile, and renews the covenant in Moab. Moses says the secret things belong to the LORD, but the things revealed belong to us, that we may follow all the words of this law (29:29). What does this reveal about the practice of obedience?
q2: Deuteronomy sets blessings and curses before Israel; Revelation 22:3–4 (Day 358) says, "No longer will there be any curse," and "his servants will serve him. They will see his face." How are these two passages similar or different? What does this reveal about God's people as servants who will see his face?
q3: In light of the things God has revealed to be followed, how might obedience take shape in your life this week?
identity: Servants who will see his face

main_theme: God promises to bring Israel back after exile and circumcise their hearts, and calls them to choose life; Joshua is commissioned and the law is to be read publicly.
primary_threads: Exile and return; Covenant; Blessing and curse; Law and wisdom
pre_where: Moses has set out blessings and curses. Today he looks beyond exile to a return and commissions Joshua to lead the people into the land.
pre_watch: Watch for the promise in 30:6, how near the word is in 30:11–14, and the choice set before Israel in 30:19–20.
q1: God promises to bring Israel back after exile and circumcise their hearts, and calls them to choose life; Joshua is commissioned and the law is to be read publicly. Moses says the command is not too difficult or beyond reach; the word is very near, in your mouth and in your heart (30:11, 14). What does this reveal about the practice of meditating on Scripture?
q2: Paul quotes Deuteronomy 30:12–14 in Romans 10:6–8 (Day 297). How does Paul use these words? Romans 10:13 says, "Everyone who calls on the name of the Lord will be saved"; what does this reveal about God's people as those who call on the name of the Lord?
q3: In light of the word being near, in your mouth and in your heart, how might meditating on Scripture take shape in your life this week?
identity: Those who call on the name of the Lord

main_theme: Moses’ song recounts the LORD’s care for Israel, Israel’s turning to other gods, and the LORD’s judgment; Moses blesses the tribes and dies after seeing the land.
primary_threads: Blessing and curse; The people of God; Covenant
pre_where: Moses has commissioned Joshua. Today Moses sings a final song, blesses the tribes and dies after seeing the land from Mount Nebo.
pre_watch: Watch for how the song describes God in 32:4 and 32:10–11, Moses' final words in 33:26–29, and what the LORD shows Moses in 34:1–4.
q1: Moses’ song recounts the LORD’s care for Israel, Israel’s turning to other gods, and the LORD’s judgment; Moses blesses the tribes and dies after seeing the land. Moses' song begins, "Oh, praise the greatness of our God!" (32:3). What does this reveal about the practice of worship?
q2: Paul urges believers to offer themselves as a living sacrifice (Romans 12:1, Day 298) and later quotes Deuteronomy 32:35 when instructing them not to take revenge (Romans 12:19–21).
