How does Paul use Moses' words, and how might his instructions about responding to enemies relate to offering ourselves as a living sacrifice?
q3: In light of Moses' song praising God's greatness, how might worship take shape in your life this week?
identity: Those who offer themselves as a living sacrifice

main_theme: God commissions Joshua to be strong and keep the law; Rahab hides the spies, and Israel crosses the Jordan on dry ground and sets up memorial stones.
primary_threads: Law and wisdom; Exodus and redemption; Temple and God's presence; The people of God
pre_where: Moses has died. Today the book of Joshua opens as God speaks to Moses' successor, and Israel prepares to cross the Jordan.
pre_watch: Watch for God's words to Joshua in 1:6–9, Rahab's words in 2:9–11, and why the stones are set up in 4:6–7 and 4:21–24.
q1: God commissions Joshua to be strong and keep the law; Rahab hides the spies, and Israel crosses the Jordan on dry ground and sets up memorial stones. God tells Joshua to keep the Book of the Law on his lips and meditate on it day and night (1:8). What does this reveal about the practice of meditating on Scripture?
q2: Hebrews 11:31 (Day 340) says that by faith Rahab "was not killed with those who were disobedient," because she welcomed the spies. How does Hebrews describe Rahab? Hebrews 11:39 says, "These were all commended for their faith"; what does this reveal about God's people as those commended for their faith?
q3: In light of God's command to meditate on his law day and night, how might meditating on Scripture take shape in your life this week?
identity: Those commended for their faith

article_title: What Happens When We Read the Bible Together?
main_theme: Israel is circumcised and keeps Passover, Jericho falls, Achan's theft brings defeat at Ai, and the covenant is renewed at Mount Ebal.
primary_threads: Covenant; Blessing and curse; Exodus and redemption; Law and wisdom
pre_where: Israel has crossed the Jordan. Today the men are circumcised, Israel keeps the Passover in the land, and the manna stops.
pre_watch: Watch for the commander of the LORD's army in 5:13–15, what Achan admits in 7:20–21, and the reading of the law in 8:34–35.
q1: Israel is circumcised and keeps Passover, Jericho falls, Achan's theft brings defeat at Ai, and the covenant is renewed at Mount Ebal. Joshua falls facedown before the commander of the LORD's army and takes off his sandals, for the place is holy (5:14–15). What does this reveal about the practice of worship?
q2: The commander's words, "Take off your sandals, for the place where you are standing is holy" (5:15), repeat God's words to Moses at the burning bush (Exodus 3:5, Day 17). How do these two meetings compare? Exodus 19:6 (Day 23) calls Israel a holy nation; what does this reveal about God's people as a holy nation?
q3: In light of Joshua falling facedown on holy ground, how might worship take shape in your life this week?
identity: A holy nation

main_theme: The Gibeonites trick Israel into a treaty, the LORD fights for Israel as the sun stands still, and the kings of the south and north are defeated.
primary_threads: The people of God; Kingdom and kingship; Covenant
pre_where: Jericho and Ai have fallen. Today the Gibeonites deceive Israel into a treaty, and the kings of the south and north gather to fight.
pre_watch: Watch for what Israel fails to do in 9:14, how Israel keeps its oath in 9:19–20, and Joshua's words to the LORD and his command concerning the sun and moon in 10:12–14.
q1: The Gibeonites trick Israel into a treaty, the LORD fights for Israel as the sun stands still, and the kings of the south and north are defeated. Israel's leaders do not inquire of the LORD before making the treaty (9:14). What does this reveal about the practice of prayer?
q2: Israel keeps its oath to the Gibeonites even after the deception (9:19–20); Psalm 15:1, 4 asks who may dwell with God and answers, the one "who keeps an oath even when it hurts." How are these two passages similar or different? What does this reveal about God's people as those who may dwell with God?
q3: In light of Israel's failure to inquire of the LORD, how might prayer take shape in your life this week?
identity: Those who may dwell with God

main_theme: The land is divided among the tribes, Caleb receives Hebron, and cities of refuge and Levitical towns are set apart; none of the LORD's promises fail.
primary_threads: Covenant; The people of God; Law and wisdom
pre_where: The main campaigns are over. Today the land is divided among the tribes, a long record of borders and towns.
pre_watch: Watch for Caleb's request in 14:6–12, Zelophehad's daughters again in 17:3–6, and the summary in 21:43–45.
q1: The land is divided among the tribes, Caleb receives Hebron, and cities of refuge and Levitical towns are set apart; none of the LORD's promises fail. Caleb says he followed the LORD wholeheartedly and asks for the hill country the LORD promised (14:8–12). What does this reveal about the practice of trust?
q2: Hebrews 4:8–9 (Day 336) says that if Joshua had given them rest, God would not have spoken later about another day, and that a Sabbath-rest remains for the people of God. How does Hebrews use Joshua's story? What does this reveal about God's people as a people for whom a Sabbath-rest remains?
q3: In light of Caleb trusting God's promise after forty-five years, how might trust take shape in your life this week?
identity: A people for whom a Sabbath-rest remains

main_theme: An altar built by the eastern tribes nearly causes war; Joshua urges faithfulness, and at Shechem the people choose to serve the LORD and renew the covenant.
primary_threads: Covenant; The people of God; Blessing and curse; Law and wisdom
pre_where: The land has been divided. Today the eastern tribes go home, and Joshua, now old, gathers Israel at Shechem.
pre_watch: Watch for the misunderstanding over the altar in chapter 22, Joshua's retelling of Israel's history in 24:2–13, and the choice in 24:14–15.
q1: An altar built by the eastern tribes nearly causes war; Joshua urges faithfulness, and at Shechem the people choose to serve the LORD and renew the covenant. Joshua says, "As for me and my household, we will serve the LORD" (24:15). What does this reveal about the practice of service?
q2: Joshua calls Israel to put away other gods and serve the LORD (24:14, 23). Paul calls the Thessalonians loved by God and describes their turning from idols to serve the living and true God (1 Thessalonians 1:4, 9, Day 325). How do these accounts compare, and what does Paul's description invite you to reflect on about being loved by God and serving him?
q3: In light of Joshua's choice for himself and his household, how might service take shape in your life this week?
identity: Those loved by God

main_theme: Israel fails to drive out the Canaanites and serves their gods; the LORD raises up Othniel, Ehud and Shamgar to deliver them.
primary_threads: Blessing and curse; The people of God; The Spirit; Exodus and redemption
pre_where: Joshua has died. Judges opens with the tribes trying to take the rest of the land, and with a new generation that does not know the LORD.
pre_watch: Watch for the pattern described in 2:11–19, and how the LORD raises up deliverers, including Othniel, Ehud and Shamgar.
q1: Israel fails to drive out the Canaanites and serves their gods; the LORD raises up Othniel, Ehud and Shamgar to deliver them. When the Israelites cry out to the LORD, he raises up a deliverer for them (3:9, 15). What does this reveal about the practice of lament?
q2: Judges 2:16–19 describes the LORD raising up judges; Hebrews 11:32–34 (Day 340) names later judges among examples of faith. How does Hebrews describe their faith, and how does its call to run with perseverance (12:1) draw on those examples?
q3: In light of Israel crying out and the LORD answering, how might lament take shape in your life this week?
identity: Those who run the race with perseverance

main_theme: Deborah and Barak lead Israel against Sisera, Jael kills Sisera, and Deborah and Barak sing of the LORD's victory.
primary_threads: The people of God; Blessing and curse
pre_where: Ehud and Shamgar have delivered Israel. Today, after Ehud's death, Israel again does evil and is oppressed by Jabin, a king of Canaan, while Deborah is leading Israel.
pre_watch: Watch for what Deborah tells Barak in 4:6–9, who the text says routed Sisera in 4:15, and how Deborah's song begins in 5:2–3.
q1: Deborah and Barak lead Israel against Sisera, Jael kills Sisera, and Deborah and Barak sing of the LORD's victory. Deborah and Barak sing, "I will praise the LORD, the God of Israel, in song" (5:3). What does this reveal about the practice of worship?
q2: Deborah and Barak sing after the LORD's victory (5:1–3), as Moses and Miriam sang after the sea (Exodus 15:1, 20–21, Day 21). How are these two songs similar or different? Exodus 15:13 speaks of "the people you have redeemed"; what does this reveal about God's people as the people God has redeemed?
q3: In light of Deborah and Barak praising the LORD in song, how might worship take shape in your life this week?
identity: The people God has redeemed

main_theme: The LORD calls Gideon, who tears down Baal's altar and defeats Midian with three hundred men, refuses to be king, and makes an ephod that becomes a snare.
primary_threads: The Spirit; Kingdom and kingship; The people of God; Blessing and curse
pre_where: Deborah's song ended with forty years of peace. Today Israel again does evil, and Midian oppresses them for seven years.
pre_watch: Watch for how Gideon describes himself in 6:15, why the LORD reduces the army in 7:2, and Gideon's answer when he is offered kingship in 8:22–23.
q1: The LORD calls Gideon, who tears down Baal's altar and defeats Midian with three hundred men, refuses to be king, and makes an ephod that becomes a snare. The LORD reduces Gideon's army so that Israel cannot boast that its own strength saved it (7:2). What does this reveal about the practice of humility?
q2: Paul writes that God chose the weak things of the world to shame the strong, "so that no one may boast before him" (1 Corinthians 1:27–29, Day 301). How is this similar to or different from the LORD's words to Gideon in Judges 7:2? In 1:24 Paul speaks of "those whom God has called"; what does this reveal about God's people as those whom God has called?
q3: In light of the LORD's word that Israel should not boast in its own strength, how might humility take shape in your life this week?
identity: Those whom God has called

main_theme: Abimelek seizes kingship by murder and is destroyed; Jephthah defeats Ammon, makes a vow and carries it out concerning his daughter, and Ephraim fights Gilead.
primary_threads: Kingdom and kingship; Blessing and curse; The Spirit
pre_where: Gideon has died, and Israel again turns to the Baals. Today his son Abimelek seizes power, and later Jephthah leads Gilead against Ammon.
pre_watch: Watch for Jotham's story of the trees in 9:7–15, what 9:56–57 says about Abimelek's end, and what Israel does in 10:10–16.
q1: Abimelek seizes kingship by murder and is destroyed; Jephthah defeats Ammon, makes a vow and carries it out concerning his daughter, and Ephraim fights Gilead. The Israelites confess, "We have sinned," get rid of the foreign gods among them and serve the LORD (10:10, 15–16). What does this reveal about the practice of repentance?
q2: After Israel gets rid of its foreign gods, the LORD "could bear Israel's misery no longer" (10:16). In Hosea 11:8 (Day 158) the LORD says, "How can I give you up, Ephraim?… all my compassion is aroused." How are these two passages similar or different? Hosea 11:1 says, "out of Egypt I called my son"; what does this reveal about God's people as God's son, called out of Egypt?
q3: In light of Israel getting rid of its foreign gods and serving the LORD, how might repentance take shape in your life this week?
identity: God's son, called out of Egypt

main_theme: The angel of the LORD announces Samson’s birth; Samson marries a Philistine woman, and the Spirit of the LORD comes upon him as he fights the Philistines.
primary_threads: The Spirit; The people of God
pre_where: Jephthah and the judges after him have died. Today Israel again does evil, the Philistines rule them for forty years, and an angel announces a son to Manoah's wife.
pre_watch: Watch for the instructions in 13:4–5, Manoah's prayer in 13:8, and the times the text says the Spirit of the LORD came powerfully on Samson (14:6, 19; 15:14).
q1: The angel of the LORD announces Samson’s birth; Samson marries a Philistine woman, and the Spirit of the LORD comes upon him as he fights the Philistines. Manoah prays to the LORD to teach them how to bring up the boy, and God hears him (13:8–9). What does this reveal about the practice of prayer?
q2: An angel announces Samson's birth with instructions that he be a Nazirite (13:3–5); in Luke 1:13–17 (Day 267) an angel announces John's birth and says he is "never to take wine or other fermented drink." How are these two announcements similar or different? Luke 1:17 says John will "make ready a people prepared for the Lord"; what does this reveal about God's people as a people prepared for the Lord?
q3: In light of Manoah asking the LORD to teach them how to raise the boy, how might prayer take shape in your life this week?
identity: A people prepared for the Lord

main_theme: Delilah betrays Samson, who dies destroying a Philistine temple; Micah makes idols and hires a priest, and the tribe of Dan takes the idols and priest and captures Laish.
primary_threads: The people of God; Kingdom and kingship
pre_where: Samson has led Israel for twenty years. Today Delilah betrays him, and the book turns to a man named Micah and the tribe of Dan.
pre_watch: Watch for what Samson does not know in 16:20, the phrase in 17:6 and 18:1, and what Micah says in 17:13.
q1: Delilah betrays Samson, who dies destroying a Philistine temple; Micah makes idols and hires a priest, and the tribe of Dan takes the idols and priest and captures Laish. Micah makes an idol and appoints a priest, expecting the LORD to bless him (17:4–5, 13). What does this reveal about the dangers of worship shaped by our own expectations?
q2: Micah makes an idol of silver and expects the LORD to be good to him (17:4–13). In Acts 17:24–25, 29 (Day 287) Paul says God "is not served by human hands" and that we should not think the divine being is like gold or silver. How are these two passages similar or different? Paul says God did this "so that they would seek him and perhaps reach out for him and find him" (17:27); what does this reveal about God's people as those who seek him?
q3: How might you examine your worship this week in light of Micah's choices?
identity: Those who seek him

main_theme: A Levite’s concubine is abused in Gibeah and dies, civil war nearly destroys Benjamin, and the book ends with everyone doing what is right in their own eyes.
primary_threads: The people of God; Kingdom and kingship
pre_where: Dan has taken Laish and set up Micah's idol. Today the book's final chapters tell of a crime in Gibeah and the war that follows.
pre_watch: Watch for the old man's hospitality in 19:16–21, how Israel inquires of the LORD in 20:18, 23 and 26–28, and the book's last verse, 21:25.
q1: A Levite’s concubine is abused in Gibeah and dies, civil war nearly destroys Benjamin, and the book ends with everyone doing what is right in their own eyes. The Israelites go up to Bethel, weep before the LORD and fast (20:26). What does this reveal about the practice of lament?
q2: Hosea recalls the days of Gibeah (Hosea 9:9; 10:9, Day 157) and calls Israel to sow righteousness and seek the LORD (10:12). How does this call compare with the events of Judges 19–21? What does this reveal about God's people as those who return to the LORD (Hosea 6:1)?
q3: In light of Israel weeping and fasting before the LORD, how might lament take shape in your life this week?
identity: Those who return to the LORD

article_title: Rethinking Redemption With a Kinsman Redeemer in the Bible
main_theme: Naomi returns from Moab bitter, Ruth stays loyal to her, and Boaz redeems the family land and marries Ruth; their son becomes King David's grandfather.
primary_threads: Exodus and redemption; The people of God; Blessing and curse
pre_where: Judges ended with no king in Israel. Ruth is set in the days when the judges ruled (1:1), when famine sends one family from Bethlehem to Moab.
pre_watch: Watch for Ruth's words to Naomi in 1:16–17, Boaz's blessing in 2:12, and the family line in 4:17–22.
q1: Naomi returns from Moab bitter, Ruth stays loyal to her, and Boaz redeems the family land and marries Ruth; their son becomes King David's grandfather. Boaz tells Ruth, "This kindness is greater than that which you showed earlier" (3:10). What does this reveal about the practice of kindness?
q2: Ruth calls herself a foreigner (2:10), yet Matthew 1:5 (Day 236) names her in the family line of Jesus. How does Matthew include her? Ephesians 2:19 (Day 318) says, "you are no longer foreigners and strangers, but fellow citizens with God's people"; what does this reveal about God's people as fellow citizens with God's people?
q3: In light of the kindness shown between Ruth and Boaz, how might kindness take shape in your life this week?
identity: Fellow citizens with God's people

main_theme: Hannah prays for a son and gives Samuel to the LORD; Eli's sons abuse the priesthood, and the LORD calls Samuel and announces judgment on Eli's house.
primary_threads: Temple and God's presence; The people of God; Blessing and curse; Kingdom and kingship
pre_where: Ruth ended with the family line of David. 1 Samuel opens with Hannah, who has no children, at the house of the LORD at Shiloh.
pre_watch: Watch for Hannah's prayer in 1:10–11, her song in 2:1–10, and Samuel's answer in 3:10.
q1: Hannah prays for a son and gives Samuel to the LORD; Eli's sons abuse the priesthood, and the LORD calls Samuel and announces judgment on Eli's house. In deep anguish Hannah prays to the LORD, weeping bitterly (1:10). What does this reveal about the practice of prayer?
q2: Hannah's song (2:1–10) and Mary's song in Luke 1:46–55 (Day 267) both praise God for lifting up the lowly. How are these songs similar or different? Luke 1:50 says, "His mercy extends to those who fear him"; what does this reveal about God's people as those who fear him?
q3: In light of Hannah pouring out her anguish to the LORD, how might prayer take shape in your life this week?
identity: Those who fear him

article_title: Does a “Most-Accurate” Bible Translation Exist?
main_theme: The Philistines capture the ark and Eli's house falls; the ark afflicts its captors and returns, Samuel leads Israel, and the people demand a king like the nations.
primary_threads: Temple and God's presence; Kingdom and kingship; Blessing and curse; The people of God
pre_where: The LORD has called Samuel. Today Israel takes the ark into battle against the Philistines.
pre_watch: Watch for why Israel brings the ark in 4:3, the name Ichabod in 4:21–22, Samuel's words in 7:3, and what the LORD tells Samuel in 8:7.
q1: The Philistines capture the ark and Eli's house falls; the ark afflicts its captors and returns, Samuel leads Israel, and the people demand a king like the nations. Samuel tells Israel to rid themselves of the foreign gods and serve the LORD only, and they do (7:3–4). What does this reveal about the practice of repentance?
q2: The LORD tells Samuel that in asking for a king the people "have rejected me as their king" (8:7), and in John 19:15 (Day 266) the chief priests answer Pilate, "We have no king but Caesar." Jesus describes his kingdom as not of this world and says everyone on the side of truth listens to him (John 18:36–37, Day 265). How does this help you compare the responses to kingship in 1 Samuel 8:7 and John 19:15? What does this reveal about God's people as those on the side of truth?
q3: In light of Israel putting away its foreign gods and serving the LORD only, how might repentance take shape in your life this week?
identity: Those on the side of truth

main_theme: God chooses Saul, Samuel anoints him, the Spirit comes on him, and he is confirmed as king; Samuel warns Israel to fear and serve the LORD.
primary_threads: Kingdom and kingship; The Spirit; Blessing and curse
pre_where: Israel has asked for a king. Today God leads Samuel to Saul, a young Benjamite searching for lost donkeys.
pre_watch: Watch for the signs Samuel gives Saul in 10:1–7, where Saul is found in 10:22, and Samuel's words in 12:20–24.
q1: God chooses Saul, Samuel anoints him, the Spirit comes on him, and he is confirmed as king; Samuel warns Israel to fear and serve the LORD. Samuel says, "Far be it from me that I should sin against the LORD by failing to pray for you" (12:23). What does this reveal about the practice of prayer?
q2: Samuel says it would be a sin against the LORD to stop praying for the people (12:23); Hebrews 7:25 (Day 338) says Jesus "always lives to intercede for them." How are these two pictures of intercession similar or different? Hebrews 7:25 speaks of "those who come to God through him"; what does this reveal about God's people as those who come to God through him?
q3: In light of Samuel's commitment to keep praying for the people, how might prayer take shape in your life this week?
identity: Those who come to God through him

main_theme: Saul offers a sacrifice without waiting for Samuel and is told his kingdom will not last; Jonathan trusts the LORD to save, and Saul's rash oath endangers him.
primary_threads: Kingdom and kingship; Blessing and curse
pre_where: Saul has been confirmed as king. Today Israel faces the Philistines at Mikmash, and Saul does not wait for Samuel.
pre_watch: Watch for Saul's explanation in 13:11–12, Samuel's words in 13:13–14, and what Jonathan says in 14:6.
q1: Saul offers a sacrifice without waiting for Samuel and is told his kingdom will not last; Jonathan trusts the LORD to save, and Saul's rash oath endangers him. Jonathan says, "Nothing can hinder the LORD from saving, whether by many or by few" (14:6). What does this reveal about the practice of trust?
q2: Paul recalls God's choice of David (Acts 13:22, Day 285; 1 Samuel 13:14), then says God brought Israel the Savior Jesus from David's descendants (Acts 13:23). How does Paul connect David with Jesus? In Acts 13:38–39 Paul announces forgiveness and freedom through Jesus for those who believe. What does this reveal about God's people as those who are set free?
q3: In light of Jonathan's words that the LORD can save by many or by few, how might trust take shape in your life this week?
identity: Those who are set free

main_theme: Saul disobeys God's command concerning Amalek and is rejected as king; Samuel anoints David, the Spirit comes on him, and David defeats Goliath in the LORD's name.
primary_threads: Kingdom and kingship; The Spirit; Sacrifice and atonement; The people of God
pre_where: Saul has been told his kingdom will not endure. Today he is given a command concerning the Amalekites, and Samuel goes to Bethlehem.
pre_watch: Watch for Samuel's words in 15:22, what the LORD tells Samuel in 16:7, and David's words to Goliath in 17:45–47.
q1: Saul disobeys God's command concerning Amalek and is rejected as king; Samuel anoints David, the Spirit comes on him, and David defeats Goliath in the LORD's name. Samuel says, "To obey is better than sacrifice" (15:22). What does this reveal about the practice of obedience?
q2: Samuel says, "To obey is better than sacrifice" (15:22). In Mark 3:35 (Day 251) Jesus says, "Whoever does God's will is my brother and sister and mother." How are these two sayings similar or different? What does this reveal about God's people as those who do God's will?
q3: In light of Samuel's words that obeying is better than sacrifice, how might obedience take shape in your life this week?
identity: Those who do God's will

main_theme: David's success makes Saul jealous and murderous, while Jonathan makes a covenant with David and helps him escape.
primary_threads: Covenant; Kingdom and kingship
pre_where: David has defeated Goliath. Today he serves in Saul's court, where his success turns Saul against him.
pre_watch: Watch for what Jonathan gives David in 18:3–4, the covenant in 20:16–17, and their parting in 20:41–42.
q1: David's success makes Saul jealous and murderous, while Jonathan makes a covenant with David and helps him escape. Jonathan makes a covenant with David because he loves him as himself (18:3). What does this reveal about the practice of friendship?
q2: Jonathan loves David as himself (18:3; 20:17); in John 15:13–15 (Day 264) Jesus says, "Greater love has no one than this: to lay down one's life for one's friends." How are these two passages similar or different? Jesus says, "I have called you friends" (15:15); what does this reveal about God's people as Jesus' friends?
q3: In light of Jonathan's covenant loyalty to David, how might friendship take shape in your life this week?
identity: Jesus' friends

main_theme: David flees from Saul, Saul has the priests of Nob killed, and David spares Saul's life because he is the LORD's anointed.
primary_threads: Kingdom and kingship
pre_where: Jonathan has warned David to flee. Today David runs from Saul, first to Nob, then to Gath, and into the wilderness.
pre_watch: Watch for what David asks of the priest in 21:1–9, what happens at Nob in chapter 22, and David's words to Saul in 24:6 and 24:12.
q1: David flees from Saul, Saul has the priests of Nob killed, and David spares Saul's life because he is the LORD's anointed. David says to Saul, "May the LORD judge between you and me… but my hand will not touch you" (24:12). What does this reveal about the practice of trust?
q2: David leaves judgment to the LORD rather than harming Saul (24:12). First Peter 2:23 (Day 343) says that when Jesus suffered, "he entrusted himself to him who judges justly." How are these two responses similar or different? First Peter 2:21 speaks of following in his steps; what does this reveal about God's people as those who follow in his steps?
q3: In light of David leaving judgment to the LORD, how might trust take shape in your life this week?
identity: Those who follow in his steps

main_theme: Abigail persuades David not to take revenge on Nabal, David spares Saul a second time, and he takes refuge among the Philistines.
primary_threads: Kingdom and kingship; Law and wisdom
pre_where: David has spared Saul in the cave. Today, after Samuel's death, David meets Nabal and Abigail, and spares Saul a second time.
pre_watch: Watch for Abigail's words in 25:28–31, David's response in 25:32–33, and his words in 26:23.
q1: Abigail persuades David not to take revenge on Nabal, David spares Saul a second time, and he takes refuge among the Philistines. David praises the LORD for Abigail's good judgment in keeping him from bloodshed and from avenging himself (25:32–33). What does this reveal about the practice of humility?
q2: Abigail turns David from taking revenge (25:32–33); James 3:17–18 (Day 341) says the wisdom that comes from heaven is "peace-loving" and that "peacemakers who sow in peace reap a harvest of righteousness." How are these two passages similar or different? What does this reveal about God's people as peacemakers?
q3: In light of David accepting Abigail's counsel against taking revenge, how might humility take shape in your life this week?
identity: Peacemakers

main_theme: Saul consults a medium at Endor and hears of his defeat; David rescues his people from the Amalekites, and Saul and his sons die on Mount Gilboa.
primary_threads: Kingdom and kingship; Blessing and curse
pre_where: David has taken refuge among the Philistines. Today the Philistines gather against Israel, and Saul, afraid, receives no answer from the LORD.
pre_watch: Watch for how the LORD does not answer Saul in 28:6, David's response in 30:6, and how he shares the plunder in 30:23–25.
q1: Saul consults a medium at Endor and hears of his defeat; David rescues his people from the Amalekites, and Saul and his sons die on Mount Gilboa. In great distress, David finds strength in the LORD his God (30:6). What does this reveal about the practice of trust?
q2: David finds strength in the LORD his God (30:6). Paul describes learning contentment in plenty and in need and says, "I can do all this through him who gives me strength" (Philippians 4:11–13, Day 322). How are these two passages similar or different? What does this reveal about God's people as those to whom he gives strength?
q3: In light of David finding strength in the LORD in his distress, how might trust take shape in your life this week?
identity: Those to whom he gives strength

main_theme: David mourns Saul and Jonathan and is anointed king over Judah, and war between his house and Saul's continues until Abner is killed.
primary_threads: Kingdom and kingship; The people of God
pre_where: 1 Samuel ended with the deaths of Saul and his sons. 2 Samuel opens as the news reaches David at Ziklag.
pre_watch: Watch for David's lament in 1:19–27, his question to the LORD in 2:1, and his response to Abner's death in 3:31–39.
q1: David mourns Saul and Jonathan and is anointed king over Judah, and war between his house and Saul's continues until Abner is killed. David takes up a lament concerning Saul and his son Jonathan (1:17). What does this reveal about the practice of lament?
q2: David mourns Saul and Jonathan (1:17–27); Romans 12:15 (Day 298) says, "mourn with those who mourn." How are these two passages similar or different? Romans 12:5 says, "in Christ we, though many, form one body"; what does this reveal about God's people as one body in Christ?
q3: In light of David mourning Saul and Jonathan, how might lament take shape in your life this week?
identity: One body in Christ

article_title: Can We Trust God in Difficult Times?
main_theme: David becomes king over all Israel, takes Jerusalem and brings the ark there, and God promises that David's house and kingdom will endure forever.
primary_threads: Kingdom and kingship; Covenant; Temple and God's presence
pre_where: David has been king over Judah at Hebron. Today the tribes of Israel come to make him king over all Israel.
pre_watch: Watch for David dancing before the LORD in 6:14–15, his wish to build a house for the ark in 7:1–3, and God's promise in 7:11–16.
q1: David becomes king over all Israel, takes Jerusalem and brings the ark there, and God promises that David's house and kingdom will endure forever. David dances before the LORD with all his might (6:14). What does this reveal about the practice of worship?
q2: God promises David, "your throne will be established forever" (7:16); in Luke 1:32–33 (Day 267) the angel tells Mary that God will give Jesus "the throne of his father David" and that "his kingdom will never end." How does Luke echo this promise? Mary calls herself the Lord's servant (Luke 1:38), and her song speaks of God helping his servant Israel in remembrance of his mercy (1:54–55). What does this reveal about God's people as the Lord's servants?
q3: In light of David dancing before the LORD with all his might, how might worship take shape in your life this week?
identity: The Lord's servants

main_theme: David shows kindness to Mephibosheth, takes Bathsheba and has Uriah killed, and confesses his sin when Nathan confronts him; the child dies and Solomon is born.
primary_threads: Kingdom and kingship; Covenant; Blessing and curse
pre_where: God has promised David a lasting house. Today David seeks out Jonathan's son, and then, at the height of his power, sins against Uriah.
pre_watch: Watch for David's question in 9:1, Nathan's story in 12:1–7, and David's words in 12:13.
q1: David shows kindness to Mephibosheth, takes Bathsheba and has Uriah killed, and confesses his sin when Nathan confronts him; the child dies and Solomon is born. When Nathan confronts him, David says, "I have sinned against the LORD" (12:13). What does this reveal about the practice of confession?
q2: The heading of Psalm 51 (the daily psalm on Day 51) links it to Nathan's visit after David's sin (2 Samuel 12:1–13). How does the psalm pray in response to sin (Psalm 51:1–4, 10–12)? Psalm 51:17 speaks of a broken and contrite heart; what does this reveal about God's people as those with a broken and contrite heart?
q3: In light of David's confession to Nathan, how might confession take shape in your life this week?
identity: Those with a broken and contrite heart

main_theme: Amnon assaults Tamar, Absalom kills Amnon and later rebels, and David flees Jerusalem.
primary_threads: Kingdom and kingship; Blessing and curse
pre_where: Nathan told David that the sword would never depart from his house (12:10). Today trouble begins within David's own family.
pre_watch: Watch for Tamar's words in 13:12–13, David's response when Absalom returns in 14:33, and Ittai's words to David in 15:21.
q1: Amnon assaults Tamar, Absalom kills Amnon and later rebels, and David flees Jerusalem. As he flees, David sends the ark back and says, "let him do to me whatever seems good to him" (15:25–26). What does this reveal about the practice of trust?
q2: David goes up the Mount of Olives weeping and places himself in the LORD's hands (15:25–26, 30). On the Mount of Olives Jesus prays, "Yet not what I will, but what you will" (Mark 14:26, 36, Day 256). How are these two moments similar or different? Jesus tells his disciples, "Watch and pray" (14:38); what does this reveal about God's people as those who watch and pray?
q3: In light of David placing his future in the LORD's hands, how might trust take shape in your life this week?
identity: Those who watch and pray

main_theme: Absalom sleeps with David’s concubines, Hushai’s advice is accepted over Ahithophel’s, and Absalom is killed during the battle; David mourns him.
primary_threads: Kingdom and kingship; Blessing and curse
pre_where: David has fled Jerusalem. Today Absalom takes the city, and the advice of two counselors decides what happens next.
pre_watch: Watch for David's response to Shimei in 16:10–12, what 17:14 says about Ahithophel's advice, and David's grief in 18:33.
q1: Absalom sleeps with David’s concubines, Hushai’s advice is accepted over Ahithophel’s, and Absalom is killed during the battle; David mourns him. David weeps, "O my son Absalom! My son, my son Absalom! If only I had died instead of you" (18:33). What does this reveal about the practice of lament?
q2: David grieves for the son who rebelled against him (18:33); in Luke 15:20 (Day 274) a father runs to welcome back a son who left. How are these two fathers similar or different? The father says his son "was lost and is found" (15:32); what does this reveal about God's people as those who were lost and are found?
q3: In light of David's grief over his son, how might lament take shape in your life this week?
identity: Those who were lost and are found

main_theme: David returns to Jerusalem amid tribal rivalry, Sheba’s revolt is put down, and David hands over seven of Saul’s descendants to the Gibeonites after learning of Saul’s bloodshed against them.
primary_threads: Kingdom and kingship; Covenant
pre_where: Absalom has died. Today David returns to Jerusalem, but the tribes quarrel over the king.
pre_watch: Watch for David's words to Shimei in 19:22–23, Mephibosheth's words in 19:24–30, and what David asks the Gibeonites in 21:3.
q1: David returns to Jerusalem amid tribal rivalry, Sheba’s revolt is put down, and David hands over seven of Saul’s descendants to the Gibeonites after learning of Saul’s bloodshed against them. When Abishai wants Shimei put to death, David says, "Should anyone be put to death in Israel today?" and spares him (19:21–23). What does this reveal about the practice of justice and mercy?
q2: Abishai wants Shimei put to death, but David refuses (19:21–23). In Luke 9:54–55 (Day 271) James and John ask to call down fire on a Samaritan village, and Jesus rebukes them. Earlier Jesus teaches that "it is the one who is least among you all who is the greatest" (9:46–48) and calls his followers to deny themselves (9:23). How might Jesus' teaching on humility and self-denial inform your comparison of these responses to calls for punishment? What does this reveal about God's people as disciples who deny themselves?
q3: In light of David sparing Shimei, how might justice and mercy take shape in your life this week?
identity: Disciples who deny themselves

main_theme: David sings of the LORD his rock and deliverer, speaks of an everlasting covenant, and his census brings a plague that ends with a sacrifice at Araunah's threshing floor.
primary_threads: Kingdom and kingship; Covenant; Sacrifice and atonement
pre_where: David's reign is near its end. Today he sings a song of praise, speaks his last words, and orders a census.
pre_watch: Watch for how the song describes the LORD in 22:2–3, David's last words in 23:2–5, and his words to Araunah in 24:24.
q1: David sings of the LORD his rock and deliverer, speaks of an everlasting covenant, and his census brings a plague that ends with a sacrifice at Araunah's threshing floor. David tells Araunah, "I will not sacrifice to the LORD my God burnt offerings that cost me nothing" (24:24). What does this reveal about the practice of worship?
q2: Paul quotes David's song, "Therefore I will praise you among the Gentiles" (Romans 15:9, Day 299; 2 Samuel 22:50). How does Paul use these words? Romans 15:7 says, "Accept one another, then, just as Christ accepted you"; what does this reveal about God's people as those Christ has accepted?
q3: In light of David refusing to offer what cost him nothing, how might worship take shape in your life this week?
identity: Those Christ has accepted

main_theme: Solomon succeeds David over Adonijah's claim and secures his throne, then asks God for wisdom to govern, which God grants along with riches and honor.
primary_threads: Kingdom and kingship; Law and wisdom
pre_where: 2 Samuel ended with David's altar on Araunah's threshing floor. 1 Kings opens with David old, and a struggle over who will be king after him.
pre_watch: Watch for David's charge to Solomon in 2:2–4, Solomon's request in 3:7–9, and what God says in 3:10–14.
q1: Solomon succeeds David over Adonijah's claim and secures his throne, then asks God for wisdom to govern, which God grants along with riches and honor. Solomon says, "I am only a little child and do not know how to carry out my duties," and asks for a discerning heart (3:7–9). What does this reveal about the practice of humility?
q2: Solomon asks God for a discerning heart (3:9); James 1:5 (Day 341) says, "If any of you lacks wisdom, you should ask God, who gives generously to all without finding fault." How are these two passages similar or different? James speaks of those who love God receiving the crown of life (1:12) and inheriting the promised kingdom (2:5); what does this reveal about God's people as those who inherit the kingdom he promised?
q3: In light of Solomon admitting his need and asking for a discerning heart, how might humility take shape in your life this week?
identity: Those who inherit the kingdom he promised

main_theme: Solomon's wisdom and wealth grow, and he builds the temple and his palace.
primary_threads: Temple and God's presence; Kingdom and kingship; Law and wisdom
pre_where: God has given Solomon wisdom. Today the text describes his rule and the building of the temple.
pre_watch: Watch for the date in 6:1, the LORD's word to Solomon in 6:11–13, and how long each building takes in 6:38 and 7:1.
q1: Solomon's wisdom and wealth grow, and he builds the temple and his palace. The LORD tells Solomon that if he follows his decrees, "I will live among the Israelites" (6:12–13). What does this reveal about the practice of obedience?
q2: Stephen says, "it was Solomon who built a house for him. However, the Most High does not live in houses made by human hands" (Acts 7:47–48, Day 282). How does Stephen speak of the temple? First Corinthians 3:16 (Day 302) says, "you yourselves are God's temple"; what does this reveal about God's people as God's temple?
q3: In light of the LORD's instructions to Solomon concerning obedience (1 Kings 6:11–13), how might attending to God's commands take shape in your life this week?
identity: God's temple

main_theme: The ark enters the temple and God's glory fills it; Solomon prays at its dedication, God answers with promise and warning, and the queen of Sheba praises Solomon's wisdom.
primary_threads: Temple and God's presence; Covenant; Kingdom and kingship; Blessing and curse; Exile and return
pre_where: The temple is finished. Today the ark is brought in, and Solomon dedicates the temple with a long prayer.
pre_watch: Watch for what fills the temple in 8:10–11, Solomon's question in 8:27, his prayer for the foreigner in 8:41–43, and the LORD's answer in 9:3–9.
q1: The ark enters the temple and God's glory fills it; Solomon prays at its dedication, God answers with promise and warning, and the queen of Sheba praises Solomon's wisdom. Solomon asks God to hear from heaven when his people pray toward this place, and to forgive (8:30). What does this reveal about the practice of prayer?
q2: Solomon asks, "will God really dwell on earth?" (8:27). In John 4:21–24 (Day 259) Jesus says a time is coming when the Father will be worshiped neither on that mountain nor in Jerusalem. How are these two passages similar or different? Jesus speaks of "the true worshipers" (4:23); what does this reveal about God's people as true worshipers?
q3: In light of Solomon's prayer asking God to hear and forgive, how might prayer take shape in your life this week?
identity: True worshipers

main_theme: Solomon's wives turn his heart to other gods, the kingdom splits under Rehoboam, Jeroboam sets up golden calves, and a man of God denounces the altar at Bethel.
primary_threads: Kingdom and kingship; Covenant; Blessing and curse
pre_where: Solomon has dedicated the temple and grown famous. Today his heart turns away from the LORD, and after his death the kingdom splits in two.
pre_watch: Watch for what 11:4 says about Solomon's heart, the advice Rehoboam rejects in 12:6–11, and why Jeroboam makes the golden calves in 12:26–28.
q1: Solomon's wives turn his heart to other gods, the kingdom splits under Rehoboam, Jeroboam sets up golden calves, and a man of God denounces the altar at Bethel. The elders advise Rehoboam that if he will be a servant to the people, they will always be his servants (12:7). What does this reveal about the practice of service?
q2: Jesus says, "whoever wants to become great among you must be your servant" (Mark 10:42–45, Day 254). How does this compare with Rehoboam's choice in 12:6–14? Galatians 5:13 (Day 317) says, "serve one another humbly in love"; what does this reveal about God's people as servants of one another?
q3: In light of the elders' advice that a king should serve the people, how might service take shape in your life this week?
identity: Servants of one another

main_theme: Prophets announce judgment on Jeroboam's house, Judah and Israel sin under a series of kings, and Ahab marries Jezebel and serves Baal.
primary_threads: Kingdom and kingship; Blessing and curse
pre_where: The kingdom has split into Israel in the north and Judah in the south. Today a series of kings rule both, most of them doing evil.
pre_watch: Watch for Ahijah's message to Jeroboam's wife in 14:7–11, Asa's actions in 15:11–14, and how Ahab is described in 16:30–33.
q1: Prophets announce judgment on Jeroboam's house, Judah and Israel sin under a series of kings, and Ahab marries Jezebel and serves Baal. Asa does what is right in the eyes of the LORD and gets rid of all the idols his ancestors had made (15:11–12). What does this reveal about the practice of worship?
q2: Asa removes the idols from the land (15:12–13); Colossians 3:5 (Day 324) calls believers to put to death what belongs to their earthly nature, including "greed, which is idolatry." How are these two passages similar or different? Colossians 3:12 calls them "God's chosen people, holy and dearly loved"; what does this reveal about God's people as God's chosen people, holy and dearly loved?
q3: In light of Asa removing the idols, how might worship take shape in your life this week?
identity: God's chosen people, holy and dearly loved

main_theme: Elijah announces drought; the LORD provides for him and a widow, answers by fire on Carmel, and speaks to Elijah at Horeb after a gentle whisper.
primary_threads: Blessing and curse; Temple and God's presence; The people of God
pre_where: Ahab has married Jezebel and serves Baal. Today the prophet Elijah announces a drought.
pre_watch: Watch for the widow's flour and oil in 17:14–16, Elijah's prayer in 18:36–37, and how the LORD speaks in 19:11–13.
q1: Elijah announces drought; the LORD provides for him and a widow, answers by fire on Carmel, and speaks to Elijah at Horeb after a gentle whisper. Elijah prays, "Answer me, LORD, answer me, so these people will know that you, LORD, are God" (18:37). What does this reveal about the practice of prayer?
q2: Paul quotes Elijah's complaint and God's answer about the seven thousand who have not bowed to Baal (Romans 11:2–5, Day 297; 1 Kings 19:10, 18). How does Paul use this moment? Romans 11:5 speaks of "a remnant chosen by grace"; what does this reveal about God's people as a remnant chosen by grace?
q3: In light of Elijah's prayer that the people would know the LORD is God, how might prayer take shape in your life this week?
identity: A remnant chosen by grace

main_theme: The LORD gives Ahab victories over Aram; Jezebel arranges Naboth’s death and Ahab takes his vineyard; Ahab dies in battle as Micaiah prophesied.
primary_threads: Kingdom and kingship; Blessing and curse
pre_where: Elijah has met the LORD at Horeb. Today Ahab fights Aram, takes Naboth's vineyard, and goes to battle against the word of a prophet.
pre_watch: Watch for Naboth's answer in 21:3, Ahab's response to Elijah in 21:27–29, and Micaiah's words in 22:14.
q1: The LORD gives Ahab victories over Aram; Jezebel arranges Naboth’s death and Ahab takes his vineyard; Ahab dies in battle as Micaiah prophesied. Micaiah says, "As surely as the LORD lives, I can tell him only what the LORD tells me" (22:14). What does this reveal about the practice of speaking the truth?
q2: Micaiah speaks the LORD's word though pressed to agree with the other prophets (22:13–14). In Acts 4:19–20 (Day 280) Peter and John say, "we cannot help speaking about what we have seen and heard." How are these two passages similar or different? The believers pray, "enable your servants to speak your word with great boldness" (4:29); what does this reveal about God's people as servants who speak God's word with boldness?
q3: In light of Micaiah speaking only what the LORD told him, how might speaking the truth take shape in your life this week?
identity: Servants who speak God's word with boldness

main_theme: Elijah confronts King Ahaziah and is taken up to heaven in a whirlwind; Elisha receives a double portion of his spirit, and Moab is defeated.
primary_threads: Kingdom and kingship
pre_where: 1 Kings ended with Ahab's death in battle. 2 Kings opens with his son Ahaziah injured and sending messengers to ask Baal-Zebub, the god of Ekron, whether he will recover.
pre_watch: Watch for Elijah's question in 1:3, Elisha's request in 2:9, and what the company of prophets says in 2:15.
q1: Elijah confronts King Ahaziah and is taken up to heaven in a whirlwind; Elisha asks for a double portion of Elijah's spirit, and the company of prophets recognizes that Elijah's spirit rests on Elisha (2:9–15), and Moab is defeated. Elijah asks the king's messengers, "Is it because there is no God in Israel that you are going off to consult Baal-Zebub?" (1:3). What does this reveal about the practice of trust?
q2: Elijah is taken up to heaven in a whirlwind (2:11); in Mark 9:2–7 (Day 254) Elijah appears with Moses as Jesus is transfigured, and a voice from the cloud says, "This is my Son, whom I love. Listen to him!" How does Mark present Elijah alongside Jesus? What does this reveal about God's people as those who listen to God's Son?
q3: In light of Elijah's question about turning to other gods, how might trust take shape in your life this week?
identity: Those who listen to God's Son

main_theme: Elisha's miracles provide for a widow, raise a Shunammite's son and heal Naaman, and Samaria is rescued from an Aramean siege as Elisha foretold.
primary_threads: Blessing and curse; The people of God; Exodus and redemption
pre_where: Elisha has received a double portion of Elijah's spirit. Today a series of events shows the LORD's care through him, for Israelites and for a foreign commander.
pre_watch: Watch for the widow's oil in 4:1–7, what the servant girl says in 5:3, Naaman's words in 5:15, and what the four men with leprosy say in 7:9.
q1: Elisha's miracles provide for a widow, raise a Shunammite's son and heal Naaman, and Samaria is rescued from an Aramean siege as Elisha foretold. The four men with leprosy say, "This is a day of good news and we are keeping it to ourselves" (7:9). What does this reveal about the practice of witness?
q2: The men with leprosy decide they must not keep the good news to themselves (7:9). In Romans 10:14–15 (Day 297) Paul asks how people will hear without someone preaching and quotes, "How beautiful are the feet of those who bring good news!" How are these two passages similar or different? What does this reveal about God's people as those who bring good news?
q3: In light of the men refusing to keep the good news to themselves, how might witness take shape in your life this week?
identity: Those who bring good news

main_theme: Jehu is anointed and destroys Ahab's house and Baal worship in Israel; in Judah, Athaliah seizes power until Joash is crowned and the covenant is renewed.
primary_threads: Kingdom and kingship; Covenant; Blessing and curse
pre_where: Elisha's ministry continues. Today Jehu is anointed king over Israel, and in Judah the king's mother, Athaliah, seizes the throne.
pre_watch: Watch for how the young Joash is hidden in 11:2–3, the covenant Jehoiada makes in 11:17, and the people's response in 11:18–20.
q1: Jehu is anointed and destroys Ahab's house and Baal worship in Israel; in Judah, Athaliah seizes power until Joash is crowned and the covenant is renewed. Jehoiada makes a covenant that the king and people will be the LORD's people, and the people tear down the temple of Baal (11:17–18). What does this reveal about the practice of worship?
q2: Jehosheba hides Joash from Athaliah (11:1–3), and after Joash is crowned the people renew their covenant with the LORD (11:17–18). Matthew describes the Magi worshiping Jesus and Joseph taking him to Egypt to escape Herod (Matthew 2:11–16, Day 236). How do these accounts connect threatened kingship and worship, and what does Matthew invite us to consider about worshiping Jesus?
q3: In light of the people renewing their covenant to be the LORD's people, how might worship take shape in your life this week?
identity: Those who come to worship him

main_theme: Joash repairs the temple, later kings of Israel and Judah do right or evil in the LORD’s sight, and Elisha dies.
primary_threads: Temple and God's presence; Kingdom and kingship; Covenant
pre_where: Joash has been crowned in Judah. Today he repairs the temple, and the story follows the kings of Israel and Judah to Elisha's death.
pre_watch: Watch for how the temple money is handled in 12:9–15, why the LORD is gracious to Israel in 13:23, and the law Amaziah follows in 14:6.
q1: Joash repairs the temple, later kings of Israel and Judah do right or evil in the LORD’s sight, and Elisha dies. The men who pay the workers are not asked to account for the money, because they act with complete honesty (12:15). What does this reveal about the practice of integrity?
q2: The workers' pay is handled with complete honesty (12:15); Paul takes care to handle the gift for Jerusalem by doing what is right "not only in the eyes of the Lord but also in the eyes of man" (2 Corinthians 8:20–21, Day 312). How are these two passages similar or different? What does this reveal about God's people as those who take pains to do what is right?
q3: In light of the temple money being handled with complete honesty, how might integrity take shape in your life this week?
identity: Those who take pains to do what is right

main_theme: Israel's kings fall in quick succession, Assyria conquers Samaria and exiles Israel for abandoning the LORD's covenant, and foreigners resettle the land.
primary_threads: Exile and return; Covenant; Kingdom and kingship; Blessing and curse
pre_where: Elisha has died. Today Israel's kings fall in quick succession, and Assyria rises against them.
pre_watch: Watch for the reasons the text gives in 17:7–18 and what the resettled peoples do in 17:33.
q1: Israel's kings fall in quick succession, Assyria conquers Samaria and exiles Israel for abandoning the LORD's covenant, and foreigners resettle the land. The text says the Israelites would not listen and were as stiff-necked as their ancestors (17:14). What does this reveal about the danger of refusing to listen to the LORD?
q2: Israel would not listen and was stiff-necked (17:14). Hebrews 3:12–15 (Day 336) warns, "Today, if you hear his voice, do not harden your hearts," and urges, "encourage one another daily." How are these two passages similar or different? What does this reveal about God's people as those who encourage one another daily?
q3: In light of Israel's refusal to listen to the LORD's warnings, how might obedience take shape in your life this week?
identity: Those who encourage one another daily

main_theme: Hezekiah trusts the LORD and reforms worship; when Assyria threatens Jerusalem he prays in the temple, Isaiah relays God's answer, and the angel of the LORD strikes Assyria's army.
primary_threads: Kingdom and kingship; Temple and God's presence; Exodus and redemption
pre_where: Assyria has exiled the northern kingdom of Israel. Today Hezekiah reigns in Judah, and Assyria's army comes against Jerusalem.
pre_watch: Watch for what 18:5–6 says about Hezekiah, the field commander's question in 18:19–20, and Hezekiah's prayer in 19:15–19.
q1: Hezekiah trusts the LORD and reforms worship; when Assyria threatens Jerusalem he prays in the temple, Isaiah relays God's answer, and the angel of the LORD strikes Assyria's army. Hezekiah spreads the letter out before the LORD and prays that all kingdoms may know that he alone is God (19:14–19). What does this reveal about the practice of prayer?
q2: Hezekiah prays, "You have made heaven and earth" (19:15). When threatened, the believers in Acts 4:24–30 (Day 280) raise their voices together in prayer: "Sovereign Lord… you made the heavens and the earth." How are these two prayers similar or different? What does this reveal about God's people as a people who pray together?
q3: In light of Hezekiah spreading the threat before the LORD, how might prayer take shape in your life this week?
identity: A people who pray together

main_theme: Hezekiah is healed but shows his treasures to Babylon, Manasseh's evil brings judgment on Judah, and Josiah responds to the rediscovered Book of the Law.
primary_threads: Kingdom and kingship; Exile and return; Law and wisdom; Blessing and curse
pre_where: The LORD has delivered Jerusalem from Assyria. Today Hezekiah falls ill, and after him come Manasseh, Amon and the young king Josiah.
pre_watch: Watch for Hezekiah's prayer in 20:2–3, what Isaiah says in 20:16–18, and Josiah's response to the Book of the Law in 22:11–13, 19.
q1: Hezekiah is healed but shows his treasures to Babylon, Manasseh's evil brings judgment on Judah, and Josiah responds to the rediscovered Book of the Law. When the Book of the Law is read to him, Josiah tears his robes, and the LORD says his heart was responsive and he humbled himself (22:11, 19). What does this reveal about the practice of humility?
q2: Josiah responds to the words of the Book of the Law by humbling himself (22:11, 19). James 1:22–25 (Day 341) says, "Do not merely listen to the word… Do what it says." How are these two responses to God's word similar or different? What does this reveal about God's people as those who do what the word says?
q3: In light of Josiah humbling himself when he heard the law, how might humility take shape in your life this week?
identity: Those who do what the word says

main_theme: Josiah renews the covenant and removes idolatry, yet Babylon destroys Jerusalem and the temple and exiles Judah; the captive king Jehoiachin is released from prison.
primary_threads: Covenant; Exile and return; Temple and God's presence; Kingdom and kingship; Blessing and curse
pre_where: Josiah has heard the Book of the Law. Today he renews the covenant, and after him Judah's last kings fall to Babylon.
pre_watch: Watch for Josiah's covenant in 23:1–3, the Passover in 23:21–23, and the release of Jehoiachin in 25:27–30.
q1: Josiah renews the covenant and removes idolatry, yet Babylon destroys Jerusalem and the temple and exiles Judah; the captive king Jehoiachin is released from prison. Josiah reads the Book of the Covenant to all the people and renews the covenant to follow the LORD and keep his commands with all his heart and soul (23:2–3). What does this reveal about the practice of obedience?
q2: Josiah reads the Book of the Covenant to all the people (23:2). In Nehemiah 8:1–10 (Day 217) Ezra reads the Book of the Law to the people who have returned from exile. How are these two readings similar or different? Nehemiah 8:10 says, "the joy of the LORD is your strength"; what does this reveal about God's people as those whose strength is the joy of the LORD?
q3: In light of Josiah's covenant to follow the LORD with all his heart and soul, how might obedience take shape in your life this week?
identity: Those whose strength is the joy of the LORD

main_theme: The LORD charges Judah with rebellion and empty worship, calls them to seek justice, and envisions nations streaming to his house as judgment purifies Zion.
primary_threads: Temple and God's presence; The day of the Lord; Blessing and curse; Law and wisdom
pre_where: 2 Kings ended with Judah in exile in Babylon. Today the plan turns to the prophets, beginning with Isaiah, who spoke in Judah during the reigns of Uzziah, Jotham, Ahaz and Hezekiah (1:1).
pre_watch: Watch for what the LORD says about their offerings in 1:11–17, the invitation in 1:18, and the vision of the nations in 2:2–4.
q1: The LORD charges Judah with rebellion and empty worship, calls them to seek justice, and envisions nations streaming to his house as judgment purifies Zion. The LORD says, "Learn to do right; seek justice. Defend the oppressed. Take up the cause of the fatherless; plead the case of the widow" (1:17). What does this reveal about the practice of justice and mercy?
q2: Isaiah's vision of the nations streaming to the mountain of the LORD's temple (2:2–4) appears almost word for word in Micah 4:1–3 (Day 164). How do the two prophets use this vision? Micah 4:2 says, "He will teach us his ways, so that we may walk in his paths"; what does this reveal about God's people as those who walk in his paths?
q3: In light of the LORD's call to seek justice and defend the oppressed, how might justice and mercy take shape in your life this week?
identity: Those who walk in his paths

main_theme: The song of the vineyard announces judgment, Isaiah sees the LORD enthroned and is sent, and King Ahaz is offered the sign of Immanuel.
primary_threads: Blessing and curse; Temple and God's presence; Kingdom and kingship
pre_where: Isaiah has called Judah to seek justice. Today he sings of a vineyard, describes his vision of the LORD, and brings a sign to King Ahaz.
pre_watch: Watch for the question in 5:4, the seraphim's words in 6:3, Isaiah's response in 6:5–8, and the sign in 7:14.
q1: The song of the vineyard announces judgment, Isaiah sees the LORD enthroned and is sent, and King Ahaz is offered the sign of Immanuel. Isaiah says, "Woe to me!… I am a man of unclean lips," and a seraph touches his lips and says his guilt is taken away (6:5–7). What does this reveal about the practice of confession?
q2: Isaiah gives Ahaz the sign of a child called Immanuel (7:14). Matthew 1:22–23 (Day 236) quotes this verse about the birth of Jesus and explains that the name means "God with us." How does Matthew use Isaiah's words? What does this reveal about God's people as those God is with?
q3: In light of Isaiah confessing his unclean lips before the holy LORD, how might confession take shape in your life this week?
identity: Those God is with

main_theme: Isaiah announces a child who will reign on David's throne with justice and a shoot from Jesse on whom the Spirit rests; Assyria will fall and a remnant return.
primary_threads: The promised Messiah; Kingdom and kingship; The Spirit; Exile and return
pre_where: Isaiah has given Ahaz the sign of Immanuel. Today he speaks of light for those in darkness and of a child who will reign on David's throne.
pre_watch: Watch for the names in 9:6, the shoot from Jesse in 11:1–5, and the song in 12:1–6.
q1: Isaiah announces a child who will reign on David's throne with justice and a shoot from Jesse on whom the Spirit rests; Assyria will fall and a remnant return. Isaiah's song says, "Give praise to the LORD, proclaim his name; make known among the nations what he has done" (12:4). What does this reveal about the practice of worship?
q2: Matthew 4:13–16 (Day 237) quotes Isaiah 9:1–2: "the people living in darkness have seen a great light." How does Matthew use these words? Jesus then calls, "Come, follow me" (4:19); what does this reveal about God's people as those who follow him?
q3: In light of Isaiah's call to make known among the nations what the LORD has done, how might worship take shape in your life this week?
identity: Those who follow him

main_theme: Oracles announce the day of the LORD against Babylon and the fall of its king, with judgment on Assyria, Philistia, Moab and Damascus.
primary_threads: The day of the Lord; Kingdom and kingship; Exile and return
pre_where: Isaiah has spoken of a king from David's line. Today begin his oracles against the nations, starting with Babylon.
pre_watch: Watch for the day of the LORD in 13:6–11, the promise to Israel in 14:1–2, and the taunt against the king of Babylon in 14:12–15.
q1: Oracles announce the day of the LORD against Babylon and the fall of its king, with judgment on Assyria, Philistia, Moab and Damascus. The king of Babylon said in his heart, "I will ascend to the heavens… I will make myself like the Most High," but he is brought down (14:13–15). What does this reveal about the danger of pride?
q2: The king of Babylon tries to raise himself up and is brought down (14:13–15). In Luke 14:11 (Day 274) Jesus says, "all those who exalt themselves will be humbled, and those who humble themselves will be exalted." How are these two passages similar or different? What does this reveal about God's people as those who humble themselves?
q3: In light of the king of Babylon's fall from his pride, how might humility take shape in your life this week?
identity: Those who humble themselves

main_theme: Oracles address Cush, Egypt and other nations, promising that Egypt and Assyria will worship with Israel; Jerusalem is rebuked for revelry when the LORD calls for weeping and mourning.
primary_threads: The people of God; Blessing and curse; The day of the Lord
pre_where: Isaiah's oracles against the nations continue, now addressing Cush, Egypt and others, and then Jerusalem itself.
pre_watch: Watch for the promise for Egypt and Assyria in 19:23–25, and what the people do instead of mourning in 22:12–13.
q1: Oracles address Cush, Egypt and other nations, promising that Egypt and Assyria will worship with Israel; Jerusalem is rebuked for revelry when the LORD calls for weeping and mourning. When the LORD calls them to weep and wail, the people feast instead, saying, "Let us eat and drink, for tomorrow we die!" (22:12–13). What does this reveal about the danger of ignoring God's call to turn back?
q2: Paul quotes Isaiah 22:13, "Let us eat and drink, for tomorrow we die," in 1 Corinthians 15:32 (Day 308). How does Paul use these words? In 15:58 he urges believers to give themselves fully to the work of the Lord; what does this reveal about God's people as those who give themselves fully to the work of the Lord?
q3: In light of the LORD's call to weep and turn rather than feast, how might repentance take shape in your life this week?
identity: Those who give themselves fully to the work of the Lord

main_theme: After judgment on Tyre, the earth is laid waste; then the LORD prepares a feast for all peoples on his mountain, swallows up death, and gathers Israel.
primary_threads: The day of the Lord; Temple and God's presence; Exile and return
pre_where: Isaiah has addressed Jerusalem; today he turns to Tyre and then widens the vision to the whole earth. The vision moves from judgment to a feast on the LORD's mountain.
pre_watch: Watch for the feast and the promise in 25:6–8, the song in 26:3–4, and the gathering in 27:12–13.
q1: After judgment on Tyre, the earth is laid waste; then the LORD prepares a feast for all peoples on his mountain, swallows up death, and gathers Israel. Isaiah says, "You will keep in perfect peace those whose minds are steadfast, because they trust in you" (26:3). What does this reveal about the practice of trust?
q2: Isaiah says the LORD will swallow up death forever and wipe away the tears from all faces (25:8). Revelation 21:4 (Day 358) says, "He will wipe every tear from their eyes. There will be no more death." How does Revelation echo this promise? Revelation 21:7 says those who are victorious will be God's children; what does this reveal about God's people as those who are victorious?
q3: In light of the promise of perfect peace for those who trust in the LORD, how might trust take shape in your life this week?
identity: Those who are victorious

main_theme: Judah's leaders are condemned for scoffing and for trusting Egypt, yet the LORD lays a tested cornerstone in Zion and longs to be gracious.
primary_threads: Blessing and curse; The people of God
pre_where: Isaiah has described a feast for all peoples. Today he returns to Jerusalem's leaders, who scoff at his message and seek help from Egypt.
pre_watch: Watch for the cornerstone in 28:16, the words in 29:13, and the LORD's invitation in 30:15 and 30:18.
q1: Judah's leaders are condemned for scoffing and for trusting Egypt, yet the LORD lays a tested cornerstone in Zion and longs to be gracious. The LORD says, "In repentance and rest is your salvation, in quietness and trust is your strength, but you would have none of it" (30:15). What does this reveal about the practice of trust?
q2: Peter quotes Isaiah 28:16 about a precious cornerstone laid in Zion (1 Peter 2:6, Day 343). How does Peter use this verse? In 2:5 he calls believers "living stones" being built into a spiritual house; what does this reveal about God's people as living stones?
q3: In light of the LORD's words, "in quietness and trust is your strength," how might trust take shape in your life this week?
identity: Living stones

main_theme: Judah is warned against relying on Egypt; a righteous king will reign, the Spirit will be poured out, nations are judged, and the redeemed return to Zion with joy.
primary_threads: Kingdom and kingship; The Spirit; The day of the Lord; Exodus and redemption
pre_where: Judah's leaders have looked to Egypt for help. Today Isaiah warns them again and speaks of a righteous king and of the redeemed returning to Zion.
pre_watch: Watch for the warning in 31:1, the Spirit poured out in 32:15–18, and the signs of return in 35:3–10.
q1: Judah is warned against relying on Egypt; a righteous king will reign, the Spirit will be poured out, nations are judged, and the redeemed return to Zion with joy. Isaiah says, "Strengthen the feeble hands, steady the knees that give way; say to those with fearful hearts, 'Be strong, do not fear'" (35:3–4). What does this reveal about the practice of encouragement?
q2: Hebrews 12:12–13 (Day 340) echoes Isaiah 35:3: "strengthen your feeble arms and weak knees." Hebrews 12:22–24 then says believers have come to Mount Zion and to the church of the firstborn, as Isaiah pictures the redeemed entering Zion with singing (35:10). How do these descriptions of coming to Zion relate to the call to strengthen weak knees? What does this reveal about God's people as the church of the firstborn?
q3: In light of Isaiah's call to strengthen the weak and say to the fearful, "Be strong," how might encouragement take shape in your life this week?
identity: The church of the firstborn

main_theme: Assyria threatens Jerusalem, Hezekiah prays and the LORD delivers the city, and Hezekiah is healed after praying.
primary_threads: Kingdom and kingship; Temple and God's presence; Exodus and redemption
pre_where: Isaiah has spoken of the redeemed returning to Zion. Today the book turns to narrative: Assyria threatens Jerusalem in Hezekiah's fourteenth year (36:1).
pre_watch: Watch for the field commander's words in 36:4–10, Hezekiah's prayer in 37:15–20, and his song after his healing in 38:9–20.
q1: Assyria threatens Jerusalem, Hezekiah prays and the LORD delivers the city, and Hezekiah is healed after praying. After he recovers, Hezekiah writes, "The living, the living—they praise you, as I am doing today" (38:19). What does this reveal about the practice of gratitude?
q2: Hezekiah writes that the living praise God (38:19); Hebrews 13:15 (Day 340) says, "let us continually offer to God a sacrifice of praise—the fruit of lips that openly profess his name." How are these two passages similar or different? What does this reveal about God's people as those who offer a sacrifice of praise?
q3: In light of Hezekiah's song of thanks after his healing, how might gratitude take shape in your life this week?
identity: Those who offer a sacrifice of praise

article_title: What Does Isaiah 40:31 (Wings Like Eagles Verse) Mean?
main_theme: Hezekiah shows Babylon his treasures and Isaiah foretells exile; the LORD comforts his people, comes as a shepherd, and renews the strength of those who hope in him.
primary_threads: Exile and return; Creation and new creation; The people of God
pre_where: Hezekiah has been healed. Today envoys from Babylon visit him, and then the book's tone changes: "Comfort, comfort my people" (40:1).
pre_watch: Watch for Isaiah's words to Hezekiah in 39:5–7, the voice in 40:3, and the promise in 40:29–31.
q1: Hezekiah shows Babylon his treasures and Isaiah foretells exile; the LORD comforts his people, comes as a shepherd, and renews the strength of those who hope in him. Isaiah says, "those who hope in the LORD will renew their strength" (40:31). What does this reveal about the practice of hope?
q2: Mark begins his Gospel by quoting Isaiah 40:3: "a voice of one calling in the wilderness, 'Prepare the way for the Lord'" (Mark 1:2–3, Day 250). How does Mark use these words? Jesus then proclaims, "Repent and believe the good news!" (1:15); what does this reveal about God's people as those who believe the good news?
q3: In light of the promise that those who hope in the LORD will renew their strength, how might hope take shape in your life this week?
identity: Those who believe the good news

article_title: What Does Isaiah 41:10 (Do Not Fear, for I Am With You) Mean?
main_theme: The LORD presents his servant, on whom his Spirit rests, to bring justice to the nations; he promises to redeem Israel, pour out his Spirit, and exposes idols as nothing.
primary_threads: Exodus and redemption; The Spirit; The people of God; Creation and new creation
pre_where: The LORD has comforted his people. Today he presents his servant and promises to redeem Israel.
pre_watch: Watch for the servant in 42:1–4, the LORD's words to Israel in 43:1–2, and how idols are described in 44:9–20.
q1: The LORD presents his servant, on whom his Spirit rests, to bring justice to the nations; he promises to redeem Israel, pour out his Spirit, and exposes idols as nothing. The LORD tells Israel, "Do not fear, for I have redeemed you; I have summoned you by name; you are mine" (43:1). What does this reveal about the practice of trust?
q2: Matthew 12:17–21 (Day 241) quotes Isaiah 42:1–4 about Jesus: "Here is my servant whom I have chosen." How does Matthew use these words? The quotation ends, "In his name the nations will put their hope"; what does this reveal about God's people as those who put their hope in his name?
q3: In light of God's words, "I have summoned you by name; you are mine," how might trust take shape in your life this week?
identity: Those who put their hope in his name

main_theme: God names Cyrus his anointed to free the exiles, declares there is no other God, and calls Israel to leave Babylon.
primary_threads: Exile and return; Kingdom and kingship; Creation and new creation
pre_where: The LORD has promised to redeem Israel. Today he names Cyrus, a Persian king, as the one who will free the exiles.
pre_watch: Watch for what the LORD calls Cyrus in 45:1, the invitation in 45:22, and the call in 48:20.
q1: God names Cyrus his anointed to free the exiles, declares there is no other God, and calls Israel to leave Babylon. The LORD says, "Turn to me and be saved, all you ends of the earth; for I am God, and there is no other" (45:22). What does this reveal about the practice of worship?
q2: The LORD says, "Before me every knee will bow; by me every tongue will swear" (45:23). After describing every knee bowing and every tongue acknowledging Jesus as Lord, Paul calls his readers to obedience without grumbling or arguing (Philippians 2:10–15, Day 321). How does that response relate to Isaiah's call to turn to the LORD (Isaiah 45:22–23)? What does this reveal about God's people as those who shine like stars?
q3: In light of the LORD's call to turn to him, for there is no other God, how might worship take shape in your life this week?
identity: Those who shine like stars

main_theme: The servant is called to restore Israel and be a light to the nations; God has not forgotten Zion, and the servant does not turn back from suffering.
primary_threads: The people of God; Exile and return; Exodus and redemption
pre_where: The LORD has named Cyrus to free the exiles. Today the servant speaks, called to restore Israel and to be a light for the nations.
pre_watch: Watch for the servant's calling in 49:6, the LORD's answer to Zion in 49:14–16, and the servant's words in 50:4–7.
q1: The servant is called to restore Israel and be a light to the nations; God has not forgotten Zion, and the servant does not turn back from suffering. When Zion says, "The LORD has forsaken me," the LORD answers, "I will not forget you! See, I have engraved you on the palms of my hands" (49:14–16). What does this reveal about the practice of lament?
q2: Paul and Barnabas quote Isaiah 49:6, "I have made you a light for the Gentiles," as the Lord's command to them (Acts 13:47, Day 285). How do they use these words? Acts 13:52 says the disciples were filled with joy and with the Holy Spirit; what does this reveal about God's people as disciples filled with joy and the Holy Spirit?
q3: In light of Zion bringing her complaint and the LORD answering, how might lament take shape in your life this week?
identity: Disciples filled with joy and the Holy Spirit

main_theme: The LORD announces good news to Zion; his servant is despised and wounded and bears the sin of many, and the LORD promises a covenant of peace.
primary_threads: Sacrifice and atonement; Covenant; Exodus and redemption
pre_where: The servant has spoken of his calling and suffering. Today comes good news for Zion and the fullest description of the servant who suffers.
pre_watch: Watch for the messenger in 52:7, the description in 53:3–6, and the promise in 54:10.
q1: The LORD announces good news to Zion; his servant is despised and wounded and bears the sin of many, and the LORD promises a covenant of peace. Isaiah says, "How beautiful on the mountains are the feet of those who bring good news" (52:7). What does this reveal about the practice of witness?
q2: In Acts 8:30–35 (Day 282) an Ethiopian official reads Isaiah 53:7–8, and Philip, beginning with that very passage, tells him the good news about Jesus. How does Philip use this passage? Acts 8:4 says those who had been scattered preached the word wherever they went; what does this reveal about God's people as those who preach the word wherever they go?
q3: In light of Isaiah's picture of those who bring good news, how might witness take shape in your life this week?
identity: Those who preach the word wherever they go

main_theme: The LORD invites the thirsty to come, promises an everlasting covenant tied to his promises to David, welcomes foreigners who keep his covenant, and revives the contrite but rebukes idolatry.
primary_threads: Covenant; The people of God; Temple and God's presence
pre_where: Isaiah has described the suffering servant and a covenant of peace. Today the LORD invites everyone who is thirsty to come.
pre_watch: Watch for the invitation in 55:1–3, the comparison in 55:8–11, and the promise to foreigners in 56:6–7.
q1: The LORD invites the thirsty to come, promises an everlasting covenant tied to his promises to David, welcomes foreigners who keep his covenant, and revives the contrite but rebukes idolatry. Isaiah calls his hearers to seek the LORD while he may be found and call on him while he is near (55:6). What does this reveal about the practice of prayer?
q2: In the temple courts Jesus quotes Isaiah 56:7, "My house will be called a house of prayer for all nations" (Mark 11:15–17, Day 255). How does Jesus use these words? He later tells his disciples, "Have faith in God" (11:22); what does this reveal about God's people as those who have faith in God?
q3: In light of Isaiah's call to seek the LORD and call on him (55:6), how might prayer take shape in your life this week?
identity: Those who have faith in God

main_theme: God rejects fasting without justice; Israel's sins separate them from God, the Redeemer will come to Zion, and the nations will come to its light.
primary_threads: Law and wisdom; Exodus and redemption; The Spirit; Temple and God's presence
pre_where: The LORD has invited the thirsty to come. Today he answers a people who fast and ask why he does not notice.
pre_watch: Watch for the people's question in 58:3, the fast the LORD chooses in 58:6–7, and the light in 60:1–3.
q1: God rejects fasting without justice; Israel's sins separate them from God, the Redeemer will come to Zion, and the nations will come to its light. The LORD says the fast he chooses is to loose the chains of injustice, share food with the hungry and provide the poor wanderer with shelter (58:6–7). What does this reveal about the practice of justice and mercy?
q2: The LORD calls for sharing food with the hungry and clothing the naked (58:7). In Matthew 25:35–40 (Day 248) Jesus says, "I was hungry and you gave me something to eat." How are these two passages similar or different? Jesus calls them "you who are blessed by my Father" (25:34); what does this reveal about God's people as those blessed by the Father?
q3: In light of the fast the LORD chooses, how might justice and mercy take shape in your life this week?
identity: Those blessed by the Father
