main_theme: One anointed by the Spirit proclaims good news and freedom, Zion receives a new name, the LORD comes in judgment, and the people plead for him to come down.
primary_threads: The Spirit; Exodus and redemption; The day of the Lord
pre_where: The LORD has promised light for Zion. Today one anointed by the Spirit proclaims good news.
pre_watch: Watch for the speaker's mission in 61:1–3, the new name in 62:2–4, and the people's plea in 64:1 and 64:8.
q1: One anointed by the Spirit proclaims good news and freedom, Zion receives a new name, the LORD comes in judgment, and the people plead for him to come down. The people plead, "Oh, that you would rend the heavens and come down" (64:1). What does this reveal about the practice of prayer?
q2: Jesus reads Isaiah's announcement of good news to the poor and says it is fulfilled in their hearing (Luke 4:18–21, Day 269; Isaiah 61:1–2). What does this invite us to consider about God's people as those to whom good news is proclaimed?
q3: In light of the people's plea for the LORD to come down, how might prayer take shape in your life this week?
identity: Those to whom good news is proclaimed

main_theme: The LORD says he made himself available to those who did not ask for him, judges the rebellious, promises new heavens and a new earth, and gathers all nations to see his glory.
primary_threads: Creation and new creation; The day of the Lord; Temple and God's presence; The people of God
pre_where: The people have pleaded for the LORD to come down. Today he answers, and Isaiah ends with new heavens and a new earth.
pre_watch: Watch for what the LORD says in 65:1, the new heavens and new earth in 65:17–25, and the one the LORD esteems in 66:2.
q1: The LORD says he made himself available to those who did not ask for him, judges the rebellious, promises new heavens and a new earth, and gathers all nations to see his glory. The LORD says, "These are the ones I look on with favor: those who are humble and contrite in spirit, and who tremble at my word" (66:2). What does this reveal about the practice of humility?
q2: The LORD promises new heavens and a new earth (65:17). Second Peter 3:13 (Day 345) says, "in keeping with his promise we are looking forward to a new heaven and a new earth, where righteousness dwells." How does Peter echo this promise? What does this reveal about God's people as those who look forward to a new heaven and a new earth?
q3: In light of the LORD's favor on those who are humble and tremble at his word, how might humility take shape in your life this week?
identity: Those who look forward to a new heaven and a new earth

main_theme: The LORD appoints Jeremiah as a prophet to the nations and charges Judah with forsaking him for other gods, while calling unfaithful Israel to return.
primary_threads: Covenant; Blessing and curse; Exile and return; The people of God
pre_where: Isaiah has ended with new heavens and a new earth. Today the plan turns to Jeremiah, who prophesied in Judah from the reign of Josiah until Jerusalem's exile (1:1–3).
pre_watch: Watch for Jeremiah's objection and the LORD's answer in 1:6–8, the two sins in 2:13, and the call to return in 3:12–14.
q1: The LORD appoints Jeremiah as a prophet to the nations and charges Judah with forsaking him for other gods, while calling unfaithful Israel to return. The LORD says, "My people have committed two sins: They have forsaken me, the spring of living water, and have dug their own cisterns, broken cisterns that cannot hold water" (2:13). What does this reveal about the danger of forsaking the LORD for what cannot satisfy?
q2: The LORD calls himself "the spring of living water" (2:13). Revelation 22:17 (Day 358) invites the thirsty to "take the free gift of the water of life." How does this invitation relate to the LORD's description of himself in Jeremiah 2:13? How does Revelation portray the bride who joins the Spirit in saying "Come" (Revelation 21:2, 9–10; 22:17)?
q3: In light of the LORD's call to unfaithful Israel to return, how might repentance take shape in your life this week?
identity: The bride

main_theme: Jeremiah warns of disaster from the north, calls Judah to circumcise their hearts and wash the evil from them, and laments a people who refuse correction.
primary_threads: Blessing and curse; The people of God
pre_where: The LORD has called Israel to return. Today Jeremiah warns of disaster coming from the north.
pre_watch: Watch for the call in 4:3–4, the search in 5:1, and the ancient paths in 6:16.
q1: Jeremiah warns of disaster from the north, calls Judah to circumcise their hearts and wash the evil from them, and laments a people who refuse correction. The LORD calls the people to walk in the good way and find rest for their souls, but they answer that they will not walk in it (6:16). What does this reveal about the practice of obedience?
q2: Jesus says, "Take my yoke upon you and learn from me… and you will find rest for your souls" (Matthew 11:28–29, Day 241), echoing Jeremiah 6:16. How does Jesus use these words? He invites "all you who are weary and burdened"; what does this reveal about God's people as the weary who come to him?
q3: In light of the LORD's call to ask for the good way and walk in it, how might obedience take shape in your life this week?
identity: The weary who come to him

main_theme: At the temple gate Jeremiah condemns trust in the temple while injustice and idolatry continue, and he weeps over his people's coming judgment.
primary_threads: Temple and God's presence; Covenant; Blessing and curse; Law and wisdom
pre_where: Jeremiah has warned of disaster from the north. Today the LORD sends him to stand at the gate of the temple.
pre_watch: Watch for the words the people repeat in 7:4, what the LORD asks in 7:5–7, and what the LORD says to boast about in 9:23–24.
q1: At the temple gate Jeremiah condemns trust in the temple while injustice and idolatry continue, and he weeps over his people's coming judgment. The LORD calls people to boast in knowing him, and says that he exercises kindness, justice and righteousness on earth (9:24). What does this reveal about the practice of knowing God?
q2: Paul writes, "Let the one who boasts boast in the Lord" (1 Corinthians 1:31, Day 301), drawing on Jeremiah 9:24. How does Paul use these words? In 1:30 he says, "It is because of him that you are in Christ Jesus"; what does this reveal about God's people as those who are in Christ Jesus?
q3: In light of the LORD's words that the one who boasts should boast in knowing him, how might knowing God take shape in your life this week?
identity: Those who are in Christ Jesus

main_theme: Jeremiah contrasts the living God with idols, proclaims the broken covenant, faces plots against his life, and acts out Judah's ruin with a linen belt.
primary_threads: Covenant; Creation and new creation; Blessing and curse; Exile and return
pre_where: Jeremiah has stood at the temple gate. Today he contrasts the living God with idols and proclaims the broken covenant.
pre_watch: Watch for how idols are described in 10:3–5, Jeremiah's prayer in 10:23–24, his question in 12:1, and the linen belt in 13:1–11.
q1: Jeremiah contrasts the living God with idols, proclaims the broken covenant, faces plots against his life, and acts out Judah's ruin with a linen belt. Jeremiah says, "You are always righteous, LORD, when I bring a case before you. Yet I would speak with you about your justice: Why does the way of the wicked prosper?" (12:1). What does this reveal about the practice of lament?
q2: Jeremiah asks why the way of the wicked prospers (12:1); Psalm 73 (daily psalm, Day 73) describes envy at "the prosperity of the wicked" (73:3) until the psalmist enters the sanctuary of God (73:17). How are these two responses similar or different? Psalm 73:1 says, "Surely God is good to Israel, to those who are pure in heart"; what does this reveal about God's people as the pure in heart?
q3: In light of Jeremiah bringing his honest question to the LORD, how might lament take shape in your life this week?
identity: The pure in heart

main_theme: Amid drought the LORD refuses to hear prayers for Judah; Jeremiah laments his calling, and the LORD promises a new exodus and calls Judah to trust him and keep the Sabbath.
primary_threads: Blessing and curse; Exile and return; Exodus and redemption; Law and wisdom
pre_where: Jeremiah has acted out Judah's ruin with a linen belt. Today a drought falls on the land.
pre_watch: Watch for the people's confession in 14:7–9, Jeremiah's complaint in 15:15–18 and the LORD's answer in 15:19–21, and the two pictures in 17:5–8.
q1: Amid drought the LORD refuses to hear prayers for Judah; Jeremiah laments his calling, and the LORD promises a new exodus and calls Judah to trust him and keep the Sabbath. The one who trusts in the LORD is like a tree planted by the water that sends out its roots by the stream (17:7–8). What does this reveal about the practice of trust?
q2: Jeremiah describes the one who trusts in the LORD as a tree planted by the water (17:7–8); Psalm 1 (daily psalm, Day 1) uses the same picture for the one whose delight is in the law of the LORD (1:2–3). How are these two pictures similar or different? What does this reveal about God's people as those who delight in the law of the LORD?
q3: In light of the picture of a tree planted by the water, how might trust take shape in your life this week?
identity: Those who delight in the law of the LORD

main_theme: At the potter's house the LORD speaks of uprooting or building nations according to their response; Jeremiah breaks a jar, is beaten and put in stocks, and warns Judah's kings.
primary_threads: Kingdom and kingship; Blessing and curse; Exile and return
pre_where: Drought has fallen on Judah, and Jeremiah has called them to trust the LORD. Today the LORD sends him to watch a potter at work.
pre_watch: Watch for what the LORD says in 18:6–10, Jeremiah's complaint in 20:7–9, and the LORD's words about Josiah in 22:15–16.
q1: At the potter's house the LORD speaks of uprooting or building nations according to their response; Jeremiah breaks a jar, is beaten and put in stocks, and warns Judah's kings. The LORD says of King Josiah, "He defended the cause of the poor and needy… Is that not what it means to know me?" (22:16). What does this reveal about the practice of justice and mercy?
q2: The LORD says that defending the poor and needy is what it means to know him (22:16). First John 3:17–18 (Day 347) says, "let us not love with words or speech but with actions and in truth." How are these two passages similar or different? First John 3:14 says, "We know that we have passed from death to life, because we love each other"; what does this reveal about God's people as those who have passed from death to life?
q3: In light of the LORD's words about defending the poor and needy, how might justice and mercy take shape in your life this week?
identity: Those who have passed from death to life

main_theme: The LORD condemns false shepherds and prophets, promises a righteous Branch from David's line, and announces seventy years of service to the king of Babylon.
primary_threads: Kingdom and kingship; The promised Messiah; Exile and return
pre_where: Jeremiah has warned Judah's kings. Today the LORD condemns the shepherds who scatter his flock and promises a righteous Branch.
pre_watch: Watch for the promise in 23:5–6, the contrast between dreams and the LORD's word in 23:28–29, and the good figs in 24:5–7.
q1: The LORD condemns false shepherds and prophets, promises a righteous Branch from David's line, and announces seventy years of service to the king of Babylon. The LORD says, "let the one who has my word speak it faithfully" (23:28). What does this reveal about the practice of speaking the truth?
q2: The LORD condemns the shepherds who scatter his flock and promises to place shepherds over them who will tend them (23:1–4). In John 10:11–16 (Day 262) Jesus says, "I am the good shepherd." How are these two passages similar or different? Jesus speaks of "one flock and one shepherd" (10:16); what does this reveal about God's people as one flock?
q3: In light of the LORD's call to speak his word faithfully, how might speaking the truth take shape in your life this week?
identity: One flock

article_title: What Does Jeremiah 29:11 Mean? (“For I Know the Plans I Have for You”)
main_theme: Jeremiah is threatened with death for speaking against the temple, wears a yoke, confronts the prophet Hananiah, and writes to the exiles to seek Babylon's welfare.
primary_threads: Exile and return; Temple and God's presence; The people of God
pre_where: The LORD has announced seventy years of service to Babylon's king. Today Jeremiah is threatened with death for his words about the temple.
pre_watch: Watch for the elders' defense of Jeremiah in 26:17–19, the yoke in chapters 27–28, and Jeremiah's letter to the exiles in 29:4–14.
q1: Jeremiah is threatened with death for speaking against the temple, wears a yoke, confronts the prophet Hananiah, and writes to the exiles to seek Babylon's welfare. In Jeremiah's letter the LORD tells the exiles, "seek the peace and prosperity of the city to which I have carried you into exile. Pray to the LORD for it" (29:7). What does this reveal about the practice of prayer?
q2: Jeremiah's letter tells the exiles to seek the peace of the city where they live and pray for it (29:7). First Peter 2:11–12 (Day 343) addresses believers "as foreigners and exiles" and urges them to live such good lives among their neighbors that they glorify God. How are these two passages similar or different? What does this reveal about God's people as foreigners and exiles?
q3: In light of the call to seek the peace of the city and pray for it, how might prayer take shape in your life this week?
identity: Foreigners and exiles

main_theme: The LORD promises to restore Israel and Judah, make a new covenant written on their hearts, and raise up a righteous Branch; Jeremiah buys a field, for fields will again be bought in the land.
primary_threads: Covenant; Exile and return; The promised Messiah; Kingdom and kingship
pre_where: Jeremiah has written to the exiles. Today the LORD speaks of restoring Israel and Judah and of a new covenant.
pre_watch: Watch for the new covenant in 31:31–34, the field Jeremiah buys in 32:6–15, and his prayer in 32:17.
q1: The LORD promises to restore Israel and Judah, make a new covenant written on their hearts, and raise up a righteous Branch; Jeremiah buys a field, for fields will again be bought in the land. The LORD tells Jeremiah to buy a field, for "Houses, fields and vineyards will again be bought in this land" (32:15). What does this reveal about the practice of hope?
q2: The LORD promises a new covenant, with his law written on their hearts (Jeremiah 31:31–34). In 2 Corinthians 3:2–6 (Day 310) Paul tells the Corinthians, "You show that you are a letter from Christ… written not with ink but with the Spirit of the living God," and describes his own ministry as service of a new covenant. How does Paul describe the Corinthians as a letter written by the Spirit, and his ministry as service of a new covenant? What does this reveal about God's people as a letter from Christ?
q3: In light of the field Jeremiah buys as a sign that the land will be restored, how might hope take shape in your life this week?
identity: A letter from Christ

main_theme: Judah breaks its covenant to free Hebrew slaves, the Rekabites are commended for obeying their ancestor's commands, and King Jehoiakim burns Jeremiah's scroll, which is written again.
primary_threads: Covenant; Law and wisdom; Kingdom and kingship
pre_where: The LORD has promised restoration and a new covenant. Today Judah breaks a covenant to free its slaves, and King Jehoiakim hears Jeremiah's scroll read.
pre_watch: Watch for what the people do in 34:8–11, the Rekabites' answer in 35:6–10, and what the king does with the scroll in 36:23–24.
q1: Judah breaks its covenant to free Hebrew slaves, the Rekabites are commended for obeying their ancestor's commands, and King Jehoiakim burns Jeremiah's scroll, which is written again. The Rekabites keep their ancestor's command, and the LORD contrasts them with Judah, who has not obeyed him (35:14). What does this reveal about the practice of obedience?
q2: Jehoiakim cuts up and burns the scroll, yet the LORD has the words written again (36:23, 27–28). Hebrews 4:12–13 (Day 336) says, "the word of God is alive and active." How do Jeremiah 36:23, 27–28 and Hebrews 4:12–13 describe responses to God's word? How does Hebrews 4:14–16 invite its hearers to approach God? What does this reveal about God's people as those who approach the throne of grace with confidence?
q3: In light of the LORD's contrast between the Rekabites' faithfulness and Judah's disobedience, how might obedience take shape in your life this week?
identity: Those who approach the throne of grace with confidence

main_theme: Jeremiah is imprisoned and thrown into a cistern, urges King Zedekiah to surrender, and Jerusalem falls to Babylon.
primary_threads: Exile and return; Kingdom and kingship; Blessing and curse
pre_where: Jehoiakim has burned the scroll. Today, under King Zedekiah, Jeremiah is imprisoned as Babylon's army besieges Jerusalem.
pre_watch: Watch for Zedekiah's secret question in 37:17, what Ebed-Melek does in 38:7–13, and the LORD's word to him in 39:15–18.
q1: Jeremiah is imprisoned and thrown into a cistern, urges King Zedekiah to surrender, and Jerusalem falls to Babylon. Ebed-Melek, a Cushite official, goes to the king and has Jeremiah lifted out of the cistern (38:7–13). What does this reveal about the practice of justice and mercy?
q2: Ebed-Melek rescues Jeremiah from the cistern (38:7–13). Hebrews 13:3 (Day 340) says, "Continue to remember those in prison as if you were together with them in prison." How are these two passages similar or different? Hebrews 13:1 says, "Keep on loving one another as brothers and sisters"; what does this reveal about God's people as brothers and sisters?
q3: In light of Ebed-Melek acting to rescue Jeremiah, how might justice and mercy take shape in your life this week?
identity: Brothers and sisters

main_theme: After Jerusalem falls, Gedaliah is murdered, and the remnant flees to Egypt against the LORD's word, taking Jeremiah, and worships other gods there.
primary_threads: Exile and return; The people of God; Blessing and curse
pre_where: Jerusalem has fallen to Babylon. Today Gedaliah is appointed governor over those left in the land.
pre_watch: Watch for the people's promise in 42:5–6, the LORD's answer in 42:10–12, and what they do in 43:1–7.
q1: After Jerusalem falls, Gedaliah is murdered, and the remnant flees to Egypt against the LORD's word, taking Jeremiah, and worships other gods there. The people promise to obey whatever the LORD says, then refuse his answer and go to Egypt (42:5–6; 43:4–7). What does their promise and subsequent refusal reveal about the danger of seeking God's guidance but not following it?
q2: The people promise to obey the LORD and then refuse (42:5–6; 43:4). In Matthew 21:28–31 (Day 246) Jesus tells of a son who says, "I will, sir," but does not go. How are these two accounts similar or different? Jesus speaks of the kingdom given to "a people who will produce its fruit" (21:43); what does this reveal about God's people as a people who produce the kingdom's fruit?
q3: In light of the remnant's broken promise to obey, how might obedience take shape in your life this week?
identity: A people who produce the kingdom's fruit

main_theme: The LORD promises Baruch his life, and Jeremiah announces judgment on Egypt, Philistia and Moab, with a promise of restoration for Moab.
primary_threads: The day of the Lord; Exile and return; Exodus and redemption
pre_where: The remnant has fled to Egypt. Today the LORD speaks a word to Baruch, Jeremiah's scribe, and then Jeremiah announces judgment on the nations.
pre_watch: Watch for Baruch's complaint and the LORD's answer in 45:3–5, the promise to Jacob in 46:27–28, and the promise for Moab in 48:47.
q1: The LORD promises Baruch his life, and Jeremiah announces judgment on Egypt, Philistia and Moab, with a promise of restoration for Moab. The LORD tells Baruch, "Should you then seek great things for yourself? Do not seek them" (45:5). What does this reveal about the practice of humility?
q2: The LORD tells Baruch not to seek great things for himself (45:5). In Matthew 6:31–33 (Day 238) Jesus says, "seek first his kingdom and his righteousness." How are these two passages similar or different? What does this reveal about God's people as those who seek first his kingdom?
q3: In light of the LORD's word to Baruch not to seek great things for himself, how might humility take shape in your life this week?
identity: Those who seek first his kingdom

main_theme: Judgment is announced on Ammon, Edom, Damascus, Kedar, Elam and Babylon, and Israel will return seeking the LORD in an everlasting covenant.
primary_threads: Exile and return; Covenant; Exodus and redemption
pre_where: Jeremiah has announced judgment on Egypt, Philistia and Moab. Today he turns to Ammon, Edom, Damascus, Kedar and Elam, and then to Babylon.
pre_watch: Watch for the promises for Ammon and Elam in 49:6 and 49:39, the return in 50:4–5, and the Redeemer in 50:34.
q1: Judgment is announced on Ammon, Edom, Damascus, Kedar, Elam and Babylon, and Israel will return seeking the LORD in an everlasting covenant. The people of Israel and Judah will come in tears to seek the LORD and bind themselves to him in an everlasting covenant (50:4–5). What does this reveal about the practice of repentance?
q2: The LORD says, "My people have been lost sheep" (50:6), and that they will come seeking him (50:4–5). First Peter 2:25 (Day 343) says, "you were like sheep going astray, but now you have returned to the Shepherd and Overseer of your souls." How are these two passages similar or different? What does this reveal about God's people as those who have returned to the Shepherd?
q3: In light of the people coming in tears to seek the LORD, how might repentance take shape in your life this week?
identity: Those who have returned to the Shepherd

main_theme: Babylon will fall and God's people must flee it; Jerusalem's fall and the temple's burning are retold, and King Jehoiachin is released in Babylon.
primary_threads: Exile and return; Temple and God's presence; Kingdom and kingship
pre_where: Jeremiah has announced Babylon's fall. Today the oracle against Babylon continues, and the book ends by retelling the fall of Jerusalem.
pre_watch: Watch for the call to flee in 51:6 and 51:45, the scroll Seraiah reads in 51:59–64, and Jehoiachin's release in 52:31–34.
q1: Babylon will fall and God's people must flee it; Jerusalem's fall and the temple's burning are retold, and King Jehoiachin is released in Babylon. The LORD calls his people to flee Babylon and remember him (51:45, 50). What does this reveal about the practice of holiness?
q2: Revelation 18:2–5 (Day 356) echoes Jeremiah's words: "Fallen is Babylon the Great!… Come out of her, my people," so that you will not share in her sins. How does Revelation use Jeremiah's call? Revelation 17:14 speaks of the Lamb's "called, chosen and faithful followers"; what does this reveal about God's people as called, chosen and faithful followers?
q3: How might remembering the LORD and turning away from wrongdoing shape your practice of holiness this week?
identity: Called, chosen and faithful followers

main_theme: Among the exiles, Ezekiel sees the glory of the LORD on a throne and is commissioned as a watchman to rebellious Israel.
primary_threads: Temple and God's presence; Exile and return; The Spirit
pre_where: Jeremiah ended with Jerusalem fallen and the exiles in Babylon. Ezekiel, a priest, is among those exiles by the Kebar River when the heavens open (1:1–3).
pre_watch: Watch for the throne in 1:26–28, the scroll Ezekiel eats in 3:1–3, and the watchman's task in 3:17–19.
q1: Among the exiles, Ezekiel sees the glory of the LORD on a throne and is commissioned as a watchman to rebellious Israel. When he sees the likeness of the glory of the LORD, Ezekiel falls facedown (1:28). What does this reveal about the practice of worship?
q2: Ezekiel sees a throne, living creatures and a radiance like a rainbow (1:5, 26–28); in Revelation 4:2–8 (Day 351) John sees a throne encircled by a rainbow and four living creatures. How are these two visions similar or different? In Revelation 4:10–11 the elders fall down and worship him who sits on the throne; what does this reveal about God's people as those who worship him who sits on the throne?
q3: In light of Ezekiel falling facedown before the LORD's glory, how might worship take shape in your life this week?
identity: Those who worship him who sits on the throne

main_theme: Ezekiel acts out Jerusalem's siege and announces that the end has come on the land because of its idolatry.
primary_threads: Blessing and curse; The day of the Lord; Exile and return
pre_where: Ezekiel has been commissioned as a watchman among the exiles. Today the LORD tells him to act out the siege of Jerusalem.
pre_watch: Watch for the clay tablet and the days Ezekiel lies on his side in 4:1–6, the hair divided in 5:1–4, and the phrase repeated in 6:7, 10, 13–14.
q1: Ezekiel acts out Jerusalem's siege and announces that the end has come on the land because of its idolatry. The LORD says the survivors will remember him and loathe themselves for the evil they have done (6:9). What does this reveal about the practice of repentance?
q2: The LORD says the survivors will remember him and loathe themselves for their evil (6:9). In Revelation 3:19 (Day 350) Jesus says, "Those whom I love I rebuke and discipline. So be earnest and repent." How are these two passages similar or different? What does this reveal about God's people as those whom he loves?
q3: In light of the survivors remembering the LORD and recognizing their evil, how might repentance take shape in your life this week?
identity: Those whom he loves

main_theme: In a vision Ezekiel sees idolatry in the temple and the LORD's glory leaving it, yet God promises to gather the exiles and give them a new heart and spirit.
primary_threads: Temple and God's presence; Exile and return; The Spirit; Covenant
pre_where: Ezekiel has acted out Jerusalem's siege. Today, in a vision, he is taken to the temple in Jerusalem.
pre_watch: Watch for what the elders say in 8:12, the mark on those who grieve in 9:4, the glory leaving in 10:18–19 and 11:22–23, and the promise in 11:19–20.
q1: In a vision Ezekiel sees idolatry in the temple and the LORD's glory leaving it, yet God promises to gather the exiles and give them a new heart and spirit. The LORD has a mark put on those who grieve and lament over all the detestable things done in Jerusalem (9:4). What does this reveal about the practice of lament?
q2: In Ezekiel's vision a mark is put on the foreheads of those who grieve over the city's evil (9:4). In Revelation 7:3 (Day 352) a seal is put on the foreheads of "the servants of our God." How are these two visions similar or different? What does this reveal about God's people as the servants of our God?
q3: In light of the LORD marking those who grieve over evil, how might lament take shape in your life this week?
identity: The servants of our God

main_theme: Ezekiel acts out exile, condemns false prophets and elders who set up idols in their hearts, and declares that even Noah, Daniel and Job could save only themselves.
primary_threads: Exile and return; Blessing and curse
pre_where: Ezekiel has seen the LORD's glory leave the temple. Today he acts out going into exile.
pre_watch: Watch for the proverb in 12:22–25, the whitewashed wall in 13:10–12, and the elders' idols in their hearts in 14:3.
q1: Ezekiel acts out exile, condemns false prophets and elders who set up idols in their hearts, and declares that even Noah, Daniel and Job could save only themselves. The LORD says the elders have set up idols in their hearts and calls Israel to turn away from its idols (14:3, 6). What does this reveal about the dangers of divided worship?
q2: The elders have set up idols in their hearts (14:3). Paul prays "that Christ may dwell in your hearts through faith" (Ephesians 3:16–17, Day 319). How are these two passages similar or different? What does this reveal about God's people as those in whose hearts Christ dwells?
q3: In light of the LORD's warning against idols in the heart, how might worship take shape in your life this week?
identity: Those in whose hearts Christ dwells

main_theme: Jerusalem is pictured as a useless vine and an unfaithful wife, yet God will remember his covenant; a parable of eagles ends with a tender shoot planted on a high mountain.
primary_threads: Covenant; Kingdom and kingship; The people of God
pre_where: Ezekiel has warned against idols in the heart. Today the LORD pictures Jerusalem as a useless vine and as an unfaithful wife.
pre_watch: Watch for what the LORD did for Jerusalem in 16:6–14, the covenant he will remember in 16:60–63, and the tender shoot in 17:22–24.
q1: Jerusalem is pictured as a useless vine and an unfaithful wife, yet God will remember his covenant; a parable of eagles ends with a tender shoot planted on a high mountain. The LORD says, "I will remember the covenant I made with you in the days of your youth," and that Jerusalem will remember and be ashamed (16:60–63). What does this reveal about the practice of humility?
q2: Ezekiel pictures Jerusalem as a vine that is useless for anything (15:1–8). In John 15:1–6 (Day 264) Jesus says, "I am the vine; you are the branches." How are these two pictures similar or different? What does this reveal about God's people as branches that remain in the vine?
q3: In light of the LORD remembering his covenant despite Jerusalem's unfaithfulness, how might humility take shape in your life this week?
identity: Branches that remain in the vine

main_theme: Each person is responsible for their own sin and God takes no pleasure in the death of the wicked; Israel's rebellious history is recounted, with a promise to gather them.
primary_threads: Law and wisdom; Exile and return; Exodus and redemption; Covenant
pre_where: The LORD has promised to remember his covenant. Today he answers a proverb the exiles repeat about sour grapes.
pre_watch: Watch for the proverb in 18:2, the LORD's words in 18:23 and 18:30–32, and the retelling of Israel's history in chapter 20.
q1: Each person is responsible for their own sin and God takes no pleasure in the death of the wicked; Israel's rebellious history is recounted, with a promise to gather them. The LORD says, "Repent and live!" and calls them to get a new heart and a new spirit (18:31–32). What does this reveal about the practice of repentance?
q2: The LORD says he takes no pleasure in the death of the wicked, calls them to get a new heart and a new spirit, and says, "Repent and live!" (18:23, 31–32). Paul writes that "God's kindness is intended to lead you to repentance" and speaks of "circumcision of the heart, by the Spirit" (Romans 2:4, 28–29, Day 293). How might the call to get a new heart and spirit relate to Paul's description of circumcision of the heart by the Spirit? What does this reveal about God's people as those whose hearts are circumcised by the Spirit?
q3: In light of the LORD's call to repent and live, how might repentance take shape in your life this week?
identity: Those whose hearts are circumcised by the Spirit

main_theme: Babylon's sword is drawn against Jerusalem, its sins are listed, two unfaithful sisters picture Samaria and Jerusalem, and Ezekiel's wife dies as a sign of the sanctuary's loss and their response.
primary_threads: Blessing and curse; Exile and return
pre_where: The LORD has called the exiles to repent and live. Today Babylon's sword is drawn against Jerusalem.
pre_watch: Watch for the LORD's search in 22:30, and what the LORD tells Ezekiel about his wife's death and the people's response in 24:15–24.
q1: Babylon's sword is drawn against Jerusalem, its sins are listed, two unfaithful sisters picture Samaria and Jerusalem, and Ezekiel's wife dies as a sign of the sanctuary's loss and their response. The LORD looks for someone who would build up the wall and stand before him in the gap on behalf of the land, but finds no one (22:30). What might this search for someone to stand before the LORD on behalf of the land invite us to consider about intercessory prayer?
q2: The LORD looks for someone to stand in the gap on behalf of the land (22:30). Romans 8:26–27, 34 (Day 296) says the Spirit intercedes for God's people and that Christ Jesus is at the right hand of God interceding for us. How are these two passages similar or different? Romans 8:14 says "those who are led by the Spirit of God are the children of God"; what does this reveal about God's people as those led by the Spirit?
q3: In light of the LORD looking for someone to stand in the gap, how might prayer take shape in your life this week?
identity: Those led by the Spirit

main_theme: Judgment is announced on Ammon, Moab, Edom, Philistia, Tyre and Sidon, including a lament over the pride and fall of the king of Tyre.
primary_threads: Kingdom and kingship; Blessing and curse
pre_where: Babylon's sword has been drawn against Jerusalem. Today Ezekiel announces judgment on the nations around Israel, ending with Tyre and Sidon.
pre_watch: Watch for the reason given for Ammon's judgment in 25:3–6, Tyre's words in 26:2, and the king of Tyre's claim in 28:2.
q1: Judgment is announced on Ammon, Moab, Edom, Philistia, Tyre and Sidon, including a lament over the pride and fall of the king of Tyre. Ammon clapped and rejoiced with malice at the ruin of the land of Israel (25:6). What does this reveal about the danger of rejoicing at others' downfall?
q2: Ammon rejoices with malice over Israel's ruin (25:6). In Matthew 5:44–45 (Day 238) Jesus says, "Love your enemies and pray for those who persecute you, that you may be children of your Father in heaven." How are these two responses to others' trouble similar or different? What does this reveal about God's people as children of the Father in heaven?
q3: In light of the LORD's judgment on those who rejoiced at Israel's ruin, how might kindness take shape in your life this week?
identity: Children of the Father in heaven

main_theme: The LORD announces judgment on Pharaoh and Egypt for Pharaoh's claim over the Nile and Egypt's failure as a support to Israel; the day of the LORD is near.
primary_threads: The day of the Lord; Kingdom and kingship
pre_where: Ezekiel has announced judgment on Tyre and Sidon. Today he turns to Pharaoh and Egypt.
pre_watch: Watch for Pharaoh's claim in 29:3, what Egypt was to Israel in 29:6–7, and the day of the LORD in 30:3.
q1: The LORD announces judgment on Pharaoh and Egypt for Pharaoh's claim over the Nile and Egypt's failure as a support to Israel; the day of the LORD is near. Pharaoh says, "The Nile belongs to me; I made it for myself" (29:3). What does this reveal about the danger of claiming as our own what God has made?
q2: Pharaoh says, "The Nile belongs to me; I made it for myself" (29:3). In Luke 12:16–21 (Day 273) Jesus tells of a rich man who stores up things for himself but is not rich toward God, and then teaches, "Do not be afraid, little flock, for your Father has been pleased to give you the kingdom. Sell your possessions and give to the poor" (12:31–33). How does Jesus' teaching about possessions and the Father's gift of the kingdom contrast with Pharaoh's claim? What does this reveal about God's people as the little flock?
q3: In light of Pharaoh's claim that the Nile was his own, how might stewardship take shape in your life this week?
identity: The little flock

main_theme: Pharaoh is pictured as a great cedar cut down, laments are raised over Egypt, Ezekiel is again appointed watchman, and news of Jerusalem's fall reaches him.
primary_threads: Kingdom and kingship; Exile and return; Blessing and curse
pre_where: Ezekiel has announced judgment on Egypt. Today he pictures Pharaoh as a great cedar cut down, and then news arrives that Jerusalem has fallen.
pre_watch: Watch for the watchman's task in 33:1–9, the LORD's words in 33:11, and how the people listen in 33:30–32.
q1: Pharaoh is pictured as a great cedar cut down, laments are raised over Egypt, Ezekiel is again appointed watchman, and news of Jerusalem's fall reaches him. The people come to hear Ezekiel's words but do not put them into practice; to them he is like one who sings love songs (33:31–32). What does this reveal about the danger of hearing God's word without putting it into practice?
q2: The people hear Ezekiel's words but do not put them into practice (33:31–32). In Luke 6:46–49 (Day 270) Jesus asks, "Why do you call me, 'Lord, Lord,' and do not do what I say?" How are these two passages similar or different? Jesus compares the one who hears and does his words to a man who builds on rock; what does this reveal about God's people as those who build on the rock?
q3: In light of the people hearing but not practicing what they heard, how might obedience take shape in your life this week?
identity: Those who build on the rock

main_theme: God condemns Israel's shepherds and promises to shepherd his flock through his servant David, give them new hearts and his Spirit, and bring the dry bones to life.
primary_threads: Kingdom and kingship; The Spirit; Covenant; Exile and return; The promised Messiah; Temple and God's presence
pre_where: News of Jerusalem's fall has reached the exiles. Today the LORD condemns Israel's shepherds and promises to shepherd his flock himself.
pre_watch: Watch for what the LORD says he will do in 34:11–16, the new heart and spirit in 36:26–27, and the dry bones in 37:1–14.
q1: God condemns Israel's shepherds and promises to shepherd his flock through his servant David, give them new hearts and his Spirit, and bring the dry bones to life. When the people say, "Our bones are dried up and our hope is gone," the LORD promises, "I will put my Spirit in you and you will live" (37:11, 14). What does this reveal about the practice of hope?
q2: The LORD promises, "I will give you a new heart and put a new spirit in you" (36:26–27). In John 3:5–8 (Day 259) Jesus tells Nicodemus that no one can enter the kingdom of God unless they are born of water and the Spirit. How are these two passages similar or different? What does this reveal about God's people as those born of the Spirit?
q3: In light of the LORD's answer to the people's words, "our hope is gone," how might hope take shape in your life this week?
identity: Those born of the Spirit

article_title: The Exalted Horn of Psalm 148
main_theme: The LORD announces that Gog of Magog will attack a restored Israel and be defeated, and promises to pour out his Spirit and no longer hide his face from his people.
primary_threads: The day of the Lord; The Spirit; Exile and return
pre_where: The LORD has promised new life for his people. Today Ezekiel prophesies against Gog, of the land of Magog.
pre_watch: Watch for when the attack is said to come in 38:8, the purpose given in 38:23, and the promise in 39:25–29.
q1: The LORD announces that Gog of Magog will attack a restored Israel and be defeated, and promises to pour out his Spirit and no longer hide his face from his people. The LORD says, "I will show my greatness and my holiness, and I will make myself known in the sight of many nations. Then they will know that I am the LORD" (38:23). What does this reveal about the practice of knowing God?
q2: The LORD promises he will no longer hide his face from his people (39:29). Paul writes that God "made his light shine in our hearts to give us the light of the knowledge of God's glory displayed in the face of Christ" (2 Corinthians 4:6, Day 310). How are these two passages similar or different? Paul continues, "we have this treasure in jars of clay" (4:7); what does this reveal about God's people as jars of clay?
q3: In light of the LORD making himself known so that the nations will know him, how might knowing God take shape in your life this week?
identity: Jars of clay

main_theme: In a vision Ezekiel is shown a new temple and sees the glory of the LORD return to fill it.
primary_threads: Temple and God's presence; Sacrifice and atonement
pre_where: The prophecy against Gog has ended with the promise of the Spirit. Today, in the twenty-fifth year of exile, Ezekiel is shown a vision of a temple (40:1–2).
pre_watch: Watch for the measuring of the temple in chapters 40–42, the glory returning in 43:1–5, and what the LORD says in 43:7 and 43:12.
q1: In a vision Ezekiel is shown a new temple and sees the glory of the LORD return to fill it. The LORD says the whole area on top of the mountain will be most holy: "Such is the law of the temple" (43:12). What does this reveal about the practice of holiness?
q2: Ezekiel watches a man measure the temple (40:3–5); in Revelation 21:15–22 (Day 358) an angel measures the holy city, and John sees no temple there, "because the Lord God Almighty and the Lamb are its temple." How are these two visions similar or different? Revelation 21:27 says only "those whose names are written in the Lamb's book of life" will enter; what does this reveal about God's people as those whose names are written in the Lamb's book of life?
q3: In light of the law that the whole area of the temple is most holy, how might holiness take shape in your life this week?
identity: Those whose names are written in the Lamb's book of life

main_theme: The vision sets out duties for priests, offerings and the division of the land; a river flowing from the temple brings life, and the city is named "The LORD is there."
primary_threads: Temple and God's presence; The people of God; Sacrifice and atonement; Law and wisdom
pre_where: Ezekiel has seen the LORD's glory fill the temple. Today the vision continues with the priests' duties, the offerings and the division of the land.
pre_watch: Watch for what the priests are to teach in 44:23, the river in 47:1–12, and the city's name in 48:35.
q1: The vision sets out duties for priests, offerings and the division of the land; a river flowing from the temple brings life, and the city is named "The LORD is there." The land is to be divided with the foreigners who live among them, who are to be treated as native-born Israelites (47:22). What does this reveal about the practice of hospitality?
q2: In Ezekiel's vision a river flows from the temple, with trees whose leaves are for healing (47:1–12). In Revelation 22:1–2 (Day 358) the river of the water of life flows from the throne, and the leaves of the tree of life are "for the healing of the nations." Revelation 22:14 says, "Blessed are those who wash their robes, that they may have the right to the tree of life and may go through the gates into the city." How does the promise of access to the tree of life in verse 14 relate to the vision in verses 1–2? What does this reveal about God's people as those who wash their robes?
q3: In light of the command to treat the foreigners among them as native-born, how might hospitality take shape in your life this week?
identity: Those who wash their robes

main_theme: Hosea marries Gomer, and the LORD likens Israel's departure from him to marital unfaithfulness; he promises to woo Israel back and charges priests and people with rejecting knowledge.
primary_threads: Covenant; Blessing and curse; The people of God; The promised Messiah
pre_where: Ezekiel's vision ended with a city named "The LORD is there." Today the plan turns to Hosea, who prophesied to the northern kingdom of Israel (1:1).
pre_watch: Watch for the children's names in 1:6–9, the LORD's promise in 2:14–23, and the charge in 4:1 and 4:6.
q1: Hosea marries Gomer, and the LORD likens Israel's departure from him to marital unfaithfulness; he promises to woo Israel back and charges priests and people with rejecting knowledge. The LORD says, "my people are destroyed from lack of knowledge" (4:6). What does this reveal about the practice of knowing God?
q2: The LORD names Hosea's children Lo-Ruhamah and Lo-Ammi (1:6, 9), then promises, "I will say to those called 'Not my people,' 'You are my people'" (2:23). First Peter 2:10 (Day 343) says, "Once you were not a people, but now you are the people of God." How does Peter echo Hosea? What does this reveal about God's people as the people of God?
q3: In light of the LORD's charge that his people lacked knowledge of him, how might knowing God take shape in your life this week?
identity: The people of God

main_theme: Israel's love vanishes like morning mist; God desires mercy, not sacrifice, and announces judgment on their kings, idols and foreign alliances.
primary_threads: Sacrifice and atonement; Covenant; Kingdom and kingship; Blessing and curse; Exile and return
pre_where: The LORD has charged Israel with lacking knowledge of him. Today he speaks of their love vanishing like the morning mist.
pre_watch: Watch for the people's words in 6:1–3, the LORD's answer in 6:4–6, and the call in 10:12.
q1: Israel's love vanishes like morning mist; God desires mercy, not sacrifice, and announces judgment on their kings, idols and foreign alliances. The LORD says, "I desire mercy, not sacrifice, and acknowledgment of God rather than burnt offerings" (6:6). What does this reveal about the practice of justice and mercy?
q2: Jesus quotes Hosea 6:6 when he is criticized for eating with tax collectors and sinners: "Go and learn what this means: 'I desire mercy, not sacrifice'" (Matthew 9:10–13, Day 240). How does Jesus use these words? He says, "I have not come to call the righteous, but sinners"; what does this reveal about God's people as sinners whom Jesus calls?
q3: In light of the LORD's words that he desires mercy, not sacrifice, how might justice and mercy take shape in your life this week?
identity: Sinners whom Jesus calls

main_theme: God remembers loving Israel as a child brought out of Egypt, cannot give them up, and calls them to return, promising healing.
primary_threads: Exodus and redemption; Exile and return; Blessing and curse
pre_where: The LORD has desired mercy, not sacrifice. Today he remembers loving Israel as a child.
pre_watch: Watch for the LORD's words in 11:1–4 and 11:8–9, the call to return in 14:1–2, and the promise in 14:4.
q1: God remembers loving Israel as a child brought out of Egypt, cannot give them up, and calls them to return, promising healing. Hosea calls, "Return, Israel, to the LORD your God… Take words with you and return to the LORD" (14:1–2). What does this reveal about the practice of repentance?
q2: Matthew quotes Hosea's words about Israel when recounting Jesus' stay in Egypt and return (Hosea 11:1; Matthew 2:14–15, 19–21, Day 236). How does Matthew use these words? How does Galatians 4:4–7 (Day 316) describe the relationship to God of those who receive adoption through his Son?
q3: In light of Hosea's call to return to the LORD with words of repentance, how might repentance take shape in your life this week?
identity: God's children through adoption

main_theme: A locust plague devastates the land; Joel announces the day of the LORD, calls the people to return with all their heart, and records God's promise to pour out his Spirit.
primary_threads: The day of the Lord; The Spirit; Blessing and curse; Exile and return
pre_where: Hosea has called Israel to return. Today the prophet Joel describes a locust plague that has devastated the land.
pre_watch: Watch for the call in 1:13–14, the LORD's words in 2:12–13, and the promise in 2:28–32.
q1: A locust plague devastates the land; Joel announces the day of the LORD, calls the people to return with all their heart, and records God's promise to pour out his Spirit. Joel calls, "Declare a holy fast; call a sacred assembly… and cry out to the LORD" (1:14). What does this reveal about the practice of lament?
q2: Peter quotes Joel 2:28–32 at Pentecost: "In the last days, God says, I will pour out my Spirit on all people" (Acts 2:16–21, Day 279). How does Peter use Joel's words? He says, "The promise is for you and your children and for all who are far off—for all whom the Lord our God will call" (2:39); what does this reveal about God's people as all whom the Lord will call?
q3: In light of Joel's call to cry out to the LORD, how might lament take shape in your life this week?
identity: All whom the Lord will call

main_theme: The LORD announces judgment on surrounding nations and Judah, charges Israel with oppressing the poor, and calls for justice to roll on like a river.
primary_threads: Law and wisdom; The day of the Lord; Blessing and curse
pre_where: Joel has announced the day of the LORD. Today Amos, a shepherd from Tekoa, speaks to the northern kingdom of Israel (1:1).
pre_watch: Watch for the pattern "For three sins… even for four" in 1:3–2:6, what the LORD says about the day of the LORD in 5:18–20, and the call in 5:24.
q1: The LORD announces judgment on surrounding nations and Judah, charges Israel with oppressing the poor, and calls for justice to roll on like a river. The LORD says, "let justice roll on like a river, righteousness like a never-failing stream!" (5:24). What does this reveal about the practice of justice and mercy?
q2: Amos charges Israel with trampling on the poor (5:11–12). James 5:1–6 (Day 342) warns the rich who have withheld the wages of their workers, then urges, "Be patient, then, brothers and sisters, until the Lord's coming" (5:7–11). How does James move from warning oppressive rich people to encouraging his brothers and sisters to wait patiently for the Lord's coming? What does this reveal about God's people as those who wait patiently for the Lord's coming?
q3: In light of the LORD's call for justice to roll on like a river, how might justice and mercy take shape in your life this week?
identity: Those who wait patiently for the Lord's coming

main_theme: Amos sees visions of judgment and confronts the priest of Bethel; the LORD promises to restore David's fallen shelter and bring his people home.
primary_threads: Blessing and curse; Kingdom and kingship; Exile and return
pre_where: Amos has called for justice to roll on like a river. Today he warns those who feel secure and sees a series of visions.
pre_watch: Watch for the warning in 6:1–6, Amos's prayers in 7:2–6, his answer to Amaziah in 7:14–15, and the promise in 9:11–15.
q1: Amos sees visions of judgment and confronts the priest of Bethel; the LORD promises to restore David's fallen shelter and bring his people home. When the LORD shows him locusts and fire, Amos cries out, "Sovereign LORD, forgive!… How can Jacob survive? He is so small!" and the LORD relents (7:2–3, 5–6). What does this reveal about the practice of prayer?
q2: At the Jerusalem council James quotes Amos 9:11–12: "I will rebuild David's fallen tent… that the rest of mankind may seek the Lord, even all the Gentiles who bear my name" (Acts 15:15–17, Day 286). How does James use Amos's words? What does this reveal about God's people as all who bear his name?
q3: In light of Amos pleading with the LORD for Jacob, how might prayer take shape in your life this week?
identity: All who bear his name

main_theme: Edom is condemned for its pride and violence against Judah; the day of the LORD will judge the nations, and the kingdom will be the LORD's.
primary_threads: The day of the Lord; Kingdom and kingship
pre_where: Amos ended with a promise to restore David's fallen shelter. Today the shortest book of the Old Testament announces judgment on Edom, the nation descended from Esau.
pre_watch: Watch for Edom's pride in verses 3–4, what Edom did in verses 10–14, and the last line in verse 21.
q1: Edom is condemned for its pride and violence against Judah; the day of the LORD will judge the nations, and the kingdom will be the LORD's. The LORD tells Edom, "On the day you stood aloof while strangers carried off his wealth… you were like one of them" (v. 11). What does this reveal about the danger of standing aloof when others suffer?
q2: Edom stood aloof while strangers carried off Judah's wealth (v. 11). Galatians 6:2, 10 (Day 317) says, "Carry each other's burdens," and "let us do good to all people, especially to those who belong to the family of believers." How are these two passages similar or different? What does this reveal about God's people as the family of believers?
q3: In light of Edom standing aloof in Judah's trouble, how might justice and mercy take shape in your life this week?
identity: The family of believers

main_theme: Jonah flees God's call and is swallowed by a great fish, then preaches to Nineveh, which repents; God questions Jonah's anger at his compassion.
primary_threads: Blessing and curse
supporting_threads: The people of God; Exodus and redemption
pre_where: Obadiah announced judgment on Edom. Today the LORD sends the prophet Jonah to Nineveh, the great city of Assyria.
pre_watch: Watch for what Jonah says about himself in 1:9, his prayer in 2:2–9, Nineveh's response in 3:5–10, and the LORD's question in 4:10–11.
q1: Jonah flees God's call and is swallowed by a great fish, then preaches to Nineveh, which repents; God questions Jonah's anger at his compassion. The LORD asks Jonah, "should I not have concern for the great city of Nineveh…?" (4:11). What does this reveal about the practice of compassion?
q2: Jesus says the people of Nineveh "repented at the preaching of Jonah, and now something greater than Jonah is here" (Luke 11:29–32, Day 272). How does Jesus use Jonah's story? Just before this he says, "Blessed rather are those who hear the word of God and obey it" (11:28); what does this reveal about God's people as those who hear the word of God and obey it?
q3: In light of the LORD's concern for the great city of Nineveh, how might compassion take shape in your life this week?
identity: Those who hear the word of God and obey it

main_theme: Micah announces judgment on Samaria and Jerusalem for injustice, then sees nations streaming to the LORD's mountain and swords beaten into plowshares.
primary_threads: Blessing and curse; Temple and God's presence; Exile and return; Kingdom and kingship
pre_where: Jonah ended with the LORD's concern for Nineveh. Today Micah of Moresheth speaks against Samaria and Jerusalem (1:1).
pre_watch: Watch for who Micah charges in 2:1–2 and 3:9–11, how Micah describes himself in 3:8, and the vision in 4:1–5.
q1: Micah announces judgment on Samaria and Jerusalem for injustice, then sees nations streaming to the LORD's mountain and swords beaten into plowshares. Micah condemns those who covet fields and seize them, and take people's houses (2:1–2). What does this reveal about the danger of coveting what belongs to others?
q2: Micah condemns those who covet fields and seize them (2:1–2). Hebrews 13:5 (Day 340) says, "Keep your lives free from the love of money and be content with what you have, because God has said, 'Never will I leave you; never will I forsake you.'" How are these two passages similar or different? What does this reveal about God's people as those God will never leave?
q3: In light of Micah's warning against coveting what belongs to others, how might contentment take shape in your life this week?
identity: Those God will never leave

main_theme: A ruler will come from Bethlehem to shepherd Israel; the LORD requires justice, mercy and humility, and will again show compassion and hurl sins into the sea.
primary_threads: The promised Messiah; Kingdom and kingship; Law and wisdom; Covenant; Sacrifice and atonement
pre_where: Micah has seen the nations streaming to the LORD's mountain. Today he speaks of a ruler from Bethlehem and of what the LORD requires.
pre_watch: Watch for the ruler in 5:2–4, the question and answer in 6:6–8, and the closing words in 7:18–20.
q1: A ruler will come from Bethlehem to shepherd Israel; the LORD requires justice, mercy and humility, and will again show compassion and hurl sins into the sea. Micah says the LORD has shown what is good: "To act justly and to love mercy and to walk humbly with your God" (6:8). What does this reveal about the practice of justice and mercy?
q2: When Herod asks where the Messiah is to be born, the chief priests and teachers of the law quote Micah 5:2, which speaks of a ruler "who will shepherd my people Israel" (Matthew 2:4–6, Day 236). In John 10:14–16, 27–28 (Day 262) Jesus says, "I am the good shepherd," and "My sheep listen to my voice; I know them, and they follow me." How does Matthew use Micah 5:2–4 to describe the ruler, and how does Jesus describe his sheep in John 10? What does this reveal about God's people as those who listen to his voice and follow him?
q3: In light of what the LORD requires, how might justice and mercy take shape in your life this week?
identity: Those who listen to his voice and follow him

main_theme: The LORD, slow to anger but great in power, announces Nineveh's fall, which brings news of peace to Judah.
primary_threads: Blessing and curse
pre_where: Micah ended with the LORD hurling sins into the depths of the sea. Today Nahum announces the fall of Nineveh, the city that repented at Jonah's preaching.
pre_watch: Watch for how the LORD is described in 1:2–3 and 1:7, and the good news in 1:15.
q1: The LORD, slow to anger but great in power, announces Nineveh's fall, which brings news of peace to Judah. Nahum says, "The LORD is good, a refuge in times of trouble. He cares for those who trust in him" (1:7). What does this reveal about the practice of trust?
q2: Nahum describes the LORD as both avenging and "a refuge in times of trouble" (1:2, 7). Second Thessalonians 1:6–7 (Day 328) says God will "pay back trouble to those who trouble you and give relief to you who are troubled." How are these two passages similar or different? Paul speaks of the Lord being marveled at "among all those who have believed" (1:10); what does this reveal about God's people as those who have believed?
q3: In light of Nahum's words that the LORD is a refuge for those who trust in him, how might trust take shape in your life this week?
identity: Those who have believed

main_theme: Habakkuk questions God's justice in using Babylon; God answers that the righteous will live by faithfulness, and Habakkuk resolves to rejoice in God.
primary_threads: The people of God; Blessing and curse
pre_where: Nahum announced Nineveh's fall. Today Habakkuk brings his own questions to the LORD about the violence he sees in Judah.
pre_watch: Watch for Habakkuk's first question in 1:2–4, the LORD's answer in 2:2–4, and Habakkuk's resolve in 3:17–19.
q1: Habakkuk questions God's justice in using Babylon; God answers that the righteous will live by faithfulness, and Habakkuk resolves to rejoice in God. Habakkuk says, "Though the fig tree does not bud… yet I will rejoice in the LORD, I will be joyful in God my Savior" (3:17–18). What does this reveal about the practice of joy?
q2: Habakkuk 2:4 says "the righteous person will live by his faithfulness," and Paul quotes it as "The righteous will live by faith" when describing the gospel (Romans 1:16–17, Day 293). How does Paul use Habakkuk 2:4 in describing the gospel, and how does he address the people in Rome as those "loved by God and called to be his holy people" (1:7)? What does this reveal about being called to be God's holy people?
q3: In light of Habakkuk's resolve to rejoice in the LORD though crops fail, how might joy take shape in your life this week?
identity: Those called to be his holy people

main_theme: The day of the LORD is near, bringing judgment on Judah and the nations; the LORD will purify the peoples' lips, leave a humble remnant, and rejoice over Jerusalem with singing.
primary_threads: The day of the Lord; Exile and return; The people of God
pre_where: Habakkuk resolved to rejoice in God. Today Zephaniah, who prophesied in the days of Josiah king of Judah (1:1), announces that the day of the LORD is near.
pre_watch: Watch for the call in 2:3, the remnant in 3:12–13, and the LORD's rejoicing in 3:17.
q1: The day of the LORD is near, bringing judgment on Judah and the nations; the LORD will purify the peoples' lips, leave a humble remnant, and rejoice over Jerusalem with singing. Zephaniah says, "Seek the LORD, all you humble of the land… Seek righteousness, seek humility" (2:3). What does this reveal about the practice of humility?
q2: Zephaniah calls the humble to seek the LORD (2:3). First Peter 5:5–6 (Day 344) says, "God opposes the proud but shows favor to the humble. Humble yourselves, therefore, under God's mighty hand." How are these two passages similar or different? Peter tells the elders to be shepherds of "God's flock" (5:2); what does this reveal about God's people as God's flock?
q3: In light of Zephaniah's call to seek humility, how might humility take shape in your life this week?
identity: God's flock

main_theme: The returned exiles are told to rebuild the temple; the LORD promises his presence and Spirit, future glory for the house, and a signet ring for Zerubbabel.
primary_threads: Temple and God's presence; Exile and return; The Spirit
pre_where: Zephaniah promised that the LORD would gather his scattered people. Haggai speaks in the second year of King Darius of Persia, to exiles who have returned to Jerusalem but left the LORD's house in ruins (1:1–4).
pre_watch: Watch for the LORD's question in 1:4, the people's response in 1:12–14, and the promise in 2:4–5.
q1: The returned exiles are told to rebuild the temple; the LORD promises his presence and Spirit, future glory for the house, and a signet ring for Zerubbabel. Zerubbabel, Joshua and the whole remnant of the people obey the voice of the LORD and fear him (1:12). What does this reveal about the practice of obedience?
q2: The LORD stirs up the people to work on his house (1:14). Paul writes, "we are co-workers in God's service; you are God's field, God's building" (1 Corinthians 3:9–11, Day 302). How are these two passages similar or different? What does this reveal about God's people as God's building?
q3: In light of the remnant obeying the LORD's voice, how might obedience take shape in your life this week?
identity: God's building

main_theme: Zechariah sees the LORD returning to Jerusalem and Joshua cleansed; the LORD tells Zerubbabel the work will succeed by his Spirit and that he will finish the temple.
primary_threads: Temple and God's presence; The Spirit; Exile and return; Sacrifice and atonement
pre_where: Haggai has urged the returned exiles to rebuild the temple. Zechariah begins in the same year, calling the people to return to the LORD (1:1–3).
pre_watch: Watch for the call in 1:3, Joshua's clean garments in 3:3–5, and the word to Zerubbabel in 4:6.
q1: Zechariah sees the LORD returning to Jerusalem and Joshua cleansed; the LORD tells Zerubbabel the work will succeed by his Spirit and that he will finish the temple. The LORD says, "Return to me… and I will return to you" (1:3). What does this reveal about the practice of repentance?
q2: The LORD says, "Return to me… and I will return to you" (1:3). James 4:8 (Day 342) says, "Come near to God and he will come near to you." How are these two invitations similar or different? What does this reveal about God's people as those who come near to God?
q3: In light of the LORD's call to return to him, how might repentance take shape in your life this week?
identity: Those who come near to God

main_theme: Visions remove wickedness from the land; a crown is set on Joshua as the Branch is named builder of the temple, and God promises to dwell in Jerusalem.
primary_threads: Temple and God's presence; Kingdom and kingship; Blessing and curse; Exile and return
pre_where: Zechariah has seen visions of the temple being rebuilt. Today come two more visions, a crown for Joshua the high priest, and a question about fasting.
pre_watch: Watch for the question in 7:3, the LORD's answer in 7:9–10, and the promises in 8:3–8 and 8:20–23.
q1: Visions remove wickedness from the land; a crown is set on Joshua as the Branch is named builder of the temple, and God promises to dwell in Jerusalem. The LORD says, "Administer true justice; show mercy and compassion to one another. Do not oppress the widow or the fatherless, the foreigner or the poor" (7:9–10). What does this reveal about the practice of justice and mercy?
q2: Zechariah sees people from all nations saying, "Let us go with you, because we have heard that God is with you" (8:23). In 1 Corinthians 14:24–25 (Day 307) Paul describes an unbeliever who falls down and exclaims, "God is really among you!" How do these two passages compare? Paul says, "Everything must be done so that the church may be built up" (14:26); how does that instruction shape the identity of those who build up the church?
q3: In light of the LORD's call to show mercy and compassion to one another, how might justice and mercy take shape in your life this week?
identity: Those who build up the church

main_theme: Zion's king is announced as coming humbly on a donkey; the flock rejects Zechariah's shepherding, and on that day the LORD will be king over all the earth.
primary_threads: The promised Messiah; Kingdom and kingship; The day of the Lord; The Spirit
pre_where: Zechariah has seen people from all nations coming to seek the LORD. Today he announces Zion's king coming humbly on a donkey.
pre_watch: Watch for the king in 9:9–10, the thirty pieces of silver in 11:12–13, and the fountain in 13:1.
q1: Zion's king is announced as coming humbly on a donkey; the flock rejects Zechariah's shepherding, and on that day the LORD will be king over all the earth. Zion is told, "Rejoice greatly… See, your king comes to you, righteous and victorious, lowly and riding on a donkey" (9:9). What does this reveal about the practice of joy?
q2: John 12:14–16 (Day 263) quotes Zechariah 9:9 as Jesus rides into Jerusalem on a young donkey, and says the disciples understood it only after Jesus was glorified. How does John use these words? Jesus says, "Whoever serves me must follow me; and where I am, my servant also will be" (12:26); what does this reveal about God's people as servants who follow him?
q3: In light of Zion's call to rejoice at the coming of its humble king, how might joy take shape in your life this week?
identity: Servants who follow him

main_theme: The LORD affirms his love for Israel, rebukes priests for offering blemished sacrifices, and condemns faithlessness in marriage.
primary_threads: Covenant; Sacrifice and atonement; Temple and God's presence
pre_where: Zechariah ended with the LORD as king over all the earth. Malachi, the last book of the Old Testament, opens with the LORD's word to Israel: "I have loved you" (1:2).
pre_watch: Watch for the people's question in 1:2, the offerings in 1:7–8, and the covenant with Levi in 2:5–7.
q1: The LORD affirms his love for Israel, rebukes priests for offering blemished sacrifices, and condemns faithlessness in marriage. The LORD rebukes the priests for offering blind, lame and diseased animals, asking, "Try offering them to your governor!" (1:8). What does this reveal about the danger of offering the LORD what is blemished?
q2: The priests offer blind, lame and diseased animals (1:8, 13). In Mark 12:41–44 (Day 255) Jesus says a poor widow who gave two small coins "put in everything—all she had to live on," just after warning against those who "devour widows' houses" (12:38–40). How are these two offerings similar or different? Earlier in the chapter Jesus names the greatest commandment, to love the Lord "with all your heart" (12:30); what does this reveal about God's people as those who love God with all their heart?
q3: In light of the LORD's rebuke of blemished offerings (Malachi 1:8, 13–14), how might worship take shape in your life this week?
identity: Those who love God with all their heart

main_theme: The LORD will send his messenger and come to his temple to refine his people, calls them to return, and promises Elijah before the day of the LORD.
primary_threads: Temple and God's presence; The day of the Lord; Covenant; Law and wisdom
pre_where: The LORD has rebuked the priests and the people. Today he promises to send his messenger.
pre_watch: Watch for the messenger in 3:1, the call in 3:7, those who feared the LORD in 3:16–17, and Elijah in 4:5–6.
q1: The LORD will send his messenger and come to his temple to refine his people, calls them to return, and promises Elijah before the day of the LORD. Those who feared the LORD talked with each other, and the LORD listened and heard (3:16). What does this reveal about the practice of fellowship?
q2: Jesus says John the Baptist is the one of whom it is written, "I will send my messenger ahead of you," and "he is the Elijah who was to come" (Matthew 11:10, 14, Day 241). How does Jesus use Malachi's words? He adds, "Whoever has ears, let them hear" (11:15); what does this reveal about God's people as those who have ears to hear?
q3: In light of those who feared the LORD talking together while the LORD listened, how might fellowship take shape in your life this week?
identity: Those who have ears to hear

main_theme: The blessed person delights in the LORD's law, and the LORD installs his anointed king on Zion against the rebelling nations.
primary_threads: Law and wisdom; Kingdom and kingship; Blessing and curse
pre_where: The prophets have ended with Malachi's promise of Elijah. Today the plan turns to the poetry of Israel, beginning with the first two psalms.
pre_watch: Watch for the two ways in 1:1–6, the nations' plot in 2:1–3, and the closing words in 2:12.
q1: The blessed person delights in the LORD's law, and the LORD installs his anointed king on Zion against the rebelling nations. Blessed is the one whose delight is in the law of the LORD, and who meditates on his law day and night (1:2). What does this reveal about the practice of meditating on Scripture?
q2: Hebrews 1:5 (Day 335) quotes Psalm 2:7, "You are my Son; today I have become your Father," about the Son. How does Hebrews use these words? Hebrews 1:13–14 then speaks of "those who will inherit salvation," and 2:1–3 urges, "We must pay the most careful attention… to what we have heard." How does Hebrews describe those who inherit salvation and the response it urges? What does this reveal about God's people as those who will inherit salvation?
q3: In light of the blessing on the one who meditates on the LORD's law day and night, how might meditating on Scripture take shape in your life this week?
identity: Those who will inherit salvation

main_theme: Wisdom begins with the fear of the LORD; a father urges his son to seek wisdom and trust the LORD rather than his own understanding.
primary_threads: Law and wisdom; Creation and new creation
pre_where: The plan has begun Israel's poetry with Psalms 1–2. Today it turns to Proverbs, the sayings of Solomon, written for gaining wisdom and instruction (1:1–2).
pre_watch: Watch for the starting point in 1:7, the father's words in 3:5–6, and wisdom at creation in 3:19–20.
q1: Wisdom begins with the fear of the LORD; a father urges his son to seek wisdom and trust the LORD rather than his own understanding. The father says, "Trust in the LORD with all your heart and lean not on your own understanding" (3:5). What does this reveal about the practice of trust?
q2: Hebrews 12:5–6 (Day 340) quotes Proverbs 3:11–12: "the Lord disciplines the one he loves." Hebrews 12:10–11 says God disciplines us "for our good, in order that we may share in his holiness," and that discipline "produces a harvest of righteousness and peace." How does Hebrews describe the purpose and fruit of discipline? Hebrews 12:7 says, "God is treating you as his children"; what does this reveal about God's people as children God disciplines?
q3: In light of the call to trust the LORD rather than your own understanding, how might trust take shape in your life this week?
identity: Children God disciplines

main_theme: The father urges his son to get wisdom, guard his heart, avoid adultery, and shun laziness and the things the LORD hates.
primary_threads: Law and wisdom
pre_where: The father has urged his son to trust the LORD. Today he continues: get wisdom, guard your heart.
pre_watch: Watch for the call in 4:7, the instruction in 4:23, and the seven things the LORD hates in 6:16–19.
q1: The father urges his son to get wisdom, guard his heart, avoid adultery, and shun laziness and the things the LORD hates. The father says, "Above all else, guard your heart, for everything you do flows from it" (4:23). What does this reveal about the practice of holiness?
q2: The father says, "guard your heart" (4:23). Philippians 4:7–8 (Day 322) says "the peace of God… will guard your hearts and your minds in Christ Jesus," and urges, "whatever is true… think about such things." How are these two passages similar or different? What does this reveal about God's people as those whose hearts are guarded by God's peace?
q3: In light of the call to guard your heart, how might holiness take shape in your life this week?
identity: Those whose hearts are guarded by God's peace

article_title: How God’s Wisdom Leads to Joy
main_theme: The father warns against the adulterous woman; Wisdom calls out, describes her presence at creation, and invites the simple to her feast.
primary_threads: Law and wisdom; Creation and new creation
pre_where: The father has urged his son to guard his heart. Today he warns again, and then Wisdom herself calls out in the streets.
pre_watch: Watch for where Wisdom calls in 8:1–4, Wisdom at creation in 8:22–31, and the two invitations in 9:1–6 and 9:13–18.
q1: The father warns against the adulterous woman; Wisdom calls out, describes her presence at creation, and invites the simple to her feast. Wisdom says, "Blessed are those who listen to me, watching daily at my doors" (8:34). What does this reveal about the practice of seeking wisdom?
q2: Wisdom describes being with the LORD at creation (8:22–31). Colossians 2:2–3 (Day 323) speaks of Christ, "in whom are hidden all the treasures of wisdom and knowledge." How are these two passages similar or different? Colossians 2:7 speaks of being "rooted and built up in him"; what does this reveal about God's people as those rooted and built up in him?
q3: In light of Wisdom's blessing on those who listen to her daily, how might seeking wisdom take shape in your life this week?
identity: Those rooted and built up in him

main_theme: Solomon's proverbs contrast the righteous and the wicked, and the wise and the foolish, in speech, work and wealth.
primary_threads: Law and wisdom; Blessing and curse
pre_where: Wisdom has invited the simple to her feast. Today the proverbs of Solomon begin: short sayings that set the righteous beside the wicked, and the wise beside the foolish (10:1).
pre_watch: Watch for what the proverbs say about speech in 10:19 and 12:18, about work in 10:4, and about generosity in 11:24–25.
q1: Solomon's proverbs contrast the righteous and the wicked, and the wise and the foolish, in speech, work and wealth. The proverb says, "A generous person will prosper; whoever refreshes others will be refreshed" (11:25). What does this reveal about the practice of generosity?
q2: Proverbs 11:25 speaks of the generous person; Paul writes, "Whoever sows generously will also reap generously… for God loves a cheerful giver" (2 Corinthians 9:6–7, Day 313). How do Proverbs 11:25 and 2 Corinthians 9:6–7 compare, and what does Paul's description of the gift as service to the Lord's people (9:1, 12–13), including their "generosity in sharing with them and with everyone else," reveal about God's people as those generous in sharing with others?
q3: In light of the proverb about the generous person, how might generosity take shape in your life this week?
identity: Those generous in sharing with others

main_theme: Proverbs address diligence, discipline and the fear of the LORD, the power of a gentle answer, and the LORD who sees everything.
primary_threads: Law and wisdom
pre_where: The proverbs of Solomon have begun. Today they continue with sayings on diligence, discipline and speech.
pre_watch: Watch for the gentle answer in 15:1, the LORD who sees in 15:3, and the fear of the LORD in 15:16 and 15:33.
q1: Proverbs address diligence, discipline and the fear of the LORD, the power of a gentle answer, and the LORD who sees everything. The proverb says, "A gentle answer turns away wrath, but a harsh word stirs up anger" (15:1). What does this reveal about the practice of gentleness?
q2: The proverb says a gentle answer turns away wrath (15:1). James 1:19–20 (Day 341) says, "Everyone should be quick to listen, slow to speak and slow to become angry." How are these two passages similar or different? James 1:21 urges, "humbly accept the word planted in you"; what does this reveal about God's people as those who humbly accept the word planted in them?
q3: In light of the proverb about a gentle answer, how might gentleness take shape in your life this week?
identity: Those who humbly accept the word planted in them

main_theme: People plan their way but the LORD directs their steps; proverbs address pride, justice, kings, friendship and the power of the tongue.
primary_threads: Law and wisdom; Kingdom and kingship
pre_where: The proverbs have spoken of a gentle answer. Today they turn to planning, pride and the power of the tongue.
pre_watch: Watch for the sayings in 16:1–3 and 16:9, the warning in 16:18, and the tongue in 18:21.
q1: People plan their way but the LORD directs their steps; proverbs address pride, justice, kings, friendship and the power of the tongue. The proverb says, "In their hearts humans plan their course, but the LORD establishes their steps" (16:9). What does this reveal about the practice of trust?
q2: The proverb says the LORD establishes our steps (16:9). James 4:13–15 (Day 342) says, "you ought to say, 'If it is the Lord's will, we will live and do this or that.'" How are these two passages similar or different? What does this reveal about God's people as those who say, "If it is the Lord's will"?
q3: In light of the proverb that the LORD establishes our steps, how might trust take shape in your life this week?
identity: Those who say, "If it is the Lord's will"

main_theme: Proverbs address poverty and integrity, discipline, the LORD's direction of kings, and doing right rather than offering sacrifice.
primary_threads: Law and wisdom; Kingdom and kingship; Sacrifice and atonement
pre_where: The proverbs have spoken of planning and the LORD's direction. Today they continue with sayings on the poor, discipline and the LORD's purposes.
pre_watch: Watch for the saying about the poor in 19:17, the LORD's purpose in 19:21, and what pleases the LORD in 21:3.
q1: Proverbs address poverty and integrity, discipline, the LORD's direction of kings, and doing right rather than offering sacrifice. The proverb says, "Whoever is kind to the poor lends to the LORD, and he will reward them for what they have done" (19:17). What does this reveal about the practice of generosity?
q2: The proverb says kindness to the poor is lending to the LORD (19:17). In Luke 14:12–14 (Day 274) Jesus says, "invite the poor, the crippled, the lame, the blind, and you will be blessed… you will be repaid at the resurrection of the righteous." How are these two passages similar or different? What does this reveal about God's people as those who will share in the resurrection of the righteous?
q3: In light of the proverb about kindness to the poor, how might generosity take shape in your life this week?
