q2: Jesus answers John, "The blind receive sight, the lame walk… and the good news is proclaimed to the poor" (11:4–5). These words echo Isaiah 35:5–6 (Day 116), on the blind and the lame, and Isaiah 61:1 (Day 125), on good news for the poor. How does Jesus draw on these passages? Isaiah 35:10 says "those the LORD has rescued will return… with singing"; what does this reveal about God's people as those the LORD has rescued?
q3: How might you make room for rest and doing good this week?
identity: Those the LORD has rescued

main_theme: Jesus teaches in parables about the kingdom, is rejected in Nazareth, and after John is beheaded, feeds five thousand and walks on the water.
primary_threads: Kingdom and kingship; The people of God
pre_where: Jesus has been accused of driving out demons by Beelzebul. Today he teaches the crowds in parables from a boat.
pre_watch: Watch for the four soils in 13:3–9 and 13:18–23, the hidden treasure and the pearl in 13:44–46, and Peter on the water in 14:28–31.
q1: Jesus teaches in parables about the kingdom, is rejected in Nazareth, and after John is beheaded, feeds five thousand and walks on the water. The kingdom of heaven is like treasure hidden in a field; a man in his joy sells all he has and buys that field (13:44). What does this reveal about the practice of joy?
q2: A man in his joy sells all he has to buy the field with the hidden treasure (13:44). Paul writes, "I consider everything a loss because of the surpassing worth of knowing Christ Jesus my Lord" (Philippians 3:8, Day 322). How are these two passages similar or different? Philippians 3:20 says, "our citizenship is in heaven"; what does this reveal about God's people as citizens of heaven?
q3: In light of the man's joy at finding the treasure, how might joy take shape in your life this week?
identity: Citizens of heaven

main_theme: Jesus confronts traditions that set aside God's command, heals a Canaanite woman's daughter, feeds four thousand, and Peter declares him the Messiah before Jesus foretells his death.
primary_threads: The promised Messiah; Kingdom and kingship; Law and wisdom; The people of God
pre_where: Jesus has fed five thousand and walked on the water. Today Pharisees and teachers of the law come from Jerusalem with a question about tradition.
pre_watch: Watch for what Jesus says about the heart in 15:18–20, the Canaanite woman's answer in 15:27–28, and Peter's confession in 16:16.
q1: Jesus confronts traditions that set aside God's command, heals a Canaanite woman's daughter, feeds four thousand, and Peter declares him the Messiah before Jesus foretells his death. The Canaanite woman keeps asking, and Jesus says, "Woman, you have great faith! Your request is granted" (15:27–28). What does this reveal about the practice of prayer?
q2: Jesus grants the request of a Canaanite woman (15:21–28). Galatians 3:28 (Day 316) says, "There is neither Jew nor Gentile, neither slave nor free, nor is there male and female, for you are all one in Christ Jesus." How are these two passages similar or different? What does this reveal about God's people as one in Christ Jesus?
q3: In light of the Canaanite woman's persistent request, how might prayer take shape in your life this week?
identity: One in Christ Jesus

main_theme: Jesus is transfigured before three disciples and heals a boy, then teaches about humility, seeking the lost, correcting a brother and forgiving seventy-seven times.
primary_threads: Kingdom and kingship; Law and wisdom; The people of God
pre_where: Peter has declared Jesus the Messiah. Today, six days later, Jesus takes Peter, James and John up a high mountain (17:1).
pre_watch: Watch for the voice from the cloud in 17:5, who is greatest in 18:1–4, and Peter's question in 18:21–22.
q1: Jesus is transfigured before three disciples and heals a boy, then teaches about humility, seeking the lost, correcting a brother and forgiving seventy-seven times. Jesus tells Peter to forgive not seven times, but seventy-seven times (18:21–22). What does this reveal about the practice of forgiveness?
q2: Jesus tells Peter to forgive seventy-seven times and tells of a servant forgiven a great debt (18:21–35). Ephesians 4:32 (Day 319) says, "Be kind and compassionate to one another, forgiving each other, just as in Christ God forgave you." How are these two passages similar or different? Ephesians 4:25 says "we are all members of one body"; what does this reveal about God's people as members of one body?
q3: In light of Jesus' call to forgive seventy-seven times, how might forgiveness take shape in your life this week?
identity: Members of one body

video_title: Passage Insight: Jesus in the Divorce Debate
main_theme: Jesus teaches on divorce and wealth, tells the parable of the vineyard workers, foretells his death, and says he came to give his life as a ransom for many.
primary_threads: Law and wisdom; Kingdom and kingship; Sacrifice and atonement; Exodus and redemption
pre_where: Jesus has taught about forgiveness. Today he leaves Galilee for Judea, and questions come about divorce and wealth (19:1).
pre_watch: Watch for the rich young man in 19:16–22, the vineyard workers in 20:1–16, and Jesus' words in 20:26–28.
q1: Jesus teaches on divorce and wealth, tells the parable of the vineyard workers, foretells his death, and says he came to give his life as a ransom for many. Jesus says, "whoever wants to become great among you must be your servant… just as the Son of Man did not come to be served, but to serve" (20:26–28). What does this reveal about the practice of service?
q2: Jesus says the Son of Man came "not to be served, but to serve, and to give his life as a ransom for many" (20:28). In John 13:12–15 (Day 264) Jesus washes his disciples' feet and says, "you also should wash one another's feet." How are these two passages similar or different? Jesus says, "everyone will know that you are my disciples, if you love one another" (13:35); what does this reveal about God's people as disciples known by their love?
q3: In light of Jesus' words that the great must be servants, how might service take shape in your life this week?
identity: Disciples known by their love

main_theme: Jesus enters Jerusalem on a donkey, clears the temple, tells parables of rejection, and answers questions on taxes, resurrection and the greatest commandment.
primary_threads: The promised Messiah; Temple and God's presence; Kingdom and kingship; Law and wisdom
pre_where: Jesus has said he came to serve and give his life. Today he enters Jerusalem.
pre_watch: Watch for the crowds' words in 21:9, what Jesus does in the temple in 21:12–13, and the greatest commandment in 22:37–40.
q1: Jesus enters Jerusalem on a donkey, clears the temple, tells parables of rejection, and answers questions on taxes, resurrection and the greatest commandment. Jesus says the greatest commandment is to love the Lord your God with all your heart, soul and mind, and the second is to love your neighbor as yourself (22:37–39). What does this reveal about the practice of love?
q2: Jesus names love for God and love for neighbor as the greatest commandments (22:37–40). Paul writes, "Love does no harm to a neighbor. Therefore love is the fulfillment of the law" (Romans 13:8–10, Day 298). How are these two passages similar or different? Romans 13:14 says, "clothe yourselves with the Lord Jesus Christ"; what does this reveal about God's people as those clothed with the Lord Jesus Christ?
q3: In light of Jesus' two greatest commandments, how might love take shape in your life this week?
identity: Those clothed with the Lord Jesus Christ

main_theme: Jesus denounces the hypocrisy of the teachers of the law and Pharisees, laments over Jerusalem, and foretells the temple's destruction and the coming of the Son of Man.
primary_threads: Temple and God's presence; The day of the Lord; Law and wisdom
pre_where: Jesus has answered questions in the temple courts. Today he speaks to the crowds and his disciples about the teachers of the law and the Pharisees (23:1).
pre_watch: Watch for what Jesus says about titles in 23:8–12, his lament in 23:37, and his call to keep watch in 24:42–44.
q1: Jesus denounces the hypocrisy of the teachers of the law and Pharisees, laments over Jerusalem, and foretells the temple's destruction and the coming of the Son of Man. Jesus says, "Therefore keep watch, because you do not know on what day your Lord will come" (24:42). What does this reveal about the practice of watchfulness?
q2: Jesus says the Son of Man will come at an hour you do not expect (24:42–44). First Thessalonians 5:2–6 (Day 327) says "the day of the Lord will come like a thief in the night" and urges, "let us be awake and sober." How are these two passages similar or different? Paul says, "since we belong to the day, let us be sober" (5:8); what does this reveal about God's people as those who belong to the day?
q3: In light of Jesus' call to keep watch, how might watchfulness take shape in your life this week?
identity: Those who belong to the day

article_title: “Why Did Jesus Have To Die?” (A Question Worth Unpacking)
main_theme: Jesus tells parables of readiness and judgment, is anointed at Bethany, shares the Passover meal, prays in Gethsemane, and is arrested and denied by Peter.
primary_threads: Covenant; Sacrifice and atonement; Kingdom and kingship
pre_where: Jesus has called his disciples to keep watch. Today he tells two parables about readiness and faithfulness, followed by the Son of Man's description of judgment, and then the Passover arrives.
pre_watch: Watch for the parable of the bags of gold in 25:14–30, what the woman does in 26:6–13, and Jesus' prayer in 26:39.
q1: Jesus tells parables of readiness and judgment, is anointed at Bethany, shares the Passover meal, prays in Gethsemane, and is arrested and denied by Peter. The master tells the servant who put his money to work, "Well done, good and faithful servant! You have been faithful with a few things" (25:21). What does this reveal about the practice of stewardship?
q2: The master praises the servants who were faithful with what he entrusted to them (25:21, 23). Paul, describing himself and others as servants "entrusted with the mysteries God has revealed," writes, "it is required that those who have been given a trust must prove faithful" (1 Corinthians 4:1–5, Day 302). How does faithfulness in these two settings compare? Paul says that when the Lord comes, "each will receive their praise from God" (4:5); what does this reveal about God's people as those who will receive praise from God when the Lord comes?
q3: In light of the master's praise for the faithful servants, how might stewardship take shape in your life this week?
identity: Those who will receive praise from God when the Lord comes

main_theme: Jesus is tried before Pilate, mocked as king of the Jews, crucified and buried; on the third day he rises and sends his disciples to make disciples of all nations.
primary_threads: Kingdom and kingship; The promised Messiah; Temple and God's presence; The people of God
pre_where: Jesus has been arrested and Peter has denied him. Today, early in the morning, Jesus is handed over to Pilate (27:1–2).
pre_watch: Watch for the sign over his head in 27:37, the centurion's words in 27:54, the angel's message in 28:5–7, and Jesus' commission in 28:18–20.
q1: Jesus is tried before Pilate, mocked as king of the Jews, crucified and buried; on the third day he rises and sends his disciples to make disciples of all nations. The women hurry away from the tomb, afraid yet filled with joy, and run to tell his disciples (28:8). What does this reveal about the practice of witness?
q2: The angel tells the women, "He is not here; he has risen, just as he said" (28:6). Paul hands on "as of first importance" that Christ died, was buried, was raised on the third day and appeared to Cephas (1 Corinthians 15:3–5, Day 308). How are these two accounts similar or different? Paul says, "By this gospel you are saved, if you hold firmly to the word I preached to you" (15:2); what does this reveal about God's people as those saved by the gospel as they hold firmly to the message Paul preached?
q3: In light of the women running to tell the disciples, how might witness take shape in your life this week?
identity: Those saved by the gospel as they hold firmly to it

main_theme: Mark begins the good news about Jesus the Messiah; Jesus is baptized and the Spirit descends, he proclaims the kingdom, heals many, forgives a paralyzed man and calls Levi.
primary_threads: The promised Messiah; Kingdom and kingship; The Spirit; The people of God
pre_where: Matthew ended with Jesus sending his disciples to all nations. Today the plan begins Mark, which opens with "the good news about Jesus the Messiah, the Son of God" (1:1).
pre_watch: Watch for Jesus' message in 1:15, where he goes early in the morning in 1:35, and the four friends in 2:3–5.
q1: Mark begins the good news about Jesus the Messiah; Jesus is baptized and the Spirit descends, he proclaims the kingdom, heals many, forgives a paralyzed man and calls Levi. Very early in the morning, Jesus goes off to a solitary place, where he prays (1:35). What does this reveal about the practice of prayer?
q2: Jesus goes to a solitary place to pray (1:35). Hebrews 5:7–9 (Day 337) says that "during the days of Jesus' life on earth, he offered up prayers and petitions" and "became the source of eternal salvation for all who obey him." How are these two passages similar or different? What does this reveal about God's people as all who obey him?
q3: In light of Jesus going to a solitary place to pray, how might prayer take shape in your life this week?
identity: All who obey him

main_theme: Jesus heals on the Sabbath, appoints the twelve, is accused of being possessed, and teaches the parables of the sower and the growing seed before calming a storm.
primary_threads: Kingdom and kingship; Law and wisdom; The Spirit
pre_where: Jesus has called Levi and been questioned about fasting and the Sabbath. Today he heals on the Sabbath and appoints twelve.
pre_watch: Watch for Jesus' question in 3:4, who he calls his family in 3:34–35, and the disciples' question in 4:41.
q1: Jesus heals on the Sabbath, appoints the twelve, is accused of being possessed, and teaches the parables of the sower and the growing seed before calming a storm. Jesus asks, "Which is lawful on the Sabbath: to do good or to do evil, to save life or to kill?" (3:4). What does this reveal about the practice of compassion?
q2: Jesus tells of seed that falls on good soil and produces a crop (4:3–8, 14–20). Isaiah 55:10–11 (Day 123) says God's word is like rain that makes the earth bud and "will not return to me empty." How are these two pictures of God's word similar or different? Isaiah invites the thirsty to come, listen and live (55:1–3). What does this reveal about God's people as those who come and listen to him?
q3: In light of Jesus' question about doing good on the Sabbath, how might compassion take shape in your life this week?
identity: Those who come and listen to him

main_theme: Jesus frees a man from many demons, heals a bleeding woman and raises Jairus's daughter, is rejected at home, and feeds five thousand and walks on the water.
primary_threads: Kingdom and kingship; The people of God
pre_where: Jesus has calmed a storm on the lake. Today he crosses to the region of the Gerasenes (5:1).
pre_watch: Watch for what Jesus tells the healed man in 5:19, the woman's touch in 5:27–34, and Jesus' compassion in 6:34.
q1: Jesus frees a man from many demons, heals a bleeding woman and raises Jairus's daughter, is rejected at home, and feeds five thousand and walks on the water. Jesus tells the healed man, "Go home to your own people and tell them how much the Lord has done for you, and how he has had mercy on you" (5:19). What does this reveal about the practice of witness?
q2: Jesus sends the healed man home to tell how much the Lord has done for him (5:19). Psalm 66:16 (daily psalm, Day 66) says, "Come and hear, all you who fear God; let me tell you what he has done for me." How are these two passages similar or different? What does this reveal about God's people as all who fear God?
q3: In light of Jesus sending the man to tell his own people what the Lord had done, how might witness take shape in your life this week?
identity: All who fear God

main_theme: Jesus challenges human traditions, heals a Syrophoenician woman's daughter and a deaf man, feeds four thousand, and Peter declares him the Messiah before Jesus foretells his suffering.
primary_threads: The promised Messiah; Law and wisdom; Kingdom and kingship; The people of God
pre_where: Jesus has fed five thousand and walked on the water. Today Pharisees and teachers of the law from Jerusalem question his disciples' ways (7:1).
pre_watch: Watch for what Jesus says comes from the heart in 7:20–23, the woman's answer in 7:28, and Peter's confession and Jesus' teaching in 8:29–34.
q1: Jesus challenges human traditions, heals a Syrophoenician woman's daughter and a deaf man, feeds four thousand, and Peter declares him the Messiah before Jesus foretells his suffering. Jesus says, "Whoever wants to be my disciple must deny themselves and take up their cross and follow me" (8:34). What does this reveal about the practice of self-denial?
q2: Jesus quotes Isaiah 29:13: "These people honor me with their lips, but their hearts are far from me" (7:6–7; Isaiah 29:13, Day 115). How does Jesus use Isaiah's words? Isaiah 29:19 says, "Once more the humble will rejoice in the LORD"; what does this reveal about God's people as the humble who rejoice in the LORD?
q3: In light of Jesus' call to deny yourself and follow him, how might self-denial take shape in your life this week?
identity: The humble who rejoice in the LORD

article_title: The Apocalypse of Jesus
main_theme: Jesus is transfigured, teaches about serving and welcoming children, answers questions on divorce and wealth, and says he came to give his life as a ransom for many.
primary_threads: Kingdom and kingship; Law and wisdom; Sacrifice and atonement; Exodus and redemption
pre_where: Peter has declared Jesus the Messiah, and Jesus has spoken of his suffering. Today, six days later, Jesus is transfigured on a high mountain (9:2).
pre_watch: Watch for the father's words in 9:24, how Jesus receives children in 10:13–16, and Bartimaeus's request in 10:46–52.
q1: Jesus is transfigured, teaches about serving and welcoming children, answers questions on divorce and wealth, and says he came to give his life as a ransom for many. The boy's father cries out, "I do believe; help me overcome my unbelief!" (9:24). What does this reveal about the practice of trust?
q2: The father says, "I do believe; help me overcome my unbelief!" (9:24). Hebrews 11:6 (Day 340) says, "anyone who comes to him must believe that he exists and that he rewards those who earnestly seek him." How are these two passages similar or different? What does this reveal about God's people as those who earnestly seek him?
q3: In light of the father's honest prayer, "help me overcome my unbelief," how might trust take shape in your life this week?
identity: Those who earnestly seek him

main_theme: Jesus enters Jerusalem, curses a fig tree, clears the temple, and answers challenges about his authority, taxes, resurrection and the greatest commandment.
primary_threads: Temple and God's presence; Kingdom and kingship; Law and wisdom; The promised Messiah
pre_where: Jesus has healed blind Bartimaeus near Jericho. Today he approaches Jerusalem (11:1).
pre_watch: Watch for the crowd's words in 11:9–10, Jesus' words about prayer in 11:24–25, and the widow's offering in 12:41–44.
q1: Jesus enters Jerusalem, curses a fig tree, clears the temple, and answers challenges about his authority, taxes, resurrection and the greatest commandment. Jesus says, "when you stand praying, if you hold anything against anyone, forgive them" (11:25). What does this reveal about the practice of forgiveness?
q2: Jesus says to forgive anyone you hold something against when you pray (11:25). Colossians 3:13 (Day 324) says, "Bear with each other and forgive one another if any of you has a grievance against someone. Forgive as the Lord forgave you." How are these two passages similar or different? Colossians 3:15 says, "as members of one body you were called to peace"; what does this reveal about God's people as those called to peace?
q3: In light of Jesus' teaching to forgive when you pray, how might forgiveness take shape in your life this week?
identity: Those called to peace

article_title: Why Is the Lord’s Supper Significant in the Bible?
main_theme: Jesus foretells the temple's destruction and the coming of the Son of Man; he is anointed, shares the Passover meal, prays in Gethsemane, and is arrested and tried.
primary_threads: Temple and God's presence; The day of the Lord; Covenant; Sacrifice and atonement; The promised Messiah
pre_where: Jesus has answered challenges in the temple courts. Today, as he leaves the temple, he speaks of its destruction (13:1–2).
pre_watch: Watch for Jesus' warning in 13:33–37, the woman's anointing in 14:3–9, and Jesus' prayer in 14:36.
q1: Jesus foretells the temple's destruction and the coming of the Son of Man; he is anointed, shares the Passover meal, prays in Gethsemane, and is arrested and tried. When others criticize the woman who poured perfume on him, Jesus says, "She has done a beautiful thing to me" (14:6). What does this reveal about the practice of worship?
q2: Jesus quotes Zechariah 13:7, "I will strike the shepherd, and the sheep will be scattered" (14:27; Zechariah 13:7, Day 172). How does Jesus use Zechariah's words? Zechariah 13:9 says, "They will call on my name and I will answer them; I will say, 'They are my people'"; what does this reveal about God's people as those God calls his people?
q3: In light of Jesus' words about the woman's anointing, how might worship take shape in your life this week?
identity: Those God calls his people

main_theme: Jesus is handed over to Pilate, crucified as king of the Jews and buried; women find the tomb empty and are told he has risen.
primary_threads: Kingdom and kingship; The promised Messiah; Temple and God's presence
pre_where: Jesus has been questioned by the high priest. Today, very early in the morning, he is handed over to Pilate (15:1).
pre_watch: Watch for the sign in 15:26, the centurion's words in 15:39, and what the women are told in 16:6–7.
q1: Jesus is handed over to Pilate, crucified as king of the Jews and buried; women find the tomb empty and are told he has risen. Some women watch from a distance, including Mary Magdalene, who had followed Jesus and cared for his needs (15:40–41). What does this reveal about the practice of faithfulness?
q2: On the cross Jesus cries out, "My God, my God, why have you forsaken me?" (15:34), the opening words of Psalm 22 (daily psalm, Day 22). How does Mark present this cry? Psalm 22:26 says, "those who seek the LORD will praise him"; what does this reveal about God's people as those who seek the LORD and praise him?
q3: In light of the women who stayed and watched, how might faithfulness take shape in your life this week?
identity: Those who seek the LORD and praise him

article_title: How Do God’s Words Create?
main_theme: The Word who was with God and was God becomes flesh; John the Baptist calls Jesus the Lamb of God, and Jesus turns water into wine and clears the temple.
primary_threads: Creation and new creation; Temple and God's presence; Sacrifice and atonement; The promised Messiah
pre_where: Mark ended with the women at the empty tomb. Today the plan begins John, which opens, "In the beginning was the Word" (1:1).
pre_watch: Watch for the Word made flesh in 1:14, John the Baptist's words in 1:29, and Mary's words to the servants in 2:5.
q1: The Word who was with God and was God becomes flesh; John the Baptist calls Jesus the Lamb of God, and Jesus turns water into wine and clears the temple. Jesus' mother tells the servants, "Do whatever he tells you" (2:5). What does this reveal about the practice of obedience?
q2: John says, "The Word became flesh and made his dwelling among us. We have seen his glory" (1:14). First John 1:1–3 (Day 346) speaks of "the Word of life" that "we have looked at and our hands have touched." How are these two passages similar or different? First John 1:3 speaks of "fellowship… with the Father and with his Son, Jesus Christ"; what does this reveal about God's people as those who have fellowship with the Father and the Son?
q3: In light of Mary's words, "Do whatever he tells you," how might obedience take shape in your life this week?
identity: Those who have fellowship with the Father and the Son

article_title: Can We Experience Eternal Life Today?
main_theme: Jesus tells Nicodemus he must be born again and that God so loved the world; he offers living water to a Samaritan woman, who brings her town to him.
primary_threads: The Spirit; The promised Messiah; Temple and God's presence; The people of God
pre_where: Jesus has cleared the temple in Jerusalem. Today Nicodemus, a member of the Jewish ruling council, comes to him at night (3:1–2).
pre_watch: Watch for Jesus' words in 3:16–17, the Samaritan woman's questions in 4:9–20, and what she does in 4:28–29.
q1: Jesus tells Nicodemus he must be born again and that God so loved the world; he offers living water to a Samaritan woman, who brings her town to him. The woman leaves her water jar, goes back to the town and says, "Come, see a man who told me everything I ever did" (4:28–29). What does this reveal about the practice of witness?
q2: John 3:16 says that God loved the world and gave his Son. First John 4:9–10 (Day 347) says, "This is how God showed his love among us: He sent his one and only Son into the world that we might live through him." How are these two passages similar or different? First John 4:7 says, "everyone who loves has been born of God"; what does this reveal about God's people as those born of God who love?
q3: In light of the woman inviting her town to come and see Jesus, how might witness take shape in your life this week?
identity: Those born of God who love

main_theme: Jesus heals a man at the pool on the Sabbath and speaks of the Father giving him authority; he feeds five thousand and says he is the bread of life.
primary_threads: Exodus and redemption; Law and wisdom
pre_where: A Samaritan town has believed in Jesus. Today, back in Jerusalem for a festival, Jesus heals a man at the pool of Bethesda on the Sabbath (5:1–9).
pre_watch: Watch for Jesus' words about the Father in 5:19–20, the boy's loaves in 6:9, and Peter's answer in 6:68–69.
q1: Jesus heals a man at the pool on the Sabbath and speaks of the Father giving him authority; he feeds five thousand and says he is the bread of life. When many turn back, Peter says, "Lord, to whom shall we go? You have the words of eternal life" (6:68). What does this reveal about the practice of trust?
q2: Peter tells Jesus, "You have the words of eternal life" (6:68). First Peter 1:23–25 (Day 343) says, "you have been born again… through the living and enduring word of God." How are these two passages similar or different? What does this reveal about God's people as those born again through the living word of God?
q3: In light of Peter's answer, "Lord, to whom shall we go?" how might trust take shape in your life this week?
identity: Those born again through the living word of God

main_theme: At the Festival of Tabernacles Jesus offers living water, meaning the Spirit, declares he is the light of the world, and says, "Before Abraham was born, I am!"
primary_threads: The Spirit; Temple and God's presence; The promised Messiah; The people of God
pre_where: Many disciples have turned back, but Peter has said Jesus has the words of eternal life. Today Jesus goes up to Jerusalem for the Festival of Tabernacles (7:2, 10).
pre_watch: Watch for Jesus' invitation in 7:37–39, his words in 8:12, and his promise in 8:31–32.
q1: At the Festival of Tabernacles Jesus offers living water, meaning the Spirit, declares he is the light of the world, and says, "Before Abraham was born, I am!" Jesus says, "If you hold to my teaching, you are really my disciples. Then you will know the truth, and the truth will set you free" (8:31–32). What does this reveal about the practice of obedience?
q2: Jesus says, "I am the light of the world. Whoever follows me will never walk in darkness" (8:12). Ephesians 5:8 (Day 320) says, "you were once darkness, but now you are light in the Lord." How are these two passages similar or different? What does this reveal about God's people as light in the Lord?
q3: In light of Jesus' words about holding to his teaching, how might obedience take shape in your life this week?
identity: Light in the Lord

main_theme: Jesus heals a man born blind, who is questioned and thrown out, and Jesus calls himself the good shepherd who lays down his life for the sheep.
primary_threads: The promised Messiah; Sacrifice and atonement; The people of God; Temple and God's presence
pre_where: Jesus has said, "I am the light of the world." Today he heals a man who was born blind.
pre_watch: Watch for the disciples' question and Jesus' answer in 9:2–3, the man's testimony in 9:25, and the good shepherd in 10:11–16.
q1: Jesus heals a man born blind, who is questioned and thrown out, and Jesus calls himself the good shepherd who lays down his life for the sheep. The healed man says, "One thing I do know. I was blind but now I see!" (9:25). What does this reveal about the practice of speaking the truth?
q2: Jesus says, "I am the good shepherd. The good shepherd lays down his life for the sheep" (10:11). Psalm 23 (daily psalm, Day 23) begins, "The LORD is my shepherd, I lack nothing." How are these two pictures of a shepherd similar or different? Psalm 23:6 ends, "I will dwell in the house of the LORD forever"; what does this reveal about God's people as those who dwell in the house of the LORD?
q3: In light of the healed man telling what he knew under questioning, how might speaking the truth take shape in your life this week?
identity: Those who dwell in the house of the LORD

main_theme: Jesus raises Lazarus, is anointed at Bethany, enters Jerusalem as king, and says a kernel of wheat must die to produce many seeds.
primary_threads: Kingdom and kingship; The promised Messiah
pre_where: Jesus has called himself the good shepherd. Today word comes that his friend Lazarus is sick (11:1–3).
pre_watch: Watch for Jesus' words to Martha in 11:25–26, Jesus weeping in 11:35, and what Mary does in 12:3.
q1: Jesus raises Lazarus, is anointed at Bethany, enters Jerusalem as king, and says a kernel of wheat must die to produce many seeds. When Jesus sees Mary and the others weeping, he is deeply moved, and Jesus weeps (11:33–35). What does this reveal about the practice of compassion?
q2: Jesus weeps with those who mourn Lazarus and tells Martha, "I am the resurrection and the life" (11:25, 35). First Thessalonians 4:13–14 (Day 326) says, "we do not want you… to grieve like the rest of mankind, who have no hope." How are these two passages similar or different? What does this reveal about God's people as those who grieve with hope?
q3: In light of Jesus weeping with those who mourned, how might compassion take shape in your life this week?
identity: Those who grieve with hope

main_theme: Jesus washes his disciples' feet, gives a new command to love one another, says he is the way, the truth and the life, promises the Spirit, and calls himself the true vine.
primary_threads: The Spirit; Law and wisdom; The people of God; Temple and God's presence
pre_where: Jesus has entered Jerusalem. Today, just before the Passover Festival, he shares a meal with his disciples (13:1–2).
pre_watch: Watch for the new command in 13:34–35, Jesus' words in 14:6 and 14:16–17, and the vine and branches in 15:5.
q1: Jesus washes his disciples' feet, gives a new command to love one another, says he is the way, the truth and the life, promises the Spirit, and calls himself the true vine. Jesus says, "A new command I give you: Love one another. As I have loved you, so you must love one another" (13:34). What does this reveal about the practice of love?
q2: Jesus gives a new command: "As I have loved you, so you must love one another" (13:34). First John 4:11–12 (Day 347) says, "since God so loved us, we also ought to love one another… if we love one another, God lives in us." How are these two passages similar or different? What does this reveal about God's people as those in whom God lives as they love one another?
q3: In light of Jesus' new command to love one another as he has loved, how might love take shape in your life this week?
identity: Those in whom God lives as they love one another

main_theme: Jesus promises the Spirit will guide his disciples into truth, prays for them and all who will believe, and is arrested, questioned and denied by Peter.
primary_threads: The Spirit; The people of God; Kingdom and kingship
pre_where: Jesus has called himself the true vine. Today he continues speaking to his disciples, and then prays for them before his arrest.
pre_watch: Watch for the Spirit's work in 16:13, Jesus' prayer for all who will believe in 17:20–21, and his words to Pilate in 18:36–37.
q1: Jesus promises the Spirit will guide his disciples into truth, prays for them and all who will believe, and is arrested, questioned and denied by Peter. Jesus prays for those who will believe through his disciples' message, "that all of them may be one, Father, just as you are in me and I am in you" (17:20–21). What does this reveal about the practice of unity?
q2: Jesus prays that all who believe may be one (17:20–21). Philippians 2:2 (Day 321) urges believers to make Paul's joy complete "by being like-minded, having the same love, being one in spirit and of one mind." How are these two passages similar or different? Philippians 1:27 speaks of "striving together as one for the faith of the gospel"; what does this reveal about God's people as those who strive together for the faith of the gospel?
q3: In light of Jesus' prayer that all who believe may be one, how might unity take shape in your life this week?
identity: Those who strive together for the faith of the gospel

main_theme: Jesus is crucified as king of the Jews and says, "It is finished"; Mary Magdalene meets the risen Jesus, Thomas says, "My Lord and my God!", and Jesus asks Peter three times whether he loves him.
primary_threads: Kingdom and kingship; The Spirit; The people of God
pre_where: Jesus has been arrested and Peter has denied him. Today Pilate has Jesus flogged, and Jesus is crucified (19:1, 16).
pre_watch: Watch for Jesus' words to his mother in 19:26–27, Mary Magdalene at the tomb in 20:11–18, and Jesus' questions to Peter in 21:15–17.
q1: Jesus is crucified as king of the Jews and says, "It is finished"; Mary Magdalene meets the risen Jesus, Thomas says, "My Lord and my God!", and Jesus asks Peter three times whether he loves him. Jesus asks Peter three times, "Do you love me?" and tells him, "Feed my sheep" (21:15–17). What does this reveal about the practice of service?
q2: John says the soldiers did not break Jesus' legs, fulfilling Scripture (19:33–36). How does this relate to the Passover instruction in Exodus 12:46 (Day 20)? Paul writes, "Get rid of the old yeast, so that you may be a new unleavened batch—as you really are. For Christ, our Passover lamb, has been sacrificed" (1 Corinthians 5:7, Day 303); what does this reveal about God's people as a new unleavened batch?
q3: In light of Jesus' charge to Peter to feed his sheep, how might service take shape in your life this week?
identity: A new unleavened batch

main_theme: Luke sets out an orderly account; Gabriel announces the births of John and Jesus, Mary visits Elizabeth and praises God, and Zechariah prophesies at John's birth.
primary_threads: The promised Messiah; The Spirit; Kingdom and kingship; Covenant; Exodus and redemption
pre_where: John's Gospel ended with Jesus' charge to Peter. Today the plan begins Luke, written so that Theophilus may know the certainty of the things he has been taught (1:1–4).
pre_watch: Watch for Mary's response in 1:38, her song in 1:46–55, and Zechariah's song in 1:68–79.
q1: Luke sets out an orderly account; Gabriel announces the births of John and Jesus, Mary visits Elizabeth and praises God, and Zechariah prophesies at John's birth. Mary answers, "I am the Lord's servant. May your word to me be fulfilled" (1:38). What does this reveal about the practice of trust?
q2: Zechariah sings that God has remembered "the oath he swore to our father Abraham" (1:72–73). In Genesis 22:16–18 (Day 7) the LORD swears to Abraham that "through your offspring all nations on earth will be blessed." How does Zechariah's song, spoken of Israel (1:68–75), draw on this oath? Galatians 3:8–9 (Day 316) describes those who have faith as blessed along with Abraham. How does this extend the reflection on Abraham's promised blessing, and what does it reveal about God's people as those who rely on faith and are blessed along with Abraham?
q3: In light of Mary's answer, "May your word to me be fulfilled," how might trust take shape in your life this week?
identity: Those who rely on faith and are blessed along with Abraham

article_title: What Does the Bible Say about Angels and Cherubim?
main_theme: Jesus is born in Bethlehem and announced to shepherds, presented at the temple, and found in his Father's house as a boy; John preaches and Jesus is baptized.
primary_threads: The promised Messiah; Temple and God's presence; The Spirit; Exodus and redemption
pre_where: Luke has told of the births announced to Zechariah and Mary, and of John's birth. Today Caesar Augustus orders a census, and Joseph goes to Bethlehem with Mary (2:1–5).
pre_watch: Watch for the angel's message in 2:10–11, Simeon's words in 2:29–32, and John's answers in 3:10–14.
q1: Jesus is born in Bethlehem and announced to shepherds, presented at the temple, and found in his Father's house as a boy; John preaches and Jesus is baptized. When the crowd asks, "What should we do then?" John answers, "Anyone who has two shirts should share with the one who has none" (3:10–11). What does this reveal about the practice of generosity?
q2: Simeon calls the child "a light for revelation to the Gentiles, and the glory of your people Israel" (2:32), echoing Isaiah 49:6 (Day 121). How does Simeon's song draw on Isaiah? Isaiah 49:13 says, "the LORD comforts his people and will have compassion on his afflicted ones"; what does this reveal about God's people as those the LORD comforts?
q3: In light of John's answer to share with the one who has none, how might generosity take shape in your life this week?
identity: Those the LORD comforts

main_theme: Jesus is tested in the wilderness, reads Isaiah in Nazareth and says it is fulfilled, is rejected, then heals, forgives sins and calls Simon and Levi.
primary_threads: The Spirit; The promised Messiah; Exodus and redemption; Kingdom and kingship; The people of God
pre_where: Jesus has been baptized, and Luke has traced his line back to Adam. Today, full of the Holy Spirit, Jesus is led into the wilderness (4:1).
pre_watch: Watch for the Isaiah reading in 4:18–19, Simon's words in 5:5 and 5:8, and where Jesus goes in 5:16.
q1: Jesus is tested in the wilderness, reads Isaiah in Nazareth and says it is fulfilled, is rejected, then heals, forgives sins and calls Simon and Levi. Simon says, "Master, we've worked hard all night and haven't caught anything. But because you say so, I will let down the nets" (5:5). What does this reveal about the practice of obedience?
q2: Simon falls at Jesus' knees and says, "Go away from me, Lord; I am a sinful man!" and Jesus answers, "Don't be afraid; from now on you will fish for people" (5:8–10). In Isaiah 6:5–8 (Day 110) Isaiah says, "Woe to me!… I am a man of unclean lips," and then hears the Lord ask, "Whom shall I send?" How are these two callings similar or different? Jesus sends his disciples as the Father sent him (John 20:21, Day 266). What does this reveal about God's people as those Jesus sends?
q3: In light of Simon letting down the nets because Jesus said so, how might obedience take shape in your life this week?
identity: Those Jesus sends

video_title: Passage Insight: Speck in the Eye
main_theme: Jesus heals on the Sabbath, chooses the twelve, teaches blessings, woes and love for enemies, raises a widow's son, and forgives a woman who anoints his feet.
primary_threads: Law and wisdom; Blessing and curse; Kingdom and kingship; The people of God
pre_where: Jesus has called Simon and Levi. Today he heals on the Sabbath, chooses twelve apostles, and teaches a large crowd on a level place (6:12–17).
pre_watch: Watch for the blessings and woes in 6:20–26, the command in 6:35–36, and what Jesus says about the woman in 7:47.
q1: Jesus heals on the Sabbath, chooses the twelve, teaches blessings, woes and love for enemies, raises a widow's son, and forgives a woman who anoints his feet. Jesus calls his hearers to treat others as they would want to be treated and to be merciful as their Father is merciful (6:31, 35–36). What does this reveal about the practice of justice and mercy?
q2: Jesus says, "Be merciful, just as your Father is merciful" (6:36). Micah 7:18 (Day 165) asks, "Who is a God like you, who pardons sin… You do not stay angry forever but delight to show mercy." How do these passages describe God's mercy? Micah 7:14 calls God's people "the flock of your inheritance"; what does this reveal about God's people as the flock of his inheritance?
q3: In light of Jesus' teaching on treating others and showing mercy, how might justice and mercy take shape in your life this week?
identity: The flock of his inheritance

main_theme: Jesus teaches in parables, calms a storm, heals and raises a girl, feeds five thousand, is declared God's Messiah by Peter, is transfigured, and resolves to go to Jerusalem.
primary_threads: The promised Messiah; Kingdom and kingship; The people of God
pre_where: A woman has anointed Jesus' feet and been forgiven. Today Jesus travels from town to town with the Twelve and women who support them (8:1–3).
pre_watch: Watch for the women in 8:2–3, the seed on good soil in 8:15, and Peter's answer in 9:20.
q1: Jesus teaches in parables, calms a storm, heals and raises a girl, feeds five thousand, is declared God's Messiah by Peter, is transfigured, and resolves to go to Jerusalem. Jesus says the seed on good soil stands for those who hear the word, retain it, and by persevering produce a crop (8:15). What does this reveal about the practice of perseverance?
q2: Jesus says the seed on good soil stands for those who hear the word, retain it, and by persevering produce a crop (8:15). Hebrews 10:36 (Day 339) says, "You need to persevere so that when you have done the will of God, you will receive what he has promised." How are these two passages similar or different? Hebrews 10:39 says, "we do not belong to those who shrink back… but to those who have faith and are saved"; what does this reveal about God's people as those who have faith and are saved?
q3: In light of Jesus' picture of those who persevere and produce a crop, how might perseverance take shape in your life this week?
identity: Those who have faith and are saved

main_theme: Jesus sends out seventy-two, tells the parable of the good Samaritan, visits Mary and Martha, teaches his disciples to pray, and confronts Pharisees and experts in the law.
primary_threads: Law and wisdom; Kingdom and kingship; The Spirit; The people of God
pre_where: Jesus has resolved to go to Jerusalem. Today he sends out seventy-two others ahead of him (10:1).
pre_watch: Watch for why the disciples should rejoice in 10:20, Mary at Jesus' feet in 10:39–42, and the prayer Jesus teaches in 11:2–4.
q1: Jesus sends out seventy-two, tells the parable of the good Samaritan, visits Mary and Martha, teaches his disciples to pray, and confronts Pharisees and experts in the law. Mary sits at the Lord's feet listening to what he says, and Jesus says she has chosen what is better (10:39, 42). What does this reveal about the practice of listening?
q2: Jesus tells Martha that "few things are needed—or indeed only one," and that Mary has chosen what is better (10:41–42). Psalm 27:4 (daily psalm, Day 27) says, "One thing I ask from the LORD… that I may dwell in the house of the LORD… to gaze on the beauty of the LORD." How are these two passages similar or different? What does this reveal about God's people as those who seek to gaze on the beauty of the LORD?
q3: In light of Mary sitting at the Lord's feet to listen, how might listening take shape in your life this week?
identity: Those who seek to gaze on the beauty of the LORD

main_theme: Jesus warns against greed and hypocrisy, calls for readiness for the Son of Man, heals a woman on the Sabbath, and laments over Jerusalem.
primary_threads: Law and wisdom; Kingdom and kingship; The Spirit
pre_where: Jesus has taught his disciples to pray and confronted Pharisees and experts in the law. Today a crowd of many thousands gathers (12:1).
pre_watch: Watch for the rich fool in 12:16–21, the call to readiness in 12:35–40, and the woman healed on the Sabbath in 13:10–17.
q1: Jesus warns against greed and hypocrisy, calls for readiness for the Son of Man, heals a woman on the Sabbath, and laments over Jerusalem. Jesus says, "Watch out! Be on your guard against all kinds of greed; life does not consist in an abundance of possessions" (12:15). What does this reveal about the practice of contentment?
q2: Jesus warns that "life does not consist in an abundance of possessions" and tells of a rich man who was not "rich toward God" (12:15–21). First Timothy 6:17–19 (Day 331) tells the rich "to do good, to be rich in good deeds, and to be generous," so that they may "take hold of the life that is truly life." How are these two passages similar or different? What does this reveal about God's people as those who take hold of the life that is truly life?
q3: In light of Jesus' warning against greed, how might contentment take shape in your life this week?
identity: Those who take hold of the life that is truly life

main_theme: Jesus tells parables of the great banquet, the lost sheep, lost coin and lost son, the shrewd manager, and the rich man and Lazarus.
primary_threads: Kingdom and kingship; Law and wisdom; The people of God
pre_where: Jesus has lamented over Jerusalem. Today he eats at the house of a prominent Pharisee on the Sabbath (14:1).
pre_watch: Watch for the guests at the banquet in 14:21–23, the three parables in chapter 15, and the father's words in 15:31–32.
q1: Jesus tells parables of the great banquet, the lost sheep, lost coin and lost son, the shrewd manager, and the rich man and Lazarus. The father says, "we had to celebrate and be glad, because this brother of yours was dead and is alive again; he was lost and is found" (15:32). What does this reveal about the practice of joy?
q2: Jesus tells of a great banquet to which the poor, the crippled, the blind and the lame are brought in (14:15–23). Isaiah 25:6–9 (Day 114) says, "the LORD Almighty will prepare a feast of rich food for all peoples." How are these two pictures of a feast similar or different? Isaiah 25:9 says, "This is our God; we trusted in him, and he saved us"; what does this reveal about God's people as those who trusted in him and were saved?
q3: In light of the father's celebration for the son who was lost and is found, how might joy take shape in your life this week?
identity: Those who trusted in him and were saved

main_theme: Jesus teaches on forgiveness and faith, heals ten lepers, speaks of the kingdom and the day of the Son of Man, and tells parables on prayer and humility before foretelling his death.
primary_threads: Kingdom and kingship; The day of the Lord; Law and wisdom
pre_where: Jesus has told parables of lost things found and of a rich man and Lazarus. Today he teaches his disciples about forgiveness and faith (17:1–6).
pre_watch: Watch for the one healed man who returns in 17:15–18, the widow in 18:1–8, and the tax collector's prayer in 18:13.
q1: Jesus teaches on forgiveness and faith, heals ten lepers, speaks of the kingdom and the day of the Son of Man, and tells parables on prayer and humility before foretelling his death. The tax collector stands at a distance, beats his breast and says, "God, have mercy on me, a sinner" (18:13). What does this reveal about the practice of humility?
q2: The tax collector prays, "God, have mercy on me, a sinner," and Jesus says he went home justified (18:13–14). Isaiah 57:15 (Day 123) says the LORD lives "in a high and holy place, but also with the one who is contrite and lowly in spirit." How are these two passages similar or different? What does this reveal about God's people as those who are contrite and lowly in spirit?
q3: In light of the tax collector's prayer, how might humility take shape in your life this week?
identity: Those who are contrite and lowly in spirit

main_theme: Zacchaeus welcomes Jesus, who tells the parable of the minas, enters Jerusalem as king, weeps over the city, clears the temple, and answers challenges to his authority.
primary_threads: Kingdom and kingship; The promised Messiah; Temple and God's presence
pre_where: Jesus has foretold his death and healed a blind man near Jericho. Today he passes through Jericho (19:1).
pre_watch: Watch for Zacchaeus's words in 19:8, the crowd's praise in 19:37–38, and Jesus weeping over the city in 19:41–44.
q1: Zacchaeus welcomes Jesus, who tells the parable of the minas, enters Jerusalem as king, weeps over the city, clears the temple, and answers challenges to his authority. Zacchaeus says, "Here and now I give half of my possessions to the poor, and if I have cheated anybody out of anything, I will pay back four times the amount" (19:8). What does this reveal about the practice of justice and mercy?
q2: The crowd of disciples praises God: "Blessed is the king who comes in the name of the Lord!" (19:37–38), echoing Psalm 118:26 (daily psalm, Day 118). How does Luke use the psalm's words? Psalm 118:24 says, "The LORD has done it this very day; let us rejoice today and be glad"; what does this reveal about God's people as those who rejoice in what the LORD has done?
q3: In light of Zacchaeus's commitment to give to the poor and repay anyone he has cheated, how might justice and mercy take shape in your life this week?
identity: Those who rejoice in what the LORD has done

main_theme: Jesus foretells the temple's destruction and the coming of the Son of Man, shares the Passover meal, prays on the Mount of Olives, and is arrested and denied by Peter.
primary_threads: Temple and God's presence; The day of the Lord; Covenant; Sacrifice and atonement
pre_where: Jesus has cleared the temple and answered challenges to his authority. Today he notices a poor widow putting two coins into the temple treasury (21:1–4).
pre_watch: Watch for Jesus' words in 21:34–36, his teaching on greatness in 22:24–27, and his prayer on the Mount of Olives in 22:42.
q1: Jesus foretells the temple's destruction and the coming of the Son of Man, shares the Passover meal, prays on the Mount of Olives, and is arrested and denied by Peter. Jesus says, "Be always on the watch, and pray" (21:36). What does this reveal about the practice of watchfulness?
q2: At the meal Jesus speaks of the new covenant in his blood (22:20). Jeremiah 31:31–34 (Day 135) promises a new covenant with the house of Israel and the house of Judah, with God's law written on their hearts. How does Luke's account connect with Jeremiah's promise? Jeremiah 31:34 says, "they will all know me, from the least of them to the greatest"; what does this reveal about God's people as those who all know the LORD?
q3: In light of Jesus' call to be always on the watch and pray, how might watchfulness take shape in your life this week?
identity: Those who all know the LORD

article_title: How Does the Bible’s Story Lead to Jesus?
main_theme: Jesus is crucified, promises a criminal paradise, and is buried; risen, he explains the Scriptures about himself on the road to Emmaus and is taken up to heaven.
primary_threads: Kingdom and kingship; The promised Messiah; Temple and God's presence
pre_where: Jesus has been arrested and Peter has denied him. Today the council brings Jesus before Pilate (23:1).
pre_watch: Watch for the criminal's request in 23:42–43, Jesus' words in 23:46, and how the two disciples recognize Jesus in 24:30–32.
q1: Jesus is crucified, promises a criminal paradise, and is buried; risen, he explains the Scriptures about himself on the road to Emmaus and is taken up to heaven. The disciples recall how their hearts burned as Jesus explained the Scriptures to them (24:27, 32). How might their response inform the practice of meditating on Scripture?
q2: Jesus' last words, "Father, into your hands I commit my spirit" (23:46), are from Psalm 31:5 (daily psalm, Day 31). How does Luke present Jesus' use of this psalm? Psalm 31:23 calls the LORD's faithful people to love him: "Love the LORD, all his faithful people!" What does this reveal about their response to the LORD?
q3: How might you make time this week to reflect on Scripture in light of the disciples' experience?
identity: All his faithful people

article_title: Why Does the Ascension of Jesus Matter?
main_theme: Jesus is taken up to heaven, the Spirit comes at Pentecost, Peter preaches that Jesus is Lord and Messiah, and about three thousand are baptized and share life together.
primary_threads: The Spirit; The promised Messiah; The people of God; Kingdom and kingship; The day of the Lord
pre_where: Luke ended with Jesus taken up to heaven. Acts, Luke's second book to Theophilus, begins with Jesus speaking to his apostles about the kingdom of God (1:1–3).
pre_watch: Watch for Jesus' promise in 1:8, Peter's call in 2:38, and how the believers live in 2:42–47.
q1: Jesus is taken up to heaven, the Spirit comes at Pentecost, Peter preaches that Jesus is Lord and Messiah, and about three thousand are baptized and share life together. The believers devote themselves to the apostles' teaching and to fellowship, to the breaking of bread and to prayer (2:42). What does this reveal about the practice of fellowship?
q2: The believers devote themselves to fellowship and have everything in common (2:42–44). Psalm 133:1 (daily psalm, Day 138) says, "How good and pleasant it is when God's people live together in unity!" How are these two passages similar or different? What does this reveal about God's people as those who live together in unity?
q3: In light of the believers' devotion to teaching, fellowship, the breaking of bread and prayer, how might fellowship take shape in your life this week?
identity: Those who live together in unity

article_title: What Is Pentecost? And Why Is It Important?
main_theme: Peter and John heal a lame man and call people to repent in Jesus' name, are arrested and warned, and the believers pray for boldness and share their possessions.
primary_threads: The Spirit; Temple and God's presence; The people of God; The promised Messiah; Covenant
pre_where: The Spirit has come at Pentecost and the believers share life together. Today Peter and John go up to the temple at the time of prayer (3:1).
pre_watch: Watch for Peter's words to the lame man in 3:6, what the council notices in 4:13, and the believers' prayer in 4:29–30.
q1: Peter and John heal a lame man and call people to repent in Jesus' name, are arrested and warned, and the believers pray for boldness and share their possessions. The council sees the courage of Peter and John and realizes they are unschooled, ordinary men who had been with Jesus (4:13). What does this reveal about the practice of courage?
q2: The believers pray using Psalm 2:1–2: "Why do the nations rage… against the Lord and against his anointed one?" (4:25–26; Psalm 2, daily psalm Day 2). How do they apply the psalm to the opposition against Jesus (4:27–28), and what do they ask for (4:29–30)? Psalm 2:12 blesses those who take refuge in him. How does the believers' prayer in Acts 4:29–30 help you reflect on what it means to take refuge in God?
q3: In light of the courage of Peter and John, ordinary men who had been with Jesus, how might courage take shape in your life this week?
identity: All who take refuge in him

article_title: God’s Design for the Growth of the Church
main_theme: Ananias and Sapphira die after lying to the Holy Spirit, the apostles are jailed and freed, and seven are chosen to serve, including Stephen.
primary_threads: The Spirit; The people of God
pre_where: The believers have prayed for boldness and shared their possessions. Today a couple lies about a gift, and the apostles are arrested.
pre_watch: Watch for Peter's question in 5:3–4, the apostles' answer in 5:29, and how the seven are chosen in 6:2–6.
q1: Ananias and Sapphira die after lying to the Holy Spirit, the apostles are jailed and freed, and seven are chosen to serve, including Stephen. The apostles have the community choose seven men, full of the Spirit and wisdom, to oversee the daily distribution of food, so that they can give attention to prayer and the word (6:1–4). What does this reveal about the practice of service?
q2: The community chooses seven to serve so the apostles can give attention to prayer and the word (6:1–4). In 1 Timothy 3:8–13 (Day 330) Paul describes the character of deacons. How are these two passages similar or different? First Timothy 3:15 speaks of "God's household, which is the church of the living God"; what does this reveal about God's people as God's household?
q3: In light of the seven chosen to serve the community's daily needs, how might service take shape in your life this week?
identity: God's household

main_theme: Stephen recounts Israel's history and is stoned; persecution scatters the believers, and Philip preaches in Samaria and to an Ethiopian official.
primary_threads: The Spirit; Temple and God's presence; The people of God; Exodus and redemption; The promised Messiah
pre_where: Seven have been chosen to serve, including Stephen. Today Stephen is brought before the Sanhedrin.
pre_watch: Watch for Stephen's words about the temple in 7:48–50, his prayer in 7:59–60, and what the scattered believers do in 8:4.
q1: Stephen recounts Israel's history and is stoned; persecution scatters the believers, and Philip preaches in Samaria and to an Ethiopian official. As he is stoned, Stephen prays, "Lord, do not hold this sin against them" (7:60). What does this reveal about the practice of forgiveness?
q2: Stephen quotes Isaiah 66:1–2: "Heaven is my throne, and the earth is my footstool. What kind of house will you build for me?" (7:49–50). How does Stephen use Isaiah's words? Isaiah 66:2 continues, "These are the ones I look on with favor: those who are humble and contrite in spirit, and who tremble at my word"; what does this reveal about God's people as those who tremble at his word?
q3: In light of Stephen's prayer for those who were harming him, how might forgiveness take shape in your life this week?
identity: Those who tremble at his word

main_theme: Saul meets the risen Jesus on the road to Damascus and is baptized; Peter raises Tabitha, and God sends Peter to Cornelius, whose household receives the Spirit.
primary_threads: The Spirit; The people of God
pre_where: Persecution has scattered the believers, and Philip has preached in Samaria. Today Saul sets out for Damascus to arrest followers of the Way (9:1–2).
pre_watch: Watch for what Ananias is asked to do in 9:10–17, Peter's words in 10:34–35, and what happens in 10:44–47.
q1: Saul meets the risen Jesus on the road to Damascus and is baptized; Peter raises Tabitha, and God sends Peter to Cornelius, whose household receives the Spirit. Ananias obeys the Lord and addresses Saul as brother despite his earlier concerns (9:13–17). What does his welcome reveal about the practice of hospitality?
q2: Peter says, "God does not show favoritism but accepts from every nation the one who fears him and does what is right" (10:34–35). James 2:1 (Day 341) says, "believers in our glorious Lord Jesus Christ must not show favoritism." How are these two passages similar or different? What does this reveal about God's people as believers in our glorious Lord Jesus Christ?
q3: How might you welcome someone you might otherwise hesitate to receive this week?
identity: Believers in our glorious Lord Jesus Christ

main_theme: The Jerusalem church accepts the Gentile believers, disciples are first called Christians in Antioch, James is killed, and an angel frees Peter before Herod dies.
primary_threads: The people of God; The Spirit; Blessing and curse
pre_where: Peter has seen Cornelius's household receive the Spirit. Today he explains this to the believers in Jerusalem.
pre_watch: Watch for the response in 11:18, Barnabas in Antioch in 11:22–24, and the church's prayer in 12:5.
q1: The Jerusalem church accepts the Gentile believers, disciples are first called Christians in Antioch, James is killed, and an angel frees Peter before Herod dies. When Barnabas arrives in Antioch and sees what the grace of God has done, he is glad and encourages them all to remain true to the Lord (11:23). What does this reveal about the practice of encouragement?
q2: Barnabas encourages the believers in Antioch to remain true to the Lord (11:23). First Thessalonians 5:11 (Day 327) says, "encourage one another and build each other up, just as in fact you are doing." How are these two passages similar or different? First Thessalonians 5:9 says "God did not appoint us to suffer wrath but to receive salvation"; what does this reveal about God's people as those appointed to receive salvation?
q3: In light of Barnabas encouraging the believers to remain true to the Lord, how might encouragement take shape in your life this week?
identity: Those appointed to receive salvation

main_theme: The Spirit sends Barnabas and Saul out; Paul preaches in Pisidian Antioch and turns to the Gentiles, and they face opposition and Paul is stoned.
primary_threads: The Spirit; The people of God; The promised Messiah
pre_where: The church in Antioch has grown. Today, while they are worshiping and fasting, the Holy Spirit sets apart Barnabas and Saul (13:1–3).
pre_watch: Watch for how they are sent in 13:2–3, the Gentiles' response in 13:48, and what Paul and Barnabas tell the disciples in 14:22.
q1: The Spirit sends Barnabas and Saul out; Paul preaches in Pisidian Antioch and turns to the Gentiles, and they face opposition and Paul is stoned. While the church is worshiping the Lord and fasting, the Holy Spirit says to set apart Barnabas and Saul, and after more fasting and prayer they send them off (13:2–3). What does this reveal about the practice of prayer?
q2: The church sends out Barnabas and Saul after worship, fasting and prayer (13:2–3). In Matthew 9:37–38 (Day 240) Jesus tells his disciples to "ask the Lord of the harvest… to send out workers into his harvest field," and then he sends out the Twelve (10:1, 5–8). How does the prayer Jesus calls for and his sending of the Twelve compare with Acts 13:2–3? What does this reveal about being workers sent into the harvest?
q3: In light of the church's worship, fasting and prayer before sending Barnabas and Saul, how might prayer take shape in your life this week?
identity: Workers sent into the harvest field

main_theme: The Jerusalem council decides Gentile believers need not be circumcised; Paul and Silas travel on, Lydia believes, and a jailer's household is baptized after an earthquake.
primary_threads: Law and wisdom; The people of God; The Spirit
pre_where: Paul and Barnabas have returned to Antioch. Today some teach that Gentile believers must be circumcised, and the church sends them to Jerusalem (15:1–2).
pre_watch: Watch for Peter's words in 15:8–11, the council's letter in 15:28–29, and what Paul and Silas do in prison in 16:25.
q1: The Jerusalem council decides Gentile believers need not be circumcised; Paul and Silas travel on, Lydia believes, and a jailer's household is baptized after an earthquake. Peter tells the council that God "did not discriminate between us and them, for he purified their hearts by faith" (15:9). What does this reveal about the practice of unity?
q2: Peter tells the council that God "did not discriminate between us and them" (15:8–9). Ephesians 2:14–16 (Day 318) says Christ "has made the two groups one" and created "in himself one new humanity out of the two." How are these two passages similar or different? What does this reveal about God's people as one new humanity?
q3: In light of Peter's words that God did not discriminate between Jewish and Gentile believers, how might unity take shape in your life this week?
identity: One new humanity

video_title: Passage Insight: Jesus and Short Prayers
main_theme: Paul preaches in Thessalonica, Berea and Athens, where he speaks of the God who made the world, then stays in Corinth, and Apollos is taught more accurately.
primary_threads: Creation and new creation; The promised Messiah; The people of God; The day of the Lord
pre_where: Paul and Silas have been released from prison in Philippi. Today they travel on to Thessalonica (17:1).
pre_watch: Watch for what the Bereans do in 17:11, Paul's words in Athens in 17:24–28, and how Priscilla and Aquila help Apollos in 18:26.
q1: Paul preaches in Thessalonica, Berea and Athens, where he speaks of the God who made the world, then stays in Corinth, and Apollos is taught more accurately. The Bereans examine Scripture daily to test Paul's message (17:11). How might their careful attention inform the practice of meditating on Scripture?
q2: The Bereans examine the Scriptures every day (17:11). Hebrews 5:12–14 (Day 337) says "solid food is for the mature, who by constant use have trained themselves to distinguish good from evil." How are these two passages similar or different? What does this reveal about God's people as the mature who by constant use have trained themselves?
q3: How might you set aside time to examine and reflect on Scripture this week?
identity: The mature who have trained themselves

main_theme: In Ephesus disciples receive the Spirit and a riot breaks out; Paul raises Eutychus and urges the Ephesian elders to shepherd the church God bought with his own blood.
primary_threads: The Spirit; The people of God; Exodus and redemption
pre_where: Paul has stayed in Corinth, and Apollos has been taught more accurately. Today Paul arrives in Ephesus (19:1).
pre_watch: Watch for what the new believers do with their scrolls in 19:18–19, Paul's words in 20:24, and his farewell in 20:36–38.
q1: In Ephesus disciples receive the Spirit and a riot breaks out; Paul raises Eutychus and urges the Ephesian elders to shepherd the church God bought with his own blood. Many who believe openly confess what they had done, and those who had practiced sorcery burn their scrolls publicly (19:18–19). What does this reveal about the practice of repentance?
q2: The new believers in Ephesus confess their practices and burn their sorcery scrolls (19:18–19). Ephesians 4:22–24 (Day 319) instructs believers to "put off your old self" and "put on the new self, created to be like God in true righteousness and holiness." How does the Ephesian believers' confession and abandonment of sorcery compare with the instruction to put off the old self and put on the new? What does this reveal about God's people as those called to put on the new self?
q3: In light of the believers who openly confessed and burned their scrolls, how might repentance take shape in your life this week?
identity: Those called to put on the new self

main_theme: Paul goes to Jerusalem despite warnings, is seized at the temple, and tells the crowd how he met Jesus.
primary_threads: Temple and God's presence; The Spirit; The people of God
pre_where: Paul has said farewell to the Ephesian elders. Today he travels to Jerusalem despite warnings (21:4, 10–14).
pre_watch: Watch for Paul's answer in 21:13, what the believers say in 21:14, and how Paul tells his story in 22:6–16.
q1: Paul goes to Jerusalem despite warnings, is seized at the temple, and tells the crowd how he met Jesus. When Paul will not be dissuaded, the believers say, "The Lord's will be done" (21:14). What does this reveal about the practice of trust?
q2: The believers say, "The Lord's will be done" (21:14). In Colossians 4:12 (Day 324) Epaphras is "always wrestling in prayer for you, that you may stand firm in all the will of God, mature and fully assured." How does the believers' response in Acts 21:14 compare with Epaphras's prayer? What does this reveal about God's people as those for whom he prays to stand firm in God's will?
q3: In light of the believers' words, "The Lord's will be done," how might trust take shape in your life this week?
identity: Those prayed for to stand firm in God's will

main_theme: A plot against Paul leads to his transfer to Caesarea, where he defends himself before Felix and speaks of righteousness and the judgment to come.
primary_threads: The people of God
pre_where: Paul has been seized at the temple and has told the crowd how he met Jesus. Today he stands before the Sanhedrin (22:30–23:1).
pre_watch: Watch for the Lord's words to Paul in 23:11, how Paul's nephew helps in 23:16, and what Paul says to Felix in 24:16 and 24:25.
q1: A plot against Paul leads to his transfer to Caesarea, where he defends himself before Felix and speaks of righteousness and the judgment to come. Paul says, "I strive always to keep my conscience clear before God and man" (24:16). What does this reveal about the practice of integrity?
q2: Paul says he strives to keep his conscience clear before God and man (24:16). First Peter 3:15–16 (Day 344) says, "in your hearts revere Christ as Lord. Always be prepared to give an answer… with gentleness and respect, keeping a clear conscience." How are these two passages similar or different? What does this reveal about God's people as those who revere Christ as Lord?
q3: In light of Paul's effort to keep a clear conscience before God and others, how might integrity take shape in your life this week?
identity: Those who revere Christ as Lord

main_theme: Paul appeals to Caesar and tells King Agrippa of his conversion and of the Messiah who would suffer and rise, as the prophets said.
primary_threads: The promised Messiah; The people of God
pre_where: Paul has been held in Caesarea for two years (24:27). Today the new governor, Festus, hears his case.
pre_watch: Watch for Paul's appeal in 25:11, what the Lord told him in 26:16–18, and his answer to Agrippa in 26:29.
q1: Paul appeals to Caesar and tells King Agrippa of his conversion and of the Messiah who would suffer and rise, as the prophets said. Paul tells Agrippa, "I pray to God that not only you but all who are listening to me today may become what I am, except for these chains" (26:29). What does this reveal about the practice of witness?
q2: Jesus sends Paul "to open their eyes and turn them from darkness to light" (26:18). Colossians 1:12–13 (Day 323) says God "has rescued us from the dominion of darkness and brought us into the kingdom of the Son he loves." How are these two passages similar or different? What does this reveal about God's people as those brought into the kingdom of the Son?
q3: In light of Paul's prayer that his hearers would come to faith, how might witness take shape in your life this week?
identity: Those brought into the kingdom of the Son

main_theme: Paul survives a shipwreck and reaches Rome, where he proclaims the kingdom of God and teaches about Jesus with boldness.
primary_threads: Kingdom and kingship; The people of God
pre_where: Paul has appealed to Caesar. Today he sets sail for Italy as a prisoner (27:1).
pre_watch: Watch for what Paul tells those on board in 27:22–25, his actions in 27:33–36, and how Acts ends in 28:30–31.
q1: Paul survives a shipwreck and reaches Rome, where he proclaims the kingdom of God and teaches about Jesus with boldness. In the storm Paul urges everyone to eat, gives thanks to God in front of them all, and they are all encouraged (27:35–36). What does this reveal about the practice of gratitude?
q2: Paul and those on board are brought safely through the storm and shipwreck (27:41–44). Psalm 107:28–30 (daily psalm, Day 107) says, "they cried out to the LORD in their trouble… He stilled the storm to a whisper." How are these two passages similar or different? Psalm 107:2 says, "Let the redeemed of the LORD tell their story"; what does this reveal about God's people as the redeemed of the LORD?
q3: In light of Paul giving thanks to God in the middle of the storm, how might gratitude take shape in your life this week?
identity: The redeemed of the LORD

main_theme: Paul greets the Roman believers with the gospel of God's Son, descended from David, which reveals God's righteousness; he says Gentiles and Jews alike stand under God's judgment.
primary_threads: The promised Messiah; Creation and new creation; Law and wisdom; The day of the Lord; The people of God
pre_where: Acts ended with Paul in Rome, proclaiming the kingdom of God. Today the plan turns to the letter Paul wrote to the believers in Rome before he visited them (1:7, 10–13).
pre_watch: Watch for how Paul describes the gospel in 1:16–17, what he says about creation in 1:20, and his words on judging others in 2:1–4.
q1: Paul greets the Roman believers with the gospel of God's Son, descended from David, which reveals God's righteousness; he says Gentiles and Jews alike stand under God's judgment. Paul says, "I am not ashamed of the gospel, because it is the power of God that brings salvation to everyone who believes" (1:16). What does this reveal about the practice of witness?
q2: Paul says, "I am not ashamed of the gospel" (1:16). In 2 Timothy 1:7–8 (Day 332) he writes, "the Spirit God gave us does not make us timid, but gives us power, love and self-discipline. So do not be ashamed of the testimony about our Lord." How are these two passages similar or different? What does this reveal about God's people as those given a Spirit of power, love and self-discipline?
q3: In light of Paul's words, "I am not ashamed of the gospel," how might witness take shape in your life this week?
identity: Those given a Spirit of power, love and self-discipline

main_theme: Paul argues that all have sinned and are justified freely by God's grace through faith in Jesus, presented as a sacrifice of atonement, and points to Abraham's faith.
primary_threads: Sacrifice and atonement; Exodus and redemption; Covenant; Law and wisdom
pre_where: Paul has said that Gentiles and Jews alike stand under God's judgment. Today he explains how God makes people right with himself.
pre_watch: Watch for Paul's summary in 3:22–24, what Abraham believed in 4:3, and Abraham's faith in 4:18–21.
q1: Paul argues that all have sinned and are justified freely by God's grace through faith in Jesus, presented as a sacrifice of atonement, and points to Abraham's faith. Against all hope, Abraham in hope believes, being fully persuaded that God has power to do what he has promised (4:18, 21). What does this reveal about the practice of trust?
q2: Paul says Abraham believed God's promise against all hope (4:18–21). Hebrews 11:8–10 (Day 340) says that by faith Abraham obeyed and went, "even though he did not know where he was going," for "he was looking forward to the city with foundations, whose architect and builder is God." How are these two descriptions similar or different? Hebrews 11:16 says God "has prepared a city for them"; what does this reveal about God's people as those for whom God has prepared a city?
q3: In light of Abraham being fully persuaded that God could do what he promised, how might trust take shape in your life this week?
identity: Those for whom God has prepared a city

main_theme: Paul contrasts Adam's sin with Christ's gift of righteousness and life, and says those baptized into Christ have died to sin and now live to God.
primary_threads: Creation and new creation; Blessing and curse; Exodus and redemption; Sacrifice and atonement
pre_where: Paul has described Abraham's faith. Today he speaks of peace with God and of new life.
pre_watch: Watch for God's love in 5:8, the contrast between Adam and Christ in 5:18–19, and Paul's question in 6:1–2.
q1: Paul contrasts Adam's sin with Christ's gift of righteousness and life, and says those baptized into Christ have died to sin and now live to God. Paul says, "offer yourselves to God as those who have been brought from death to life; and offer every part of yourself to him as an instrument of righteousness" (6:13). What does this reveal about the practice of holiness?
q2: Paul says those baptized into Christ died to sin and now live to God (6:3–11). Colossians 3:1–3 (Day 324) says, "you have been raised with Christ… For you died, and your life is now hidden with Christ in God." How are these two passages similar or different? What does this reveal about God's people as those whose life is hidden with Christ in God?
q3: In light of Paul's call to offer every part of yourself to God as an instrument of righteousness, how might holiness take shape in your life this week?
identity: Those whose life is hidden with Christ in God

main_theme: Paul describes the struggle with sin under the law and life in the Spirit, where there is no condemnation, and declares that nothing can separate God's children from his love.
primary_threads: The Spirit; Law and wisdom; Creation and new creation; The people of God
pre_where: Paul has said believers have died to sin and live to God. Today he describes the struggle with sin under the law and life in the Spirit.
pre_watch: Watch for the cry in 7:24–25, the Spirit's work in 8:15–16 and 8:26, and the question in 8:31.
q1: Paul describes the struggle with sin under the law and life in the Spirit, where there is no condemnation, and declares that nothing can separate God's children from his love. Paul says the Spirit himself intercedes for us "through wordless groans" when we do not know what to pray for (8:26). What does this reveal about the practice of prayer?
q2: Paul says the Spirit helps us in our weakness and intercedes for us (8:26–27). In John 14:16–17 (Day 264) Jesus promises "another advocate to help you and be with you forever—the Spirit of truth… he lives with you and will be in you." How are these two passages similar or different? What does this reveal about God's people as those in whom the Spirit lives?
q3: In light of Paul's words that the Spirit intercedes when we do not know what to pray, how might prayer take shape in your life this week?
identity: Those in whom the Spirit lives

main_theme: Paul grieves for Israel and speaks of God's choosing, calls all to confess Jesus as Lord, and pictures Gentiles grafted into Israel's olive tree, saying that all Israel will be saved.
primary_threads: The people of God; Covenant; The promised Messiah
pre_where: Paul has said nothing can separate God's children from his love. Today he speaks of his grief for his own people, Israel (9:1–3).
pre_watch: Watch for Paul's grief in 9:2–3, his prayer in 10:1, and his praise in 11:33–36.
q1: Paul grieves for Israel and speaks of God's choosing, calls all to confess Jesus as Lord, and pictures Gentiles grafted into Israel's olive tree, saying that all Israel will be saved.
